author: Unknown
title: Nurcan Değirmenci: As women, we must stand together
content:
Musician and activist Nurcan Değirmenci, who performed at the "Women Stand Together, Discussing the Future" conference held in Ankara on 31 October and 1 November, spoke about women's role in art and social peace and called on women to stand together in public squares on 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.


Nurcan Değirmenci said that she began her artistic career at the Mesopotamia Cultural Center in 1995 and had struggled shoulder to shoulder with women for many years, both as a musician and as a Kurdish woman. She recalled that they established the Art for Peace Initiative (BIS) in 2009, bringing artistic production together with the struggle for peace.


Değirmenci said, "Art is an indispensable element in the existence of culture," and emphasizing that the search and struggle for identity also involved artistic resistance.


'Women will shape the language of peace'


Nurcan Değirmenci said that the central message of the conference, for her, was the importance of women standing together without denying their own stories. She expressed her belief that women would build the language of peace in this period. Değirmenci said that women had borne the greatest suffering experienced in the country, adding: "We can remain silent together, but we can also speak and struggle together. Therefore, the fact that women can stand side by side here today is an important step toward peace."


A common struggle against all forms of violence


Nurcan Değirmenci called for a collective struggle against the growing violence in society, saying: "We have recently seen an escalation of violence against women, children, animals and nature. The solution to this violence, which extends from social media to politics, is to build a common struggle."


Değirmenci said that the violence women faced at home, in the streets, in workplaces, academia and politics had the same underlying roots. She said, "As women, we must come together against the violence we face. There is no other way."


'Our priority is to develop gender consciousness'


Nurcan Değirmenci recalled that Kurdish women had waged a determined struggle for many years for Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom. She emphasized that women were at the center of this struggle. Değirmenci said, "Nothing and no one can be free unless women are free. What matters is women's strength, and our priority is to develop gender consciousness."


Değirmenci also issued a call ahead of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. She said, "Women from all sections of society must take to the streets in an organized manner. The language of peace can only be built through this solidarity."

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Making Women’s History Part of the Curriculum
content:
Two teachers from Sacred Heart Preparatory School in California, Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams, have proposed an Advanced Placement U.S. Women’s History course in response to the issue of students not learning about women’s history. The courses would allow studying women’s experiences and contributions in greater depth. Establishing this course would create a better understanding of American history as it includes the diverse experiences of women and would help students connect the historical struggles for equality to gender issues today.

Women have contributed to shaping the nation’s politics, economy, and social movements, yet their participation is often overlooked by traditional history classes. From fighting for the right to vote, challenging discrimination, and advocating for female autonomy, women have had a significant role in building the foundation of the United States today.

One of the main arguments for WAPUSH is that women’s experiences are not explored in the classroom. In the article Educational Activism: Creating an AP U.S. Women’s History Course, Serene Williams, Kristen Kelly, and Clara Robinson explain that topics such as women’s suffrage and reproductive rights receive limited attention in the current AP U.S. History curriculum. The women’s suffrage movement involved decades of organizing, political campaigning, and resistance. However, teachers may not introduce this topic to students or have enough time to examine its strategies and leaders in detail. A dedicated course would allow students to study these movements more thoroughly and understand how women helped shape American democracy.

Women’s history is much broader than the fight for voting rights. The proposed WAPUSH curriculum includes women’s labor, politics, religion, culture, war, and violence against women. It also examines how race, class, sexuality, religion, and other identities shaped women’s experiences. This approach is important because women throughout the years have never shared one universal experience. Indigenous women, Black women, Immigrant women, etc., have faced different opportunities and forms of discrimination. Studying these differences would help students develop a greater understanding of American history and that America was not built on just our founding fathers, but by women who paved the path for opportunity and development through blood, sweat, and tears.

An AP course would also help students recognize the connection between historical events and current issues. The debate over reproductive rights and other feminist struggles today cannot be fully understood without examining the laws and political movements that shaped access to contraceptives, abortion, and female economic support. Studying topics from the suffrage movement to the Equal Rights Amendment can help students understand the political equality that has developed through activism and engage in feminist discussion. Learning this history would give students the context needed to evaluate debates instead of viewing them as different events.

Establishing this course would show that women’s history is worthy of advanced academic study. The WAPUSH campaign began in 2022, and according to its website, the campaign gathered more than 4,000 petition signatures and received encouragement from College Board leadership as it worked toward launching this course. Its proposal has also received university support, while the campaign continues seeking letters from high schools willing to offer the course. This continued support brings women closer to bringing light to women’s history and giving women a space in school systems and curricula. This petition is one step closer every day to its goal to educate and inform people all across America of women’s contributions.

An AP U.S. Women’s History course would make education more comprehensive, inform students even more about the history of the U.S., and connect past struggles to present issues. Women have influenced American politics, economics, culture, and social movements, yet their experiences are not always given sufficient attention in existing courses. By offering students an opportunity to examine these experiences, the College Board could help create a more inclusive and accurate understanding of the nation’s past. Women’s history is not separate from American history but instead an essential part of it.

author: Chris Walker
title: AIPAC-Funded House Dem Loses to DSA-Backed Challenger in California
content:
Angela Gonzales-Torres is one of at least six DSA-backed candidates to win election to Congress this week.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Angela Gonzales-Torres, a Democratic candidate for Congress in California who is endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), has defeated establishment Democrat Rep. Jimmy Gomez, who has been in office since 2017.

As of Thursday morning, Gonzales-Torres led Gomez by 18.4 points, with 74 percent of the vote in so far. The race has been called by all major news networks.

A noted community organizer, Gonzales-Torres has been involved in progressive politics since she was a teenager.

“Some of my earliest memories were fighting the Afghanistan and Iraq invasions,” she said in an interview last month. Besides being anti-war, Gonzales-Torres has also advocated for affordable housing measures in the Los Angeles area, the abolition of ICE, and Medicare for All.

She is one of at least six DSA-endorsed candidates to have won their elections to Congress as part of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Both candidates have at least some progressive bona fides. But earlier this year, it was announced that the House Ethics Committee had opened an investigation into Gomez over sexual abuse allegations.

Gomez has admitted to making “personal mistakes” outside of his marriage, and has long been accused of having extramarital affairs with House staffers. House rules forbid lawmakers from having relationships with their staff, but a loophole in the rule allows members of Congress to have relationships with other members’ workers.

The inquiry was officially announced this summer. According to a lawyer representing a woman involved in the case, Gomez is under investigation by a House committee for “sexual harassment and assault.” The congressman maintains that any relationships he’s had have been consensual.

Responding to the allegations during the campaign, Gonzales-Torres called on Gomez to resign, and said it was time to “get creeps out of office.”

Beyond those allegations, however, the two candidates differed in other ways, particularly on the issue of Israel and its continued genocide of Palestinians in Gaza.

Although Gomez has called for a ceasefire in the region, he has expressed strong support for Israel, and opposed legislation that would restrict U.S. arms sales to that country. And while Gonzales-Torres has refused to take any money from the pro-Israel political action committee AIPAC, Gomez has received $2.6 million from the group during the campaign.

Announcing her victory on Tuesday night, Gonzales-Torres promised to represent voters instead of special interests while serving in Congress.

“Los Angeles doesn’t belong to AIPAC, Los Angeles doesn’t belong to Crypto or Big AI, Los Angeles doesn’t belong to corporate real estate developers. It belongs to us,” she said in a statement on X.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Dossier

Wieder einmal haben sich die Frauen und verschiedenen Bildungsarbeiterinnen von CTERA der feministischen und transfeministischen Bewegung angeschlossen und unter dem Slogan „Ni una Menos“ gegen Femizide, Transfemizide und Transvestizide im ganzen Land, im Rahmen unserer CTA-T und durch alle Basisorganisationen von CTERA, diese Forderung, die vor 9 Jahren auf die Straße ging, begleitet. (…) „Hass und Hunger töten“, gewalttätige, fremdenfeindliche, frauenfeindliche, diskriminierende, verleugnende, antifeministische und LGBT+-hassende Diskurse sind das, was tagtäglich in unserer Gesellschaft zirkuliert, ausgehend von denen, die uns regieren, einer Regierung, die es sich zur Aufgabe gemacht hat, öffentliche Politiken mit einer Gender- und Diversity-Perspektive im Hinblick auf die Menschenrechte zu entleeren

Aufruf bei der Bildungsgewerkschaft CTERA

 (maschinenübersetzt) zu landesweiten Frauenprotesten am 3. Juni 2024 – siehe mehr zum Thema und Hintergründe:


„Nos falta Nancy“: Bildungsgewerkschaft CTERA hatte am 29. Oktober zu landesweitem Lehrkräftestreik und Protesten in ganz Argentinien nach Femizid an Lehrerin Nancy aufgerufen


Femizid an Lehrerin führt zu Protesten in Argentinien


„

Buenos Aires/Esquina. Im ganzen Land hat der Gewerkschaftsverband der Lehrkräfte (CTERA) in Argentinien am vergangenen Donnerstag infolge des Femizids an der Lehrerin Nancy Godoy zu einem nationalen Trauertag und zu Streiks aufgerufen. Die Protestierenden zogen in verschiedenen Provinzen, darunter Buenos Aires, Corrientes und Córdoba, durch die Straßen und machten mit Bannern und Schildern, auf denen „Nos falta Nancy“ (Nancy fehlt uns) zu lesen war, auf den Mord an der Lehrerin aufmerksam. Mit dem Fall rücken auch die Bedingungen in den Fokus, unter denen Lehrkräfte in ländlichen Regionen arbeiten. Godoy selbst hatte sich gegen die Missstände ausgesprochen.


Die 52-Jährige war stellvertretende Leiterin der ländlichen Schule Nr. 626 im Paraje El Malezal in der subtropischen Provinz Corrientes im Nordosten Argentiniens. Unter der Woche blieb sie dort, da der Weg nach Hause bis zu drei Stunden dauerte. Mobil- und Satellitenempfang gibt es in dieser Gegend oft nicht. Ihre letzte Meldung an einen ihrer Söhne erfolgte daher rund eine Woche, bevor diese sie am 7. Oktober als vermisst meldeten. Am vergangenen Mittwoch fand die Polizei ihre Leiche. Laut vorläufigem Obduktionsbericht hatte sie Stichverletzungen und Abwehrverletzungen. Fünf Personen wurden festgenommen, gegen drei wird wegen Femizids ermittelt, gegen zwei der drei unbegrenzte Untersuchungshaft angeordnet. Gegen zwei weitere Tatverdächtige ermittelt die Staatsanwaltschaft wegen eines Tötungsdeliktes bzw. Falschaussage. Der Anwalt der Familie, Gustavo Briend, sprach von einem „Akt absoluter Barbarei“ und geht davon aus, dass mehrere Personen beteiligt waren. Er forderte, auch einen möglichen sexuellen Übergriff zu untersuchen. Auch die Justiz verfolgt diese Hypothese. (…) Die CTERA greift die Forderungen von Godoy auf und prangert sie im ganzen Land an. Sie betont, dass die Bevölkerung oftmals im Unklaren über die Zustände sei, unter denen die Lehrkräfte arbeiteten. Sie macht die Regierung von Corrientes sowie Präsident Javier Milei für die „Prekarität, Isolation und Schutzlosigkeit“ verantwortlich. Ihre Forderungen umfassen gerechtere Löhne und würdigere Arbeitsbedingungen. Weiter fordert sie, den Fall Godoy zügig und transparent aufzuarbeiten. author: anred
title: De Loan a Nancy: Corrientes se tiñe de sangre, pero nadie habla de Valdés
content:
El femicidio de Nanci Godoy, la maestra rural asesinada en Esquina (Corrientes) tras denunciar las pésimas condiciones de la escuela donde se desempeñaba, generó un impacto a nivel nacional que trascendió las fronteras provinciales. Sin embargo, muy pocos focos están puestos en el gobernador de la provincia, Juan Pablo Valdés, responsable político de la seguridad y la educación a nivel provincial.

Por El Grito del Sur.


Loan Peña es un niño correntino que desapareció el 13 de junio de 2024, cuando estaba en un almuerzo familiar en la casa de su abuela, en la localidad de 9 de Julio, en Corrientes. El juicio comenzó el 16 de junio de este año y tiene 17 imputados, pero visibiliza la complicidad policial y política de los funcionarios provinciales con la desaparición del niño, cuyo paradero aún se desconoce. La Alerta Sofía por el menor sigue vigente. Pero no es el único escándalo provincial del que (extrañamente) el gobernador Juan Pablo Valdés sale indemne.


Valdés viene vaciando la educación al ritmo que pide Milei: en marzo de 2026 descontó los días de paro de docentes que se movilizaban por mejoras salariales y edilicias. Además, los pobladores rurales denuncian la ausencia total de medidas paliativas para las inundaciones derivadas del fenómeno del Niño que han afectado campos, unidades productivas y escuelas.


La familia Valdés gobierna hace diez años: dos períodos de Gustavo y luego la sucesión en su hermano, Juan Pablo. Expresa una continuidad de 25 años de feudalismo radical en la provincia que ha sumido a Corrientes en la pobreza, laconcentración de la riqueza en pocas manos y el ataque frontal al interior provincial y la ruralidad.


El 41% de la población del Gran Corrientes se encuentra debajo de la línea de pobreza, según datos del primer semestre de 2026. También se encuentra dentro de las tres provincias con mayor mortalidad infantil del país, alcanzando el dato de 14 por cada 1.000 nacidos vivos en 2024, la más alta de Argentina para ese año. La provincia tiene datos de analfabetismo superiores al promedio nacional.


Ni hablar de la concentración de la tierra: un 81,64% de la superficie está en explotaciones mayores a 1.000 hectáreas, según consigna la Estrategia Provincial para el Sector Agroalimentario (EPSA 2022). La concentración de la tierra coincide con el despoblamiento rural: en 1970 un 42% de la gente vivía en el campo, pero para 2022 era de apenas el 12%.

author: groundxero
title: Where Women Make History: Reclaiming Agency in History and in Movements
content:
Gargi’s book is a historiographical recovery of the junctures when women fought and moved another inch towards occupying half the sky. 


 


By

 Vertika Mani 


 


The first intriguing thing to notice about V. Gargi’s

No Women, No History

 is the cover page of the book itself. Published by Virasam Books, the cover depicts women holding guns, marching with axes and also hugging trees. The image with its wide range of contrast yet a commonality of women as marchers and fighters interacts with its readers to convey the larger argument that this book seeks to make. The book was initially written as a collection of notes by V. Gargi, a revolutionary activist who dedicated this book

“To all the women who fought against overwhelming odds, made great sacrifices to the extent of even laying down their lives to make this place better for all of us…”


 


The first edition of

No Women No History: Women in Indian Movements (19th century – 2004)

 was published last year in August, at a pit stop, when the mainstream feminist discourse in India and abroad mostly associate women with power of intellect and pen, which are all quite a matter of privilege and can therefore be politically disabling at times. In that context, reading

No women No History

 is refreshing as it takes us down the road of history of women’s struggle, almost on a rampage to discover the truth of the fighting spirit that Indian women have always stood for.


 


An extraordinary range of political histories 


 


The book covers an extraordinary range of political histories and geographical contexts from 19th Century to the year 2004 covering histories of peasant and Adivasi uprisings, anti-caste struggles, labour movements, revolutionary politics, autonomous women’s organisations, ecological movements, struggles in the North-East, cultural organisations and contemporary campaigns. Its approach is broad and, for the most part, non-sectarian. Rather than treating “women’s issues” as a separate political category, Gargi locates women within the wider structures of social and political struggle, as peasants, workers, artisans, Dalits, Adivasis and members of minority communities.


 


This method of writing makes gendered oppression therefore appear not as an isolated structure but is seen in relationship with caste, class, feudal relations, economic exploitation and political power. This is among this book’s most important methodological contributions which allow the history of women’s liberation to be read as history of movements rather than that of organisations. A history of movements in which women fought over land, wages, labour, caste hierarchy, food, displacement, forests, political representation and state power. The breadth of the historical canvas is therefore significant to explore beyond conventional boundaries of women’s history.


 


Beginning with women’s participation in tribal and peasant rebellions, Gargi moves between the histories of Ranis and Begums and those of ordinary women who participated in the political ferment of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The juxtaposition prevents women’s history from becoming a gallery of exceptional female figures. It takes a dive into the political labour of ordinary women, particularly peasant, working-class, Dalit, Adivasi and other marginalised women, who have so frequently remained outside the central narrative of political history.


 


One of the salient feature of discussions around movements is the notable references made to the women pioneers, for instance, of Self-Respect Movement which is mostly associated with Periyar but more often than not misses to speak of Maniyammai, the woman who went on to lead the Kazhagam after Periyar’s death. Similarly, Gargi talks about Ambedkarite and Dalit movements including women’s role at length. Other such references include the distinctive forms of women’s participation in movements like Jail Bharo Satyagraha of 1960–65. The histories of women in the freedom struggle, women revolutionaries and communists are similarly placed alongside organisational histories that are less familiar in mainstream accounts.


 


Similarly, the book discusses collectives which are again, less talked about. For instance, The Mahila Atmaraksha Samitis (MARS), which emerged as an important form of women’s mobilisation before Partition. The further chapters trace the experiences of women during and after Partition, discovering a phase in history where …

author: CMI Argentina
title: El martirio de Nancy
content:
A Nancy Godoy el estado la dejó sola. Horas a caballo para llegar a su escuela, en medio de la nada, en el territorio de una estancia, que tenía dentro una escuela para sus peones. Llegó por primera vez y era una ruina. Lo denunció con detalles. La ignoraron. No llegó a cobrar un sueldo desde agosto. Apareció asesinada. Toda su lucha debió conocerse antes.


Por Silvana Melo


Nancy Godoy tenía ocho alumnos en una escuela pública dentro de una estancia. Es decir, en un territorio privado. Para llegar tenía que recorrer decenas de kilómetros de caminos rurales correntinos hasta ese punto de poder donde la alcanzaban hasta el paraje en el que un caballo la trasladaría durante tres horas para llegar a la escuela. Cruzando bañados, riachos y soledades escampadas que se volvían de una hostilidad imprevisible en caso de lluvias.


Tenía 52 años cuando ese 15 de agosto llegó a la escuela N° 626 del paraje El Malezal, en Esquina, Corrientes, para hacerse cargo de una suplencia. Era una casita desgastada, destruida, como si por ella hubiera pasado no sólo el tiempo, sino la desidia estatal y el desprecio privado.


Después de hacerse un panorama general de aquello a lo que se enfrentaba –suciedad extrema, ausencia de años de cualquier autoridad, falta de registros de todo tipo, situación sanitaria peligrosa, imposibilidad de habitar para ella, que debía quedarse la semana entera- el 15 de agosto escribió una carta manuscrita para enviar al ministerio de Educación de Corrientes. Y denunció cada detalle. Envió un expediente y sostuvo que la escuela estaba totalmente abandonada, sin agua, con inodoros llenos de tierra y ratas, que tuvo que acudir a una madre y a la baqueana que la acompañaba en el último tramo de su trayecto, María Rosa Leguizamón. En su casa tuvo que dormir las tres primeras noches porque la escuela era inhabitable. Esa misma mujer quedó involucrada después en la investigación por el crimen.


Decía que el techo se le caería encima, que las ventanas estaban rotas, que la humedad se comía el edificio, que las ratas y los murciélagos se habían apropiado de la casa, que el olor de sus heces era insoportable, que no había muebles suficientes, que los libros se habían mojado. Ella era docente, cocinera, portera y directora. Y era la responsable del edificio.


La carta que escribió Nancy a las autoridades educativas


Y la dejaron sola.


El estado la dejó sola. En medio de la nada, dentro de una estancia, en las manos de un propietario que hacía y deshacía, que tenía dentro de su propiedad una escuela para sus peones. Y ella debería comportarse como su maestra, directora, portera y cocinera. Con un sueldo pagado por el estado que la dejaba a la buena de dios. Sola de toda soledad.


Su denuncia fue ignorada por las autoridades educativas, sólo sostenida después de su desaparición por la comunidad de Esquina, sus docentes y su familia.


Pero esta lucha de ella debió conocerse antes de la tragedia.


No después. Cuando alguien la asesinó por el motivo que sea. Por ser mujer. Por ser maestra rural. Por tener coraje. Por denunciar.


Nancy se pasaba los días en esa escuela que tuvo que rehacer con sus manos y el fin de semana volvía con su familia. Sin señal de celular, sin comunicación de ningún tipo, su familia sabía que seguía viva cuando regresaba su sonrisa destruida por el cansancio. Pero aquel fin de semana no volvió. Y todo comenzó a volverse sombrío.


La dejaron sola. Tres horas a caballo y sin señal.


Apareció asesinada.


A metros del aula que había sabido reparar con sus manos, en la tapera del capataz, había ropa quemada.


Hay un estado que manda una trabajadora sola. A educar. Precarizada. A caballo. Sin señal de ningún tipo. Sin procurarle un transporte oficial. A que llegue como pueda. A una escuela en ruinas. Dentro de una propiedad de un estanciero. Ese estado cajonea su denuncia. Investiga su desaparición. Y la encuentra cuando fue asesinada.


En el territorio de la estancia El Curupí. En una escuela pública dentro de una zona privada.


El espacio Docentes Autoconvocados Corrientes – Sector 2019 aseguró que Nancy Godoy fue asesinada sin llegar a cobrar un solo sueldo a pesar de trabajar desde agosto.


A pesar del sacrificio para llegar. A pesar del desastre que encontró y del que nadie se hizo cargo. A pesar de que el docente que hacía años que no iba a la escuela seguía cobrando su salario.


Y ella fue asesinada por ser maestra en una escuela pública y tener que afrontar una realidad …

author: Marx-lover
title: The Cornell Case and the Left's Betrayal of Itself
content:
Here's an article about the feminist reaction to the "Cornell 7" case that has been in the news recently (October 2026). A version of it was published in "Compact." (The hyperlinks have been deleted, unfortunately.) The general point is that contemporary feminism has become an albatross for the left, and is also contributing to destructive social and cultural trends.

In the 1960s, feminists demanded that women and men have legal equality, that women be treated as mature adults who are free to make their own choices be it with regard to sex or their careers, that patriarchal paternalism be dismantled. In the 2020s, feminists demand that women be constantly protected against men, that patriarchal paternalism be resurrected, that women be legally treated as not responsible for decisions they’ve made because, in certain contexts, only men have agency. And men, they argue, are inveterate misogynists, abusers, and rapists, so the agency they manifest is almost invariably malign.

The reaction to the “Cornell 7” case is the latest example. A remarkable wave of hysteria has swept liberal and left culture, from mass media and social media to university campuses. Misandry is drenching the discourse; mobs are going after anyone who questions the dominant narrative; the guilt of the accused is automatically assumed, because the accused are men and men are by definition guilty. Is it any wonder that millions of men in recent years have turned away from the left—which seems to hate them—and fallen into the clutches of the far-right and the “manosphere”?

Consider what has transpired. Far from condemning the wildly irresponsible comments of public figures like Governor Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, which treat as established fact accusations made in a civil lawsuit, leftists themselves, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani, have talked as though the case has already been decided. This is despite the highly ambiguous evidence that has been presented, much of which tends to exonerate the alleged perpetrators of the “gang-rape.” Not only is presumption of innocence thrown out the window; it is obvious that even if the accused end up being found innocent, most liberals and leftists will remain sure of their guilt.

Lynch mobs have been out for blood. A few weeks ago, it was easy to find thousands of people “liking” public demands to kill the accused. Even innocent bystanders were victimized. The campaign of overwhelming harassment to which the journalist Michael Tracey has been subjected for questioning the “guilty until proven innocent” narrative led to his father receiving “thousands of nonstop crazed texts/calls/voicemails” threatening him with brutal violence. The current owners of Tracey’s childhood home were “inundated” with “crazed threats,” and received suspicious packages at their house. Friends and family of the accused men were harassed by thousands. So was the family of an innocent man who happens to have the same name as one of the accused.

Since liberals and leftists are refusing to stand up for decency and the rule of law, it is left to conservatives to do so—which enables them to claim the moral high ground against “lunatic” leftists and thereby score political points. It turns out that many conservatives take women more seriously as (potentially) responsible adults and moral agents than most leftists do.

Feminist moral panics may seem well-intentioned in that they’re allegedly motivated by concern for the safety of women, but these episodes illustrate the extent to which the (so-called) “left” has been corrupted and co-opted by neoliberal dynamics, particularly in the era of social media. The atomized, polarized, siloed, anti-intellectual, narcissistic soundbite culture of social media—itself a reflection of capitalist tendencies—has helped produce a liberal-left that dehumanizes others, reflexively assumes the worst of men, exploits controversies for social media clout, and contributes to the very social breakdown that leftists rightly attack neoliberalism for engendering. After all, a feminism that teaches women to hate and fear men, and to view themselves as being on a higher moral plane, doesn’t exactly promote healthy relationships. It exacerbates gender wars and culture wars, thus, again, gifting the right wing with talking points and grievances to rally around.

author: Paige Collings
title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
content:
What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?


Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. 


That's why earlier this year with the

queer arts collective

, we put out a

call for submissions

 inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom.


And we’re excited to share that the project is now live!

Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution. 


These essays and stories remind us that digital rights aren't just about the existence of technology and its deployment as existing in a vacuum, but instead about how tech tools are a way for people to express themselves freely, find communities, explore identities, and build spaces to exist and seek joy without fear. Too often, conversations about technology focus on innovation, efficiency, and the next big thing while overlooking the people and communities most affected by the systems being built. This project was an effort to break containment and make space for something different: a chance to imagine digital futures rooted in queer creativity, resistance, and possibility.


Together with the queer arts collective, we were excited to launch the magazine and celebrate the artists and ideas that brought it to life through our session at Mozilla Festival last week, ‘

Privacy x Queer Desire

,’ where we started out by co-curating a community privacy plan grounded in digital fairness before launching the magazine. 


If the stories in

Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 teach us one thing, it’s that we don't have to accept the digital future handed to us by oppressive governments and tech companies. We already have pre-Big Tech internet experiences encoded in our fondest memories that can inform our dreams for something better, and together we can build a new reality.

title: [“In a world that constantly shames us for our bodies, genders, or sexualities, we can trick…
content:
gatheringbones

:

[“In a world that constantly shames us for our bodies, genders, or sexualities, we can trick ourselves into thinking that we are “taking control” and that achieving a certain body ideal is liberation. It is far from that.

For those of us who face multiple forms of oppression, developing eating disorders is not simply wanting our bodies to meet the impossible aesthetic ideal associated with people in dominant culture. Queer and trans people don’t develop disordered eating simply because we want to assimilate to cisgender, heteronormative culture. Of course, appearances can be and often are part of the picture. But when we attribute eating disorders solely to the desire for our bodies to look a certain way, the conversation stops. And we miss out on opportunities for crucial conversations about the connections between eating disorders, trauma, and survival.

Eating disorders help us to survive trauma and oppression.

 For queer and trans folks, the way we both conceptualize and heal from eating disorders must account for the ways we are harmed by systems of power. Eating disorders help us to cope with everyday microaggressions and macroaggressions. They help us to get by in the face of food insecurity. They can keep us safe in a world in which being read as queer or trans can mean life or death.

For many people, disordered eating or behaviours are attempts at shape control, which are attempts to blend in and not become a target. For many of us, eating disorder “treatment” that aims to strip us of the very armour that has allowed us to stay alive, can actually cause more harm if there isn’t an adequate substitute or systemic change to help us to safely exist in the world. Treatment cannot simply be aimed at challenging our “distorted thoughts” or symptom reduction or cheerleading body positivity. Treatment approaches that aim at skills training (e.g., dialectical behaviour therapy) and challenging unhelpful thought patterns that fuel an eating disorder (e.g., cognitive behavioural therapy) are often crucial, but they are not enough for a true sense of feeling safe and at home in one’s body.

Most mainstream treatment approaches perpetuate white supremacist, capitalist systems of harm. Fat people are told that they are holding on to their fat as protection and that if they worked through their trauma, the weight would fall away. Thin people are told they need to restore their weight but they are not to go beyond an established “upper limit.” When we demonize “emotional eating,” there is an inherent assumption that the individual can get to a calm, neutral state at all times when their body needs or wants to be fed. Sometimes “emotional eating” is harm reduction.

Our disorders and symptoms, the things that we feel shame about, were once what helped us to get through the night. We might still be in survival mode. Or, we might have a hard time recognizing that we no longer need to be in survival mode. But before we move on, we might have to pay respect and allow ourselves to grieve how we have been called to protect ourselves in ways that are simultaneously brilliant and destructive.”]

sand c. chang, from dreaming bigger: body liberation and weight inclusivity in health care, from The Care We Dream Of: Liberatory & Transformative Justice Approaches to LGBTQ+ Health, edited by Zena Sharman, 2021

author: TGEU
title: TGEU publishes Legal developments on trans-specific healthcare: A review of national case law in the EU
content:
Court cases have been central to advancing the rights of trans people in Europe, but trans-specific healthcare remains largely untested in the courts.


Since the European Court of Human Rights’ earliest decisions on legal gender recognition, strategic litigation has driven many major advances. More recently, rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union on freedom of movement and non-discrimination have further strengthened these gains. TGEU’s

2026 Trans Rights Map

 also found that national court decisions are increasingly driving progress in trans rights, particularly where legislative and policy advances are stalled or reversed.


Trans-specific healthcare is an exception and is comparatively less litigated at the European level. Trans people across the EU face significant barriers in accessing trans-specific healthcare. Enforcing their rights to healthcare is further complicated by administrative refusals, unclear national regulations, and national court rulings that remain largely unknown. At the same time, interest is growing in using legal tools to advocate for improved access to trans-specific healthcare, and in how courts across the region handle such cases.


get the publication


Objective of the publication


This resource explains how litigation can help improve access to trans-specific healthcare by reviewing case law from national courts across EU Member States.  Beyond resolving individual cases, court rulings can expand the scope of rights claims accepted and promote respectful, non-discriminatory language, even in complex areas like healthcare and health insurance law. 


We hope this resource empowers activists and lawyers to explore legal tools to improve access to trans-specific healthcare, drawing on ideas and arguments from similar efforts across the region.


What the publication covers


The publication presents national court decisions from EU Member States and covers key topics such as cost coverage, travelling abroad for care, age limits, waiting times, and discrimination. It includes cases where trans applicants won and cases where they didn’t, so readers can see what aspects courts consider relevant to their decision. Although the publication reviews case law in nearly all Member States, relevant cases were found in only a handful of countries, including Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, France, Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands.


get the publication


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: Shefali Luthra
title: Missouri Voters Reject Effort to Overturn Their State’s Abortion Protections
content:
The measure would also have banned gender-affirming care for transgender minors, which is already illegal in the state.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Missouri voters rejected an effort to overturn their state’s abortion protections, according to a projection by Decision Desk HQ, ensuring that the procedure will remain legal and enshrined in the state constitution despite dedicated efforts by Republican leadership.

Amendment 3 would have reversed the results of a 2024 vote that enshrined abortion protections into the state constitution and made Missouri the first state with a constitutional ban on the procedure. It would also have banned gender-affirming care for transgender minors, which is already illegal in the state.

The measure’s failure offers a rebuke to efforts by Missouri’s Republican leaders, who largely oppose abortion. Amendment 3 was put forth by Republican lawmakers who, troubled by the 2024 vote’s results, hoped a second vote might result in the undoing of abortion rights. The state’s first lady, Claudia Kehoe, served as treasurer for the campaign to pass Amendment 3.

Polling conducted this summer suggested that while Missouri voters largely supported abortion rights, they opposed keeping gender-affirming care legal for trans minors, a point emphasized by Amendment 3’s backers.

“We’re trying to do everything. We’ve had canvassers knocking on thousands of doors,” Tom Estes, a Republican state Senate staffer working on the pro-Amendment 3 campaign, told The 19th earlier this year. “There are several pieces of this that resonate really well, that we may not have gotten last time. The number one piece of that is the trans issue.”

The campaign also argued that the abortion protections enacted two years ago had made the procedure unregulated and dangerous, suggesting that the new ban would protect women and children.

The reality, according to abortion providers in the state, has been different: Abortion has been highly regulated and only sporadically available. Even prior to the fall of Roe v. Wade in 2022, abortions in Missouri had become almost impossible to obtain, the result of a maze of restrictions enacted by the state’s conservative legislature. By 2022, only one clinic in the state offered abortion, in St. Louis.

“I would love to provide abortion services four to six days a week in Springfield,” Dr. Margaret Baum, the chief medical officer at Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, told The 19th at the end of August. “I think the demand is there.”

author: La Zarzamora
title: Lulén y Max, dos jóvenes trans llevan año y medio encarcelados por defenderse de su agresor
content:
Lulen y Max son una pareja de dos personas trans condenados por intento de homicidio agravado con tentativa hacia el padre adoptivo de uno de ellos.

Los hechos habrían ocurrido en febrero del 2025 cuando ambos jóvenes se reúnen en la casa del padre de Lulen “Willian Watts” en Córdoba, con el motivo de buscar algunas reliquias de su abuela quién había fallecido recientemente.

El contexto de la familia adoptiva de Lulen es clave para entender los hechos, ya que desde su adolescencia se vio enfrentado a la violencia psicológica y física que perpetuaba el padre hacia la madre; a la homofobia del padre por su orientación sexual y posteriormente por su transición de género.

El día de los hechos como era recurrente hubo una discusión. Lulen y Max se defienden golpeando a Willian Watts hasta que un vecino escucha gritos, interrumpe la pelea y llama a la policía. Watts se encontraba inconsciente por una supuesta asfixia, pero queda vivo y sin lesiones. Desde ese día en febrero del 2025 Lulen y Max se encuentran secuestrados, presos en la cárcel de Córdoba.

La fiscalía les condenó a 12 años y seis meses de cárcel por intento de homicidio agravado con tentativa, primero por el vinculo familiar, segundo por alevosía y tercero por una supuesta teoría de premeditación (tentativa).

Sin duda ha habido diferentes vulneraciones desde el sistema judicial en su totalidad, ya que no dan ninguna relevancia a los hechos de violencia consecutiva y daños previos ejercidos por Willian Watts, tampoco otorgan valor al transodio y sostienen una hipótesis de película sin entender la legítima defensa y el malestar que puede llevar a una persona a defenderse.

En palabras de su red de apoyo:

“A pesar de que cayeron casi todos los agravantes que pidió el fiscal, la condena es insólita en su dureza y no se tuvieron en cuenta las circunstancias atenuantes que pidió la defensa; la de años de abuso y violencia psicológica hacia Lulén por parte de su padre.”

“Aún transitando el dolor y la bronca, estamos dispuestos a seguir a la próxima instancia judicial para lograr un mejor resultado. Seguiremos con actividades para terminar de juntar el dinero para terminar de pagar la defensa y vamos a sostener y abrir la campaña de libertad para Lulén y Max. Porque no aceptamos este fallo y no dejaremos que todo lo que se presenció quede impune.”

“Las vidas Trans importan, y ningún fiscal transodiante ni menos un tribunal discriminatorio nos van a parar o amedrentar.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Cómo fue el ataque a las trabajadoras sexuales trans en los Bosques de Palermo
content:
En la madrugada del domingo, un grupo de ciclistas atacó a mujeres trans que estaban realizando trabajo sexual en los Bosques de Palermo. La violencia que crece.


En la misma semana en que la Ciudad de Buenos Aires se prepara para la

35 Marcha del Orgullo

, un grupo de varones que participaba de una bicicleteada nocturna atacó a trabajadoras sexuales travestis y trans en los Bosques de Palermo el domingo en la madrugada. El hecho se difundió y viralizó a partir de los videos que los agresores subieron a las redes sociales. Y desataron el repudio de gran parte de la sociedad.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Presentes (@presenteslatam)


Una mujer trans que estuvo presente cuando ocurrió la agresión contó a

Presentes

lo que vivió esa madrugada. A las chicas “las cercaron. Fue así como un torbellino, un huracán. Las rodearon a todas ellas en la esquina de Ombúes y Bello. No podías entrar a defenderlas porque eran más de 150 ciclistas”, dijo Leticia . “Fue como a las tres de la mañana. Pude zafar porque cuando vi que ellos venían con esa intención, que empezaban a insultar, a gritar y tenían cosas en la mano, me metí en el bosque”.


Desde la

Defensoría del Pueblo de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

 informaron a esta agencia que, tras la agresión, hay varias mujeres trans heridas. “Lo que pudimos saber es que por lo menos hay seis compañeras lesionadas. Una bastante grave. No corre peligro de vida, pero tiene muy afectada una de sus orejas”, sostuvo María Rachid, titular del Instituto contra la Discriminación de la Defensoría del Pueblo de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.


“Estamos trabajándolo y hablando con la fiscal Andrea Verónica Scanga, la fiscal especializada en discriminación, quien ya abrió de oficio una investigación. Vamos a aportar el testimonio de las compañeras que presenciaron la agresión, los videos y print de pantalla que tenemos”, agregó Rachid.


Qué se sabe de los hechos


Algunos de los agresores, luego de subir los videos, cambiaron la privacidad de sus cuentas mientras que otros difundieron versiones que tendrán que probar en la Justicia. Por ejemplo, “sugerir” que reaccionaron a un ataque, cuando, hasta ahora, no existe un solo video que registre el supuesto ataque. Por el contrario, varios muestran desde distintos ángulos las agresiones a las personas trans.


También dijeron que un grupo se separó del recorrido central de la bicicleteada organizada para la noche de Halloween que recorrió la Ciudad.


Desde la Federación Argentina LGBT+ (FALGBT+) presentaron una denuncia penal. “No vamos a tolerar la violencia ni la impunidad. Por eso, presentamos una denuncia penal exigiendo justicia y el esclarecimiento inmediato de los hechos. Frente al odio y los ataques, nuestra respuesta es la organización y la presencia en las calles”, expresaron a través de sus redes y convocaron a marchar el 7/11: “Que el orgullo en las calles sea nuestra resistencia”.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Federación Argentina LGBT+ (@falgbt)


Violencia permanente


No es la primera vez que las trabajadoras sexuales de esa zona de la Ciudad sufren ataques. Hace más de un año que vienen denunciando en distintas oportunidades situaciones de hostigamiento y persecución por parte de la Policía de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.


Los videos se conocieron horas antes del

Paro de Trabajadoras Sexuales

en el que, entre otros reclamos, plantearon los ataques y agresiones que se agudizaron en los últimos meses. “Estamos frente a una situación de violencia de manera permanente. Todo el tiempo nos llegan videos, mensajes, audios, denunciando violencia por parte de la policía y de los vecinos. En Palermo, en los bosques, los jóvenes van a la zona de trabajo sexual a violentar a las compañeras, filman con los celulares y suben ese contenido a TikTok o a sus redes sociales”, describió Georgina Orellano, secretaria general de la

Asociación de Mujeres Meretrices de Argentina

 (Ammar).  Ella misma fue detenida en varias oportunidades


Por el hecho interviene el

Ministerio Público de la Ciudad

, a través de la Unidad de Flagrancia Norte, a cargo de Ángel Palopoli, que dispuso iniciar actuaciones por “averiguación de lesiones”. Fuentes vinculadas con la investigación informaron a

Presentes

 que el caso se está investigando para determinar qué pasó. En el proceso se hizo un pedido para acceder al registro de las cámaras de la zona y a testigos.


Artistas …

title: Фестиваль «Дед Мороз против Путина» возвращается в Хельсинки!
content:
9 января 2027 года в столице Финляндии пройдет уже двенадцатый фестиваль «Дед Мороз против Путина».

История нашего фестиваля началась 12 лет назад, в 2014 году, с простой идеи: создать безопасное пространство в Хельсинки, где гражданские активисты могли бы открыто обсуждать политические и социальные проблемы России, делиться опытом и находить единомышленников.

С началом войны в Украине контекст радикально изменился. Сегодня наш фестиваль — это важнейшая точка сборки для всей русскоязычной эмиграции и солидарных жителей Финляндии.

Фестиваль создается для и силами новой волны российской эмиграции. Мы рады видеть антиавторитарных активистов, феминисток, антимилитаристов, антифашистов, правозащитников, художников и исследователей.

Наша площадка открыта для всех, кто был вынужден покинуть РФ, а также для жителей Финляндии, мигрантов и беженцев, которые поддерживают борьбу гражданского общества против путинского авторитарного олигархического режима.

Если вы хотите приблизить падение диктатуры, остановить войну и верите в потенциал массового оппозиционного движения — присоединяйтесь к нам!

author: Kiara Green
title: What Rights Are at Stake in the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 Term?
content:
The US Supreme Court reconvened on October 5 for its 2026-27 term which concludes in June of 2027. Cases involving the rights of immigrants, rules governing elections, LGBTQIA rights, and more, stand at the forefront this term. The Court’s decisions could have significant consequences for how federal and state laws protect individual rights.

The Court begins this term with a 6–3 conservative majority. Three of the nine justices, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, were nominated by President Donald Trump. Recent decisions, including the overturning of Dobbs and rulings affecting the enforcement of the Voting Rights Act, have already reshaped the legal landscape. This term, the justices will consider additional disputes over voting regulations and the rights of young people.

Among these cases is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, which is scheduled to be heard on December 8. The Court will decide whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship to register to vote and if the National Voter Registration Act prohibits Arizona from canceling the registrations of non-citizens within 90 days of a federal election.

Despite the lack of evidence of noncitizen voting, concerns about voter eligibility have led to policies that can create additional hurdles for eligible voters in Arizona, especially indigenous people. Arizona is home to one of the largest Indigenous reservations in the US, but was one of the last states to allow Indigenous people to vote.

Indigenous votes play a vital role in deciding the outcome of state and federal elections. In 2020, Indigenous voters from the Hopi and Navajo reservation cast nearly 60,000 votes.

The Supreme Court’s decision could affect how Arizona and other states administer voter registration and verify citizenship. It will also determine how federal law limits states’ authority to change voter registration records close to an election.

The Court will also hear International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v. Ferguson on December 7. The Administration has vilified the queer community spewing anti-trans and homophobic rhetoric in the name of religious freedom. The decision of this case will impact the livelihood of queer adolescents that struggle with their gender identity.

The case is challenging a Washington State law on whether runaway minors can seek access to gender-affirming care without parental permission. Ending gender-affirming care has been a top priority for the Trump administration pushing for hospitals to discriminate against patients based on gender orientation and identity. This pressure has led at least six hospitals to agree to refuse gender-affirming hormones and surgery for transgender young people and agreed to make payments to the federal government.

As the term continues, the Court’s decisions will shape how federal protections and state laws apply to voting access, family rights and LGBTQIA+ communities. Oral arguments will offer insight into the justices’ questions, but final rulings are expected later in the term.

The Supreme Court’s work affects people across the country, often in ways that reach beyond the specific parties involved in a case. As the midterm elections approach on November 3, make a plan to vote, bring friends, spread the word. For nonpartisan voter registration information, election dates and voting resources, visit Vote411.org/feminist.

author: Unknown
title: Başka olanın hayali: Feminist tahayyül
content:
Feminist Tahayyül Dergisi şimdilerde feminist bilgi üreten ve bu bilgiyi erişilebilir kılan hakemli bir akademik dergi olmanın ötesine geçerek konferanslar ve seminerler de düzenliyor. 


Dergi, Ekim ayında başlayan güz dönemi seminerlerini ve 29-30 Mayıs 2027’de gerçekleşecek 3. konferansını yakın zamanda duyurdu. 


Derginin editörleri Demet Gülçiçek ve Emine Erdoğan geçtiğimiz Nisan ayında düzenledikleri konferanslarının sunuşuna şu

sözlerle

başlıyor:


“Feminist Tahayyül’ün başka türlüsü mümkün değilmiş gibi görüneni sorgulamakta inat ederek ve tüm sınırlara rağmen kendinden ödün vermemeye çalışan pratiklerde ısrarcı olarak, neşesi öfkesini azaltmadan yoluna devam etmesini diliyoruz.”


“Nedir bu Feminist Tahayyül?” sorusu üzerine bianet’e konuşan Demet ve Emine, “Feminist Tahayyül” fikrinin 2018’de, doktoralarını yaptıkları yıllarda feminist birikim üzerine kafa yorarken, feminist düşünce alanlarını çoğaltma arzusuyla ortaya çıktığını söylüyor:


“

Akademik üretim süreçlerinde feminist yaklaşımların artması, çeşitlenmesi gerektiğini düşündüğümüz için bir dergi oluşturma fikri bizi çok heyecanlandırdı.”


Dergi, ismini feminist düşüncenin akademide “eril pratiklerden” farklı biçimde var olabileceği fikrinden, “başka olanın” hayalinden alıyor. Hayal etmenin politik bir eylem olduğunu ifade eden Demet ve Emine, bu yaklaşımı derginin adına yansıtmak istediklerini belirtiyor.


Ayrıca, derginin akademik üretimdeki unvana dayalı hiyerarşiden ve  “nicelleştirilmiş puan” sistemlerinden uzak durmaya çalıştığını,  tüm editoryal süreçlerin gönüllülüğe dayalı yürütüldüğünü ve derginin açık erişimli olduğunu ekliyorlar.


Feminist Tahayyül ne yapıyor? 


2020’den bu yana yılda iki kez (Şubat ve Ağustos) olmak üzere çevrimiçi formatta, pedogoji, beden, duygulanım gibi farklı temalarda 14 sayı yayımladılar. 


2024’ten bu yana ise iki konferans ve her akademik yılda dört ila altı tane olmak üzere çeşitli alanlarda seminerler düzenlediler. Önümüzdeki dönemde Ankara’da düzenlenecek etkinliklerin takvimi şöyle: 


3 Ekim 2026 -  Erkekliğin Dönüş(eme)me Çabaları: Beden, Gençlik ve İnceller


7 Kasım 2026 – Üniversitelerde Şiddet ve Cinsel Taciz


19 Aralık 2026 – “Tuhaf” Akrabalıklar: Feminizm ve İnsansonrası Çalışmalar


29-30 Mayıs 2027 – III. Feminist Tahayyül Dergisi Konferansı


Demet ve Emine, etkinlikleri birlikte düşünmeyi ve bir araya gelmeyi mümkün kılacak önemli araçlar olarak görüyorlar: 


“

Feminizmi ‘akademi’ ve ‘sokak’ olarak keskin sınırlarla ayırmanın pek mümkün olmadığını düşünüyoruz. Bu ayrım üzerine ciddi bir tartışma olsa da feminist bilgi üretimi bir şekilde iki alandan da besleniyor… Feminist Tahayyül buluşmalarında çalışmalarını paylaşan kişiler için feminist bilgi üretiminin kolektif bir düşünme pratiği olduğu fikriyle, üniversitenin kurumsal denetim mekanizmalarından olabildiğince azade, bağımsız bir ortam oluşturmaya çalışıyoruz.” 


Feminist bilgi üretimi


Derginin web sitesini ziyaret ettiğimizde hedeflerinin, “üretilecek olan feminist bilginin erişilebilirliğini ve arşivlenmesini kolaylaştırmak, aynı zamanda Türkiye’de feminist bilginin pratik ve kuramsal yönelimlerini görünür kılmak” olduğunu görüyoruz. 


Editörler bu amacın olanaklarını ve sınırlarını şöyle ifade ediyor: 


“Feminizmin sadece “feminizm çalışanları” ilgilendirmediğini düşündüğümüz için, feminizmi ayrı bir tema olarak değil, sosyal bilimler, beşerî bilimler ve doğa bilimleri dahil herhangi bir bilimsel çalışmada olması gereken bir yaklaşım olarak görüyoruz. Fakat feminist bilginin statüsünde bazı sistematik problemler var: marjinalleştirilme, ciddiye alınmama, tehdit haline getirilme, içinin boşaltılması gibi. Bunlara rağmen, ulusaşırı feminist bilgi üretme pratiklerinin inanılmaz etkileyici bir ısrarı var. Temel kavramlara dair teorik tartışmalardan kıyafet ceplerinin cinsiyetlendirilmiş kullanımına kadar geniş bir yelpazeden bahsediyoruz.”


Feminist hafıza 


Demet ve Emine, ürettikleri çalışmaların gelecekte farklı bir zaman ve bağlam üzerinden değerlendirilecek olmasının hem romantik hem de endişe verici boyutları olduğuna dikkat çekiyor. 


Feminist yayıncılık pratiklerinin tarihsel süreçte birbirinin birikimine dayanmasını meselenin “romantik” ve politik açıdan umut verici yönü olarak tanımlarken, feminist hafızanın bu şekilde inşa edildiğini belirtiyor. 


Bu tarihsel bağın, farklı dönemler ve bağlamlar arasındaki mesafeyi kısaltarak yalnızlık hissini ortadan kaldırdığını ifade ediyorlar.

author: Clare Hymer
title: Could the Way the Greens Set Policy Be About to Change?
content:
Could the way the Green party of England and Wales makes policy – and who gets to call the shots – be about to change?


Ever since

the motion stating that Zionism is racism

 passed at Green conference in October, senior figures have taken to legacy media outlets to claim that the vote shows the party’s internal democracy isn’t working. 


In an act with more than a whiff of the Corbyn-era Labour right, former co-leader and MP for Waveney Valley Adrian Ramsay told Laura Kuenssberg at the weekend that the Greens are at risk of being overrun by the “hard left”. Ellie Chowns MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not

“vulnerable to capture by extremists”

, while Green trailblazer Caroline Lucas has raised

concerns about “entryism”

. 


But it’s not just the Greens’ old guard who think the party needs a shake-up. Leader Zack Polanski wrote in

a Guardian article

 after the conference that the party’s democracy must “evolve” to meet the Greens’ newly expanded membership, “creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set… strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible”. This was followed by

a “joint leadership statement”

 last week which said a working group had been set up, and the first proposals would likely be voted on at the party’s conference in spring 2027.


As it stands, the Greens have a one-member-one-vote system: any member, regardless of how long ago they joined the party, can vote on policy and changes to the party’s constitution. This direct democracy, which is distinct from the other mainstream parties in Britain, is cherished by the membership – and any group of members who organise well around conference can change party policy, be that to declare that Zionism is racism, or for the Greens

to ditch their longstanding opposition to nuclear power

. 


The recent murmurings around change have got some members worried. An

open letter

 to Polanski and co. circulating on social media this week insists that the party sticks with the one-member-one-vote model, and that “members will not accept any move away from this model”. Meanwhile, Greens for Palestine – the members behind the Zionism is racism motion – put out

a statement

 against those seeking to “subvert the Green party’s member-led democracy because they fear a loss of control”.


Russell Warfield, author of the new book

The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future

, told Novara Media he doesn’t think Polanski’s calls for improvements to the party’s democracy are, unlike for others, “a knee-jerk reaction to fix the ‘problem’ of the Zionism motion”. But for as long as the leadership’s proposals are unspecific, Polanski risks being seen to be in a coalition with those most vocally opposed to the motion. Members are likely wondering if their leader is –

like Ramsay

 – in favour of a delegate system more similar to Labour, whereby local parties select members to send to conferences.


On Wednesday, Greens Organise, a group of ecosocialist party members,

published a model motion

 aimed at improving how conferences run and better engaging members – one it hopes will be uncontroversial. It also

called for proposals

 for the more fundamental matter of how (and crucially if) the party’s democracy should be reformed. Co-deputy leader Rachel Millward told Novara Media the leadership welcomed this initiative, in addition to a forthcoming consultation of the wider membership.


Greens Organise said: “Any changes must serve the purpose of building a mass, ecosocialist party – not a reaction to any one policy… We should not leave it to [the leadership] to decide.”


The good news for those in the ‘change nothing’ camp is that anyone wanting to see a major reform through will have a tough time. First, they’d need a two-thirds majority. Second,

many have wrangled over the party’s internal workings before

 – and yet its core structure remains the same as 30 years ago. (Warfield noted that it’s an odd reversal that the veteran Greens “clamouring” for the current review “roughly correspond to the cohort who most resisted it last time”.)


“I think it’s unlikely this is going to be easily resolved,” Warfield said.

title: Alemania: la solidaridad con Palestina no es negociable
content:
Líder de Die Linke, Elif Eralp, y manifestantes pro Palestina en Alemania (Ibrahim Ibrahim entre ellos). Foto © Instagram / @eliferalp – Wikipedia


Die Linke fue la fuerza más votada en las últimas elecciones para la Cámara de Diputados de Berlín y de las asambleas de Consejales de Distrito el 20.09. Se desplegó una campaña de agresión, odio y mentiras, ya durante la campaña electoral, que se intensificó luego de la victoria. Obtuvo 25,7 % de los votos, seguido por CDU (derecha cristiana) con el 18,8 % y el partido Grün/Verde alcanzó el 14,3%. Pero como no se llegó a la mayoría, la izquierda podrá gobernar solo si se forma una coalición. CDU se negó rotundamnete a una coalción con la izquierda. Tras semanas de discuciones y peleas mediáticas, siguen sin ponerse de acuerdo sobre los puntos más candentes, que son los puntos claves, por los que muchas personas -sobre todo de origen migrante- habían depositado su voto a favor a Die Linke y son la no criminalización a la solidaridad con Palestina y la expropiación de los inmuebles.

Por Ana Muro, corresponsal de ANRed en Alemania.


El programa para las elecciones que presentó Die Linke decía entre otros puntos: “Deben fomentarse los proyectos contra el racismo antipalestino. Las restricciones a la libertad de expresión, de ciencia y de reunión, así como a otros derechos fundamentales, deben investigarse en profundidad en relación con esta forma específica de racismo y debe combatírselas.”


“La libertad de reunión debe protegerse con más fuerza frente a las restricciones estatales. (…) Condenamos la violencia policial y las restricciones desproporcionadas a la libertad de reunión y de expresión, como las que recientemente han afectado a manifestaciones solidarias con Palestina o aactivistas climáticos. (…) Queremos sacar a la autoridad de reuniones de la Policía de Berlín.”


El 8 de octubre se publicó el “acuerdo“ sobre el inicio de las conversaciones exploratorias entre Die Linke Berlín, Bündnis 90/Die Grünen y el SPD, entre los partidos que es posible una coalición. Ese acuerdo refuerza la represión, porque la definición de antisemitismo que utiliza es tan amplia que cualquier crítica a la política de ocupación, asentamientos, apartheid y genocidio del Estado de Israel queda incluida.


Ese acuerdo además fortalece a la policía y al Verfassungsschutz (Oficina para la Protección de la Constitución), amplía su presupuesto y sus competencias, y los refuerza como garantes de unapolítica de orden público que lleva tres años criminalizando y reprimiendo la solidaridad conPalestina.


Naturalmente los votantes se sienten traicionados


El acuerdo le da poder al SPD y a los Verdes, para decidir entre las voces aceptables y las que deben silenciarse, es decir, aquellas que no se ajustan a la Staatsräson, al apoyo incondicional de Alemania hacia Israel. Ambos partidos tienen una trayectoria bastante manchada en la historia. Los verdes en los 80′ empezaron militarizando la política exterior alemana y el SPD, a pesar de ser concebida con sociales, boicoteó la revolución en 1918 de la mano de Friedrich Ebert.


El arca política no quiere que gobierne un partido de izquierda, por ello a través de este acuerdo quieren un partido más débil, más dócil, divido, para poder frenar el tema que realmente le preocupa a la derechay al centro político: la expropiación de las viviendas. El monopolio inmobiliario tiene un poder inmenso y ejerce presión en los políticos.


La campaña de desprestigio a militantes concretos como Ferat Koçak y Vanessa Emde (ambos son los que más se solidarizan con Palestina) y a la izquierda en general, no apunta a combatir el antisemitismo real, sino a castigar cualquier voz que critique la política de ocupación, de asentamientos y de apartheid del Estado de Israel, o que cuestione la razón de Estado alemana. A su vez, se acusa a Die Linke por tener conecciones con Ibrahim Ibrahim e Issa Remo, ambos acusados de estar al frente de un clan criminal. Ibrahim Ibrahim es un activista de origen palestino y representante del Comité Nacional palestino unificado, se lo vincula con el Frente Popular para la Liberación de Palestina (considerada por EE.UU. y la UE como organización terrorista).


El tema Palestina, ya fue un punto de inflección en toda Alemania, pero también dentro de toda laIzquierda. Die Linke expulsó en 2025 a Ramsis Kilani, un activista de origen propalestino, su familia fueasesinada en un ataque aereo israelí en la franja de Gaza en 2014. Luego de más …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: House Democrats Want Stevens Out of Their Caucus After Her “Despicable Betrayal”
content:
The Michigan Democratic Party’s chair removed Haley Stevens from the party for endorsing Abdul El-Sayed’s opponent.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A growing number of House Democrats are calling for Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan) to be expelled from their caucus after she seemingly broke rules in her surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers in the tight Senate race in Michigan on Sunday, marked by some as a “despicable betrayal.”

According to Politico, at least eight Democrats were supportive of some form of punishment by Democratic leaders as of Sunday afternoon, with likely many more also quietly on board. Top progressive Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), the former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said that Stevens “has shown her true colors.”

“She is supporting a candidate for Senate that is a rubber stamp for Trump’s disastrous and dangerous administration,” said Jayapal. “She has no place in our party. This is exactly why she lost the primary despite tens of millions of dollars and why she is of no relevance to the future of this country.”

Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas), who supported Stevens in the primary, told outlets he backs her ousting. “I was the first Caucus member to host a fundraiser for her Senate bid. And, I’d be the first to make the motion to remove her,” he said, per Politico.

“Capitulating to fascism, Islamophobia, racism and the policies hurting everyday Americans makes you unfit to serve with the Democratic caucus,” said Rep. Delia C. Ramirez (D-Illinois) in a post on social media. “Shame on Haley Stevens. She must be removed from the caucus.”

Democratic caucus rules specify that members can’t “participate in campaign activities for any candidate in a partisan federal election who is not a Member of the Democratic Party.” Members can be expelled by a two-thirds vote.

Stevens has already faced some retribution. As of Sunday, Stevens was removed from the House Democrats’ text chains. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr. also said that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” And a huge proportion of her staff have resigned, including her former communications director, expressing disgust with the lawmaker.

Stevens, whose political career has been marked by her vehement support of Israel, put out a shock endorsement of Rogers after appearing at a Black church service with the GOP candidate on Sunday. This came just days after saying that she was going to do a campaign event at a Black church with primary opponent Abdul El-Sayed, and after she evidently swore in private conversations with several Democrats that she wouldn’t back Rogers.

The decision set off a political earthquake just two days before the general election on Tuesday, with Stevens swearing that she is still a Democrat and backs the party in other races.

Numerous Black politicians and commentators have noted that it was especially cynical for Stevens to use Black voters — who overwhelmingly back El-Sayed in the race — and a Black church to debut her support for Rogers.

Progressive Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts) said that Stevens used Black people as a “prop.” Pressley said that Stevens personally swore in a conversation that she would back El-Sayed.

“Well, Haley, I guess in this instance you’ve chosen a white supremacist order and then have the audacity to use Black people as a prop and as a shield for your ignorance,” Pressley said.

“She used Black people as a prop to pursue an agenda of sore loser-ness,” said political organizer Stacey Abrams in an interview with MS NOW. “Her personal animus has now overtaken her respect for the Black people with whom she worshipped and for every Michigander from whom she has requested a vote.”

Stevens’s defection is a major test for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is slated to become the next House speaker if the party retakes the House.

The Democratic leader hinted at punishment for Stevens in remarks to Politico. “Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus. We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return,” Jeffries said.
