title: Σχετικά με τα περιστατικά ακραίας αστυνομικής βίας στην Θεσσαλονίκη τον Οκτώβρη του ’24
content:
Σχετικά με τα περιστατικά ακραίας αστυνομικής βίας στην Θεσσαλονίκη τον Οκτώβρη του ’24


Στις 11/11 στα δικαστήρια Θεσσαλονίκης εκδικάζονται  2 διαφορετικές υποθέσεις, που όμως έχουν την ίδια αφετηρία: Την ακραία αστυνομική βία απέναντι σε ζευγάρι γονέων μπροστά στο ανήλικο παιδί τους -τότε βρέφος 3 μηνών- στο Πάρκο του Εργατικού Κέντρου Θεσσαλονίκης. Ας πάρουμε όμως τα πράγματα από την αρχή:


Το βραδάκι της Δευτέρας 28/10/2024 το νεαρό ζευγάρι είχε βγει βόλτα μαζί με το μωρό του και κάποιους φίλους του στο Πάρκο του ΕΚΘ. Μετά από λίγη ώρα, με πρόφαση έλεγχο για ναρκωτικά, μηχανές της ομάδας ΔΙΑΣ πλησίασαν την παρέα. Και τότε άρχισε το θέατρο του παραλόγου. Όπως αναφέρει η καταγγελία της παρέας, που δημοσιεύτηκε

σε διάφορα site

 εκείνες τις ημέρες:


“…Εμείς δεν είχαμε πάνω μας ναρκωτικά και δεν είχαμε κάτι να φοβηθούμε και δεν μας ανησύχησε αυτό. Όταν ένας από την παρέα, ο πατέρας του μωρού, ζήτησε από τους μπάτσους να μην ακουμπήσουν το μωρό, καθώς είναι τριών μηνών και δεν κάνει (το ανοσοποιητικό του είναι ακόμα αδύναμο), όπως ήταν μπριζωμένοι αυτοί τον άρπαξαν και του έστριψαν το χέρι πίσω από τη πλάτη, και τον κάθισαν στο παγκάκι, ενώ ο έλεγχος σε κάποιους από μας συνεχίζονταν. Τον είχαν στο παγκάκι λέγοντας του να χαλαρώσει, αλλά αυτοί μάλλον δεν ήταν καθόλου χαλαροί, γιατί όταν τους ζήτησε να σταματήσουν να του στρίβουν το χέρι πίσω από την πλάτη, ένας από αυτούς άρχισε να τον χτυπά με γροθιές στο κεφάλι εντελώς αναίτια, μπροστά στη μητέρα και το μωρό. Αφού τον χτύπησαν, αποφάσισαν μάλλον να το δικαιολογήσουν με σύλληψη για «αντίσταση κατά της αρχής». Για να φαίνεται αυτό πειστικότερο αποφάσισαν να περάσουν χειροπέδες και σε δεύτερο φίλο μας, τον οποίο περικύκλωσαν, κλώτσησαν, έριξαν κάτω και του φόρεσαν χειροπέδες. Έπειτα τους πήγαν και τους δύο στο τμήμα στην Αριστοτέλους. Εκεί μάθαμε ότι τους υπέβαλλαν κατηγορίες για αντίσταση. Τα παιδιά λοιπόν τα χτύπησαν αναίτια, τους φόρτωσαν κατηγορίες για να δικαιολογήσουν το ξύλο που έριξαν για να ξεδώσουν…”.


Περιττό να πούμε βέβαια πως ναρκωτικά δεν βρέθηκαν στην παρέα, όμως φαίνεται πως η στάση των νεαρών, να διεκδικήσουν δηλαδή τα δικαιώματά τους και να προστατεύσουν το παιδί τους, δεν ικανοποίησε τους αστυνομικούς. Αυτές οι συλλήψεις αποτελούν λοιπόν το αντικείμενο της μίας από τις δυο υποθέσεις που εκδικάζονται στις 11/11/2026.


Δυστυχώς όμως για τους αστυνομικούς και το αφήγημά τους, η αλληλεγγύη όσων υπήρξαν μάρτυρες στο γεγονός -ακόμη και άνθρωποι εντελώς άσχετοι με την παρέα- έφερε στην επιφάνεια μια σειρά από μαρτυρίες και video, που αποτυπώνουν την αλήθεια εκείνης της ημέρας, όπως το παρακάτω που ανέβηκε στο infolibre, όπου φαίνεται καθαρά η αναίτια βία που ασκείται στον πατέρα του βρέφους, καθώς και αργότερα στον δεύτερο συλληφθέντα, ενώ ακούγεται η μητέρα να ζητάει από τους άνδρες της ΔΙΑΣ να μην αγγίξουν το παιδί:


30/10/2026: Η άγρια επίθεση της αστυνομίας σε μαγαζί εστίασης


Δυο μέρες μετά, στις 30/10/2026, στην περιοχή πραγματοποιήθηκε πορεία αλληλεγγύης, ως απάντηση στην αστυνομική βία και αυθαιρεσία. Κατά την διάρκεια της πορείας υπήρξε έντονη αστυνομική παρουσία και αυτό οδήγησε σε μικροσυμπλοκές στο πάρκο του ΕΚΘ. Κάπου εκεί όμως ξεκινάει το δεύτερο κεφάλαιο αυτής της ιστορίας, που αφορά το έτερο δικαστήριο που εκδικάζεται σε λίγες ημέρες. Η αστυνομία περικύκλωσε τον παρακείμενο πεζόδρομο της Γκαρμπολά, όπου είχε καταφύγει κομμάτι του κόσμου τη πορείας, αλλά επίσης βρίσκονταν και άλλοι, άσχετοι άνθρωποι από την γειτονιά, θαμώνες μαγαζιών κλπ, όπως και κόσμος του κινήματος -καθώς στον συγκεκριμένο πεζόδρομο στεγάζονται πολιτικοί χώροι. Δυνάμεις των ΜΑΤ στρατοπέδευσαν έξω από χώρους εστίασης, υπό τις αποδοκιμασίες της γειτονιάς.


Στην συνέχεια, εντελώς αναίτια, πραγματοποίησαν ευθεία επίθεση σε εστιατόριο, έσπασαν την τζαμαρία του, χτύπησαν κόσμο και έριξαν δακρυγόνο στο εσωτερικό του χώρου! Τα δυο παρακάτω video αναδεικνύουν την στιγμή της επίθεσης:


Παραθέτουμε επίσης κομμάτι της μαρτυρίας κατοίκου της περιοχής

σε τοπικό Μέσο

, ο οποίος ήταν παρών στο σύνολο των γεγονότων:


“…Πραγματικά, ήταν αποπνικτικό το κλίμα σε όλο το μήκος της οδού. Εκεί τα ΜΑΤ, όχι απλά δεν απομακρύνθηκαν, αλλά άρχισαν να πετάνε και επιπλέον χημικά ακριβώς έξω από το μαγαζί. Το σοκαριστικό στην όλη υπόθεση είναι πως οι αστυνομικοί είχαν ακραία επιθετική διάθεση απέναντι στον κόσμο, χωρίς να καταλαβαίνουν ότι θα μπορούσε να υπάρξει σοβαρό ατύχημα με το να χτυπάν και να πνίγουν στα χημικά το μαγαζί. Έτσι, άρχισαν να κλωτσάν και να σπάνε το μαγαζί, ενώ σε ένα …

author: anred
title: Mendoza: cárcel al abusador Mauro Aguirre, basta de impunidad patriarcal
content:
En 2018, estudiantes de la Facultad de Ciencias Políticas y Sociales (FCPyS) de la Universidad Nacional de Cuyo (UNCuyo), en Mendoza, denunciaron al profesor y dirigente de la Agrupación Universitaria Nacional (AUN), Mauro Aguirre, por abuso sexual, violaciones y violencia de género. Sin embargo, después de casi ocho años, la justicia patriarcal todavía no lo juzgó. Aguirre es un peso pesado de la política mendocina. En 1994 fue convencional constituyente por el partido derechista Modin, del golpista carapintada Aldo Rico. Antes había militado en el Frente de Izquierda Popular, de Jorge Abelardo Ramos. Tras el retroceso electoral del Modin volvió al peronismo, donde participó de la creación del Movimiento de Integración Nacional (MIN) y llegó a integrar la conducción provincial del Partido Justicialista.

Por Isadora e Izquierda Socialista Mendoza.


En agosto de 2024, la Universidad Nacional del Litoral le entregó una medalla y un diploma por su participación en la reforma constitucional de 1994. El reconocimiento a un denunciado de múltiples abusos sexuales provocó el repudio del movimiento de mujeres y de la propia UNCuyo. La universidad tuvo que dar marcha atrás, revocar la distinción y exigirle que devolviera ambos reconocimientos.


Las denuncias se hicieron públicas en diciembre de 2018, durante una asamblea de mujeres e identidades disidentes de la facultad. Seis estudiantes denunciaron hechos ocurridos entre 2010 y 2015, cuando algunas tenían apenas 18 y 19 años. Según sus testimonios, Aguirre aprovechaba su posición como docente y dirigente político para ejercer violencia sexual y psicológica.


Las denunciantes también señalaron el papel de la agrupación peronista AUN, donde se desarrollaban prácticas de aislamiento y manipulación. Integrantes de la agrupación habrían colaborado para alejar a las jóvenes de sus vínculos personales y facilitar los abusos. Por estos hechos también fueron imputados Leandro Fontán, Lucía Fernández y Mario Codoni, acusados de actuar como partícipes primarios.


En mayo de 2019, Aguirre fue detenido. Durante la pandemia obtuvo prisión domiciliaria y en 2022, tras el pago de una fianza, recuperó la libertad. Aunque la UNCuyo lo exoneró en abril de 2021 por violencia patriarcal, la causa penal continuó acumulando demoras. El abogado defensor de Aguirre, Carlos Varela Álvarez, también es conocido por representar a la monja Kumiko Kosaka en la causa por los abusos a menores con discapacidad en el instituto Próvolo.


Recién en mayo de 2025, la Justicia confirmó que Aguirre y los otros tres imputados debían enfrentar un juicio oral. El 27 de octubre de 2026 comenzó la audiencia preliminar, que pasó a un cuarto intermedio hasta mediados de noviembre. Mientras tanto, Aguirre continúa en libertad.


Las sobrevivientes llevan casi ocho años reclamando justicia. Tuvieron que enfrentar las consecuencias de los abusos denunciados, el poder político del acusado y un sistema judicial que prolonga su sufrimiento con dilaciones interminables. La impunidad también se sostiene en estas demoras, que obligan a las denunciantes a seguir esperando mientras los acusados permanecen libres.


Desde Isadora e Izquierda Socialista Mendoza acompañamos la lucha de las sobrevivientes y denunciamos la responsabilidad de esta justicia patriarcal, que después de ocho años todavía no llevó a Aguirre al banquillo de los acusados. Exigimos que se realice de inmediato el juicio oral, que se juzgue a todos los responsables y que Aguirre y sus cómplices vayan presos.


Basta de impunidad patriarcal. Justicia para las sobrevivientes. Cárcel a los abusadores y sus cómplices.

author: Unknown
title: Lilia Folt - On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness
content:
Author

: Lilia Folt

Title

: On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness

Date

: September 27

th

, 2026

Notes

: Originally published in

Dissonant Times

, a grassroots journalism and counter-info project from the Willamette Valley of Oregon.

Source

: Dissonant Times, Retrieved on 11/5/2026 from https://dissonanttimes.org/anarchic-reflections-on-anti-surveillance-mindfulness/


 Surveillance has become a ubiquitous feature of everyday life in America. Cameras watch us from businesses and homes, from bus stops, from cars, from traffic lights. Bluetooth trackers ping our smartphones as we pass by, mapping our movements. The phones themselves illuminate our paths through society by continuously pinging cell towers, providing our cell providers our location data, information that is only a subpoena away, if that. In countless ways, we’ve been made to both passively accept and actively participate in our own surveillance. This vast complex of surveillance doesn’t just gather information about us, it also shapes our behaviors, temperaments, and ways of moving through the world. Surveillance molds us down to the level of subjective, sensory, embodied experience. At that same level we can begin to shake off its hold on us and reclaim ourselves. For that, I am offering a practice I’m calling “anti-surveillance mindfulness,” a form of walking meditation that builds mindful awareness of surveillance cameras. This practice, if taken up consistently, opens onto a broader project of transforming our relationship to the places we live in, a project that itself naturally blossoms into materially transforming public space, as self expands to world in the moment-by-moment practice of mindfulness.


Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness


 Readers may or may not be familiar with the Panopticon. Designed by 18

th

 century English liberal Jeremy Bentham, the Panopticon was a model for an institutional building designed so that a single prison guard can watch all the inmates from a central watch tower. The inmates, meanwhile, cannot tell whether or not they are being watched, and therefore could be watched at any moment. To quote Bentham:


 The more constantly the persons to be inspected are under the eyes of the persons who should inspect them, the more perfectly will the purpose of the establishment have been attained. (...) This being impossible, the next thing to be wished for is, that, at every instant, seeing reason to believe as much, and not being able to satisfy himself to the contrary, he should

conceive

 himself to be so.


 A lot has changed since the 1700’s, but the disciplinary paradigm of surveillance has remained the same. If anything, it has expanded beyond specific institutions to encompass much of society.


 There are cameras everywhere, and we are being watched, and while we are aware of this, we tend to see it as normal and unremarkable, an inevitability we must resign ourselves to. Consciousness of being surveilled fades into the background, becoming a constant assumption of being watched that we internalize. This surveillance consciousness is running us all the more effectively because it is not distinct, because it is

un

conscious. That is why the first step in anti-surveillance mindfulness is becoming conscious of surveillance.


 Mindfulness is at the same time a means and an end, the seed and the fruit. When we practice mindfulness in order to build up concentration, mindfulness is a seed. But mindfulness itself is the life of awareness: the presence of mindfulness means the presence of life, and therefore mindfulness is also the fruit. — Thích Nhất Hạnh,

The Miracle of Mindfulness


 “Mindfulness” is a practice originating in various sects of Buddhism. The mindfulness practices and concepts I’m familiar with have largely been within the school of Zen Buddhism

[1]

.


 The classic mindfulness practice is watching the breath, and that is a great starting point. Take a breath in, the air entering through your nose, your stomach and chest softly expanding as you inhale. Then exhale through the mouth, the stomach and chest settling back down, gently exhaling for a little longer than your inhale. Repeat this several times, deepening your breaths slightly. From there, start to check in with your body. Notice how it feels to be sitting down, or to be standing if you are standing; notice how it feels to be holding this piece of paper, holding your phone, or looking at your computer, however it is that you are reading …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Air Creebec hit by administrative data breach affecting employees and passengers
content:
Air Creebec, a regional Quebec airline owned by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee, reported a data breach Wednesday affecting both customers and staff.

In a press release, the company announced “an unauthorized intrusion targeting some of its administrative systems.”

The release stresses that the breach did not compromise any systems associated with aircraft, flight operations or flight safety, noting the company’s administrative systems were not connected with aircraft and flight systems, which it said operate independently.

“Initial findings indicate that administrative files were exfiltrated,” states the release. “These files may contain personal information relating mainly to current and former employees, as well as passengers. Others may also contain operational, administrative or financial information related to customers and partners. The review is ongoing.”

Based in the airport of Val d’Or in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of western Quebec, roughly 520 kilometres northwest of Ottawa, Air Creebec offers flights to 16 destinations in Quebec and Ontario. The company’s fleet consists of 21 Dash-8 turboprop regional airliners, along with one ATR 72 turboprop air-freighter for cargo, and carries 200,000 passengers per year.

Cybersecurity experts assessing damage

Air Creebec director for Marketing and Business Development Edward Trahan said the breach was identified in October after which company officials immediately brought in cybersecurity experts to analyze the situation.

“They’re currently evaluating what’s going on and what the breach actually contained,” Trahant told APTN News. “The experts are still conducting their review, so there’s no numbers [of victims] at this time that we can give.”

He added that for security reasons, he was not presently willing to name the cybersecurity team currently helping with post-breach recovery.

He said because the attack was designed to go undetected it was hard to determine the date upon which it began, and for how long attackers were able to access Air Creebec’s systems prior to being discovered.

“What I can assure you of is that as soon as [we were] made aware of [it], we acted immediately and did not wait.”

At the moment, Trahant said the attack appeared to have stolen information “related to our employees, past employees too, and maybe even our passengers.”

“But it’s hard to confirm at the moment.”

Company will contact affected parties

He added that a priority for Air Creebec is contacting every one of their staff or customers whose information has been compromised, which cybersecurity experts would undertake to carry out as soon as possible.

“A part of what the cybersecurity experts are doing for us is gathering information to [determine] what kind of protection packages we can provide to people that had their information involved,” said Trahan.

“Those people will be directly contacted in probably the next few days — [but] probably more like [the next] day — about what package they will receive, what protection they’re going to have and how long it’s going to last.”

Trahan said the cybersecurity team was currently in the process of securing all possible intrusion points, but he said the nature of cybersecurity is that 100 per cent protection is impossible.

“It’s just the way of the world,” he said, “but they are closing every possible way to get in and they are getting to the very end of that. As for how they got in initially, we don’t know yet and I don’t want to speculate while the review is still underway.”

Trahan said he and Air Creebec are taking the situation very seriously and are committed to supporting all those affected, and the company said it would be in touch with affected people to offer “appropriate protective measures,” including the possibility of credit-monitoring and identity-protection services.

“Those services will be based on the nature of the information exposed and the risks that were identified,” he said. “So individuals that are eligible to receive this protection will be informed directly and will be given a list of steps to follow in the very near future.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

author: EDRi
title: EU governments call it ‘simplification,’ but their Data Omnibus deal considerably weakens our rights
content:
EU governments have agreed on their position on the Digital Omnibus, retaining changes that threaten fundamental rights to privacy and data protection. With negotiations moving to the European Parliament, MEPs must reject the proposed weakening of GDPR safeguards for AI and pseudonymised data, protect individual rights, and defend ePrivacy against new tracking exemptions. Genuine simplification should make our rights easier to exercise and enforce, not give companies more freedom to exploit our data.

When the European Commission presented its Digital Omnibus in November 2025, it promised to simplify Europe’s digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. Yet, as EDRi and others warned at the time, a majority of its proposals, particularly those regarding General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy, went far beyond reducing administrative burdens. They are part and parcel of a broad deregulatory wave that is devouring most of our rights and safeguards in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and sovereignty.

On 21 October 2026, EU governments agreed on their negotiating position, which has timidly corrected some of the Commission’s most questionable choices, but has mainly endorsed changes that could make exploiting personal data easier while making abuses even harder to challenge.

The result is a deal that weakens important safeguards and makes redress harder. There is also little evidence that weakening these protections will improve Europe’s competitiveness. Some changes may instead reinforce the advantages of Big Tech companies that already control and abuse enormous volumes of information about us and the people around us.

One of the most worrying changes concerns the use of personal data for AI.

The Council retained a dedicated provision, Article 88bis (Article 88c in the Commission’s proposal), explicitly recognising the possibility of relying on the GDPR’s ‘legitimate interest’ legal basis to use personal data when developing or operating AI systems. Under the GDPR, companies can already use this legal basis in certain circumstances, provided they demonstrate a legitimate interest, prove that processing is necessary, and establish that people’s rights do not override that interest.

The Council clarifies that AI development does not automatically constitute a legitimate interest and that existing conditions still apply. But if legitimate interests can already justify certain AI processing, why introduce a special provision?

The concern is that Article 88bis could tilt the legitimate interest assessment in favour of AI companies, giving preferential treatment to a vaguely defined set of technologies primarily owned by autocracy-supporting billionaires, regardless of the exact purpose for which our personal data is going to be used. As recent legal analysis explains, this risks changing how the existing balancing test between legitimate interest and data protection safeguards is applied, even without formally removing its requirements.

Companies could invoke this legislative endorsement to justify extensive data reuse, even when people never reasonably expected their information to be used for AI training. And who benefits most? The same dominant Big Tech corporations that have spent decades accumulating the most intimate information about billions of people.

The Council also retains an exception for sensitive personal data appearing incidentally in AI datasets (proposed Article 9(2)(k) and 9(2)), including information revealing health, political opinions or religious beliefs. Companies must try to avoid collecting and, where collected, remove such data, but may retain them under safeguards when removal proves technically impossible or requires manifestly disproportionate effort.

These conditions might look important, but risk turning difficulties in cleaning datasets into a justification for retaining highly sensitive information. In opaque AI systems, verifying whether such data have genuinely been isolated may often be impossible. In this regard we should bear in mind that companies are mandated to protect our data and rights, and technical choices should not determine how far our fundamental rights extend.

There is some, even if limited, good news. The Council has rejected the Commission’s attempt to rewrite the GDPR’s definition of personal data in Article 4.1 and dropped its proposed Article 41a, which would have allowed the Commission to specify when certain …

author: Scott Timcke
title: The Stories Shaping Africa’s AI Future
content:
In the boardrooms of Addis Ababa and the tech hubs of Nairobi, a new worldmaking project is underway. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the central arenas where African states negotiate their position in an unequal global order. To speak of “AI in Africa” is not simply to describe the arrival of a technology, but to encounter a set of competing discursive frames through which political desires, developmental ambitions, ethical claims, and governance priorities are translated into technical agendas. As national strategies and regional protocols are rolled out, what comes into view is a struggle over how Africa is imagined within this machine age, and what kinds of futures that imagination makes thinkable.


These frames are not simply different ways of describing a new technology. They are competing scripts for what Africa is, what AI is for, and who ought to shape its future. Some cast the continent as a site of leapfrogging and renewal; others as a zone of exposure, extraction, sovereignty, moral repair, or improvised adaptation. Each brings some actors and possibilities into focus while pushing others to the margins. That is why the issue is not only what AI means for Africa, but what pictures of Africa are being called into view through AI discourse.


The first terrain is shaped by promise and protection. One of the most pervasive registers is promissory. In the African renaissance 2.0 frame, visible in the

AU Continental AI Strategy

, AI appears as a

leapfrogging

 device through which Africa can bypass the chokepoint of traditional industrialization and enter prosperity through technical modernization. Here, the ethical subject is the developmental state or planner charged with delivering growth, inclusion, and renewal. What comes into view is capacity, competitiveness, and beneficial transformation. What recedes from view are the historical and political-economic conditions that make acceleration so attractive in the first place: debt, infrastructural dependence, uneven ownership, and the possibility that AI may deepen rather than overcome inherited asymmetries.


Running alongside this is a protective register. In this vulnerability frame, Africa is not late but exposed to surveillance, bias, exclusion, and systems introduced into settings where safeguards are weak and redress is limited. As the

CIVICUS report on AI surveillance in Africa

 suggests, the issue is not only future risk but already existing forms of technologically mediated harm. The ethical subject here is the harm-bearing population—the data subject, precarious worker, surveilled citizen, and linguistically marginal user most likely to absorb the costs of badly governed AI. This frame is ethically indispensable because it foregrounds rights, harm, and institutional fragility, including the uneven but growing architecture of data protection on the continent. Its limit, however, is that it can cast Africa chiefly as a site to be protected rather than one from which technological futures are actively contested and shaped.


A second terrain is shaped by structure and sovereignty. Alongside these promissory and protective registers sits a more structural critique. In the

anti-colonial frame

, AI appears as a socio-technical order built through unequal material relations: not only data extraction, but also mineral supply chains, outsourced labor, environmental degradation, foreign-owned infrastructures, and asymmetrical control over the institutions that govern digital life. From this perspective, Africa is not outside the AI order looking in; it is already deeply inserted into it, though often on subordinated terms. The ethical subject is the dispossessed worker, community, or polity whose labor, resources, and data are drawn into AI systems while ownership and value are captured elsewhere. What becomes visible is the political economy of AI—an approach that makes it harder to sustain the comforting idea that Africa’s main problem is simply one of readiness or delayed entry. But the frame has limits. In foregrounding dispossession, it can flatten internal differentiation, externalize agency too completely, and become so totalizing that the uneven realities of negotiation and strategic inhabitation recede from view.


The sovereignty frame shifts the question from extraction to control: AI is cast as a problem of authority over infrastructure, procurement, standards, and rulemaking, a concern visible in South Africa’s

National …

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be …

title: The Dark Side of the “Machine God”: 5 Unsettling Truths About Big Tech’s AI Obsession
content:
Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

This concentration of power exposes a jarring central paradox: the exact same tech CEOs who claim AI will solve humanity’s greatest challenges simultaneously warn that the technology could trigger civilizational extinction, openly describing their pursuit as “summoning the demon.” Rather than pausing development, these executives have accelerated an apocalyptic arms race to build ultra-powerful systems, framing themselves as indispensable guardians of human survival.

To understand where artificial intelligence is truly taking society, we must look past corporate marketing and examine the underlying worldviews, historical lineages, and material harms driving the tech elite. Moving beyond superficial consumer hype reveals how a toxic mix of fringe ideologies, extractive labor practices, and authoritarian state alliances is steering Silicon Valley toward what critical theorists and legal scholars call “techno-fascism.”

To make sense of Silicon Valley’s relentless drive toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), one must understand the bizarre ideological framework shaping its leaders. Coined by philosopher Emile Torres and computer scientist Timnit Gebru, the acronym TESCREAL encapsulates a bundle of tightly interwoven worldviews: Transhumanism, Extropianism, Singularitarianism, Cosmism, Rationalism, Effective Altruism, and Longtermism.

Dr. Emile Torres highlights a critical historical truth at the heart of this ideology: transhumanism is fundamentally “eugenics on steroids.” Unlike nineteenth-century eugenics, which sought merely to optimize the existing human species through selective breeding, transhumanism seeks to use radical technology to completely replace and transcend humanity, engineering an entirely new posthuman species. Within Silicon Valley AI circles, this hypothetical superintelligence is explicitly referred to as a “Machine God.” Tech CEOs effectively act as high priests, competing to bring an all-knowing digital deity into physical existence.

This radical ideology shapes corporate roadmaps in concrete, disturbing ways:

Sam Altman (OpenAI): In a blog post titled “The Merge,” Altman argued that AI surpassing human intellect is inevitable, framing un-merged human beings as a temporary “biological bootloader” for digital intelligence that will ultimately fade into an evolutionary side-branch. Altman notably paid $10,000 to join a brain-uploading waitlist with Nectome and co-founded a brain-computer interface venture to facilitate digital integration.

Ray Kurzweil & Demis Hassabis (DeepMind): Representing Extropianism and Singularitarianism, Kurzweil champions the doctrine of living long enough to achieve digital immortality, targeting a self-improving “singularity” by 2032. Hassabis, DeepMind’s co-founder, operates under a similar singularitarian impulse to engineer self-evolving intellect.

Eliezer Yudkowsky (Rationalism): A foundational figure in modern rationalist thought who famously posited a utilitarian moral calculation arguing that forcing a single person to endure 50 years of relentless torture is ethically preferable to an unfathomable number of people experiencing the mild inconvenience of a speck of dust in their eye.

author: Nolan Higdon
title: AI Techno-Utopianism and Doomsday Threats Distract From Big Tech’s Current Harms
content:
The industry uses fantasies of technological dominance to paper over financial shortcomings and demands for regulation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

During a September 2026 visit to Ireland, President Donald Trump declared, “We’re leading China in AI [artificial intelligence]. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” His remarks arrived after months of calls from the public and tech industry insiders to slow AI development. These concerns were triggered by revelations that foundational models from Anthropic, Gemini, Meta, and OpenAI had bypassed safety protocols, accessed networks without authorization, and carried out illicit intrusions. These revelations fueled public panic that tech firms had created superintelligence — an AI exceeding human capability that posed an existential threat to humanity — even though no such breakthrough had actually been achieved.

Public concern intensified in October 2026 when cybersecurity firm Wiz revealed it had used AI tools from Google and OpenAI to identify critical security flaws in PHP: the programming language powering roughly 70% of the web. Although developers quickly released a patch, once the vulnerability was made public hacking attempts surged. In response, the governments of the Netherlands, France, Denmark, and Finland temporarily took several official websites offline.

Widespread panic over AI yielded little legislative action, as lawmakers refused to regulate or tax the industry out of fear that doing so would handicap domestic innovation and yield ground to China. However, the core threat to human existence lies neither in a lost geopolitical race nor in muted technological growth, but rather in the ubiquitous rollout of non-autonomous systems falsely hailed as artificial intelligence.

Big Tech was built on state-funded innovation, with core technologies like the internet, Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and touchscreen displays originating in public institutions. Yet during the deregulation and privatization waves of the 1980s and 1990s, lawmakers sheltered these emerging tech monopolies through minimal taxation and oversight. Most notable was Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which insulates platforms from liability for content posted by third parties. Without this protection, social media as we know it would cease to exist. Section 230 absolves tech firms of responsibility for architectures that foster misinformation, even as research confirms that the platforms themselves, not just user posts, are responsible for accelerating the spread of falsehoods over truth.

Lawmakers’ opposition to regulation is rooted in techno-utopianism, the ideological premise that technological progress inherently benefits society. Lawmakers operated under the assumption that any taxation or regulatory oversight would stifle innovation and ultimately harm consumers. Indeed, in 1997, then-President Bill Clinton wrote in an Executive Order “governments attempts to establish technical standards to govern the Internet would only risk inhibiting technological innovation.”

Without meaningful regulation, Big Tech rapidly consolidated into lucrative monopolies — collectively known as FAANG (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, and Google) or GAMMA (Google (Alphabet), Apple, Meta (formerly Facebook), Microsoft, and Amazon) conglomerates. Their vast wealth is powered by surveillance capitalism: an economic model that treats human experience as free raw material to be extracted, analyzed, and commercialized. Under this economic order, data is systematically mined through “smart” devices — where “smart” is merely a euphemism for active, continuous monitoring, including the collection of biometric data. This wholesale erosion of privacy has proven extraordinarily lucrative for Big Tech. By feeding this extracted data into algorithms, these firms build detailed psychographic profiles on users and sell the insights to insurance companies determining coverage premiums, employers screening job applicants, and law enforcement agencies evaluating security threats.

Absent meaningful government oversight, Big Tech has been left to police itself. Take the moral panic over fake news after the 2016 Presidential Election, when politicians warned that election meddling in the form of disinformation online was harming a defining feature of the U …

author: Amina Khan
title: EU transforms Frontex into a high-tech deportation command centre
content:
Yesterday, 27 October 2026, the European Commission tabled a new Regulation for Frontex, the EU’s border agency, expanding its powers and refocusing its mandate on deportations, preventing arrivals, and surveillance beyond EU territories and into social media. This would effectively turn Frontex into the EU’s deportation agency, equivalent of ICE in the United States.

At the centre of this reform is a budget that would almost double to nearly €12 billion for 2028–2034, leading to a massive expansion of the EU security and surveillance industrial complex. Frontex will test and deploy new technology to repress migrants, funnelling billions of taxpayer money to surveillance, security and defence contractors. EU’s hostile border security regime has for years produced systemic and massive human rights violations of migrants, refugees and racialised people, and those who stand in solidarity with them. This proposal will accelerate that.

Frontex as an ICE-style deportation enforcement agency

The proposal operationalises the recently adopted Deportations Regulation and deepens Frontex’s position as the central actor of a Europe-wide deportation machine. This will make the agency responsible for collecting and analysing data from Member States in order to “predict” deportation needs, and allocating resources to them. Frontex will now have a “Deportation Coordination Centre” that is expected to act at all stages of the deportation procedure, from detecting and identifying people that may be expulsed, booking or arranging flights and escorts, to monitoring their “reintegration” in the destination country.

Alarmingly, it expands Frontex’s powers to deport outside of the EU’s borders. Based on a simple status agreement, Frontex will be able to deport people from one third country to another, with the aim of preventing people from even reaching the EU. This will likely mean sharing sensitive data with third countries and countries of origin, where individuals may be at risk of persecution or harm.

The Frontex mandate reform comes in a package with a proposal to digitalise the management of deportation cases. The border control agency is given a key role in the harmonised technical design of EU and national digital systems, to exchange data on deportations, including sensitive data transfers to third countries (biometric data, travel documents and history, grounds for deportation, health data, etc.), and automate certain steps of the procedure, such as adding deportation orders in the Schengen Information System (SIS) to detect people.

Increased data processing and content policing

With this reform, Frontex’s practice of “debriefing interviews” is codified, particularly during the screening procedure introduced by the Migration Pact. The agency conducts these covert “voluntary” interrogations of people immediately after they disembark or cross the border. During these interviews, the agency extracts data from migrants deemed to be “suspects” of “cross-border crime”, without the possibility for migrants to seek legal counsel. Debriefing interviews have been rightfully criticised for their absence of fundamental rights monitoring and their unfairness as they take place when a person is detained and lacks privacy.

A new “Online Monitoring and Response Centre” will also surveil social media platforms to identify “suspicious behaviours or trends” in people’s movements at the EU borders, and before that, in the countries of origin and transit. Aggregated data collected online will be fed into Frontex’s “risk analysis” to guide border forces’ deployment and reaction. Social media monitoring was already declared as carrying high-risk for violating the fundamental rights of people affected, and was banned by the European Data Protection Supervisor in 2019 when first implemented by the EU Agency for Asylum.

Frontex will also seek designation as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act (DSA), allowing the agency to report pieces of online content to platforms for removal, effectively giving the agency extrajudicial powers to police the internet. It may also recommend national authorities to issue binding take-down notices. Frontex depriving people from finding legal support, sharing their stories or expressing solidarity is undoubtedly a serious infringement of freedom of expression.

All information collected during debriefings and online monitoring activities will contribute to Frontex’s border surveillance intelligence …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Cyberlibel complaints vs journalists strengthen calls to decriminalize libel
content:
The criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Libel complaints were recently filed against journalists and media company executives. For a journalists’ group, these validate the previous calls to decriminalize libel.

The GMA chapter of the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) stressed that libel laws silence journalism. “[C]riminalizing speech only undermines the public’s fundamental right to know,” the chapter said in a statement.

Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte filed libel and cyberlibel complaints against GMA executives and broadcast journalists which stemmed from the network’s report about alleged cash deliveries to the Dutertes claimed by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Duterte filed the complaint before the Davao City Prosecutor’s Office on October 23, more than two weeks after his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, made a joke about filing a multimillion-peso libel case against GMA Network. Her remarks happened during a press conference on October 6 while reading her affidavit which answers Gracioso’s claims.

Among the respondents were GMA executives Felipe Gozon and Gilberto Duavit, as well as journalists Mel Tiangco, Vicki Morales, Emil Sumangil, Darlene Cay, Marvin Parado, Joel San Luis, and other unidentified individuals.

In a statement released on October 23, the TV network said that they have not yet received the complaints.

Gracioso and National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) director Melvin Matibag were also named as respondents.

Meanwhile, veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on October 24 over a cyberlibel complaint reportedly filed by Mans Carpio, Sara’s husband. He was unaware of the complaint, according to his legal counsel. He was released on bail on the same day.

NUJP has been campaigning for the decriminalization of libel, echoing the views of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Committee that the criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Right(s) Up: Why journalists and advocates push for decriminalization of libel

On September 18, NUJP released its policy review on libel laws, stating that the high court has already identified the problem of these laws but reform requires legislation. The review, to name a few, cited Justice Marvic Leonen’s opinion in Disini, Jr. v. Secretary of Justice which stated that libel was unconstitutional as penal sanctions impose “an invidious chilling effect.”

It added that removing jail time alone, as proposed by some legislators, is not decriminalization because of limitations of a fine-only regime, saying that if the accused cannot pay, subsidiary imprisonment may follow.

The review cited the data obtained from the Office of Cybercrime of the Department of Justice (DOJ), indicating that 3,770 cyberlibel cases had been filed, as of May 2022, since the enactment of the Cybercrime Prevention Act. More than 2,500 cases remained pending in courts and before the prosecution level. There were already 12 convictions.

In the 2023 study by NUJP, 61.5% of the libel cases against 50 journalists from 2021 to 2023 were filed by politicians.

ML Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima said that filing a libel suit against journalists and media workers for doing their job sends a “chilling message” to other members of the press. Parties being accused can just respond to the allegations, she wrote in a Facebook post.

Under the Journalist’s Code of Ethics approved by media groups, journalists shall recognize the duty to air the other side and the duty to correct substantive errors promptly.

“Contrary to allegations of malice or unverified reporting, the report went through standard, multi-layered editorial and legal verification procedures,” the NUJP GMA Chapter said. “The team conducted due diligence—verifying information through official sources, law enforcement documents, and background checks—and obtained proper clearance from network leadership and legal counsel before airing the story.”

In the subject report, the reporter, Cay, and anchor Tiangco mentioned that they were trying to get the comments of the people implicated by Gracioso, including the Dutertes, but they did not receive a response when the report was aired …

title: Osman: Over 238 children killed or injured in military attacks in Bashur over the past 30 years
content:
Kameran Osman, a member of the Community Peacemaker Teams (CPT), spoke at a panel titled “Being a Victim of War, Crisis and Displacement During Childhood”, held as part of the International Scientific Conference on Children and Youth at the University of Sulaymaniyah (Silêmani).


Speaking about the impact of war on children, Osman shared new data. He said that more than 238 children have been killed or injured in military attacks by the Turkish and Iranian armies in the Kurdistan Region over the past 30 years. He emphasised that the effects of war on children are not limited to physical casualties.


He noted that children displaced by war often lose or see their ties weakened with the countries, communities and lands where they live. Osman also highlighted how war deeply affects children's mental health, identity, education, language and dignity.


People in border villages still wake up to the sound of bombs


Osman recalled that schools and educational institutions in villages have also been targeted in military attacks by the Turkish army and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), stating that children's safety has been disregarded.


He pointed out that international and regional organisations working with children tend to focus on urban centres, while children living in border villages are excluded from these initiatives and left without their basic needs being met. He added: “Children's safety has been neglected. Most international and regional organisations focus primarily on children in towns, districts and cities. As a result, they cannot reach children in border villages or meet their needs.”


Osman said that the perception that there is no active war in Kurdistan does not reflect reality, explaining that war continues to be part of everyday life in border regions. He added: “There is a perception that there is currently no active war in Kurdistan. However, this perception is completely wrong. War remains part of the daily lives of people and children in Kurdistan's border villages. We don't have to look very far: early this morning, people and children in villages around Xelifan woke up to the sound of two drone attacks on their area.”

title: K. C. Sinclair - Proudhon, Slavery, and the American Civil War
content:
Author

: K. C. Sinclair

Title

: Proudhon, Slavery, and the American Civil War

Date

: November 2026

Source

: Retrieved on November 5, 2026 from

historykeepshappening.wordpress.com


 In a passing remark made by the renowned historian of anarchism, Paul Avrich, in his 1988 book,

Anarchist Portraits

 (pg.20), we are told that the infamous French anarchist, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, did not support the side of the North (otherwise known as the Union) in the American Civil War.


 Avrich, uncharacteristically, provided no source for this, as if it was already common knowledge, neglecting to clarify whether Proudhon opposed both sides of the war, or perhaps worse, supported the South. He also left us hanging as to whether he’d gleaned this information from Proudhon’s own words in French, from secondary sources in English, or from both. Not much of Proudhon’s work had been translated into English at the time, but perhaps Avrich accessed the French documentation. The subject in the chapter in question was not Proudhon but instead a passionate supporter of the North, the Russian anarchist Mikhail Bakunin, and Proudhon was only mentioned as a point of contrast, so perhaps this is the simplest explanation for Avrich’s failure to provide a citation.


 Whether Avrich knew it or not, the subject of Proudhon’s position on the war had already been addressed by the presumably non-anarchist musician and writer, Thomas A. Sancton, in his 1979 academic journal article,

The Myth of French Worker Support


for the North in the American Civil War

.

 Decades later, in 2021, Sancton greatly expanded that article with his book,

Sweet Land of Liberty: America in the Mind of the French Left, 1848-1871

.


 In the 1979 article, Sancton referenced both published works and private letters of Proudhon’s in order to show that if the French anarchist had opposed both sides of the war, for different reasons, he still more strongly opposed the North than the South. Sancton, unfortunately quoted Proudhon out of chronological order and without translation, so I have rearranged and translated those quotes for the purposes of this article.


 Proudhon, in a September 1862 letter to Gustave Chaudey asked, “we have no faith in the North’s philanthropy; we do not accept that the Federal Constitution prevents secession; …. what’s more, the forces of the North are suffering one setback after another; England, Belgium, and France — consumed by poverty — call for cotton; and if the imperial [French] government, by a stroke of good luck links the two issues of Mexico and the Confederates, restoring relations between Europe and New Orleans, will you still attack it on that front?”


 Proudhon refers here to the

Second Franco-Mexican War

. Imperialist France had invaded Mexico in early 1862, a few months after the American Civil War began.


 Sancton doesn’t provide his own analysis of this particular quote beyond noting that it proves that Proudhon’s anti-Yankee sentiment was not isolated to his published works. But, for our part, we can note that Proudhon, for an anarchist, sounds oddly defensive about both the government of the American secessionists and that of his own French Empire, particularly given that the defense of slavery was very much the South’s reason for seccession.


 Proudhon, in a letter to (Lucien?) Jottrand in October of 1864, wrote, “I am not, I admit, a friend of the Anglo-Saxons, and I believe that few people are fond of them. Also, I deplored the policy of our emperor, who could have, if he had wanted… obtained from the South the promise of emancipation for the blacks, and intervening then as an interested party in the present war, would have, at the time I am writing to you, brought those in the North to their senses.”


 Again, Sancton does not comment on the specifics of Proudhon’s words here, only elaborating to the extent of pointing out that Proudhon had some influence on the French labour movement, even if he was not its official spokesman. We, on the other hand, can note that Proudhon’s opposition to the North is clearly stronger than his opposition to the South, and that he was strangely naive about the South’s willingness to part with slavery.


 In his 1865 book,

On the Political Capacity of the Working Classes

,

 Proudhon even commented publicly on the war. Sancton uses an extended quotation from that book, the translation here being taken from the one done by Shawn P. Wilbur, while the truncations are …

author: Eibhlin Priestley
title: After the Revolution, Before the War: Tracing Khartoum’s Syrian Community
content:
On 18 March 2023, Arwa Ahmed, an architect, and photographer of the Sudanese revolution, and I stood chatting in the shade of the Grand Hotel on Nile Street in Khartoum. We had spent the morning jumping in and out of Arwa’s white Hyundai photographing buildings of historic significance for the Syrian community. The quiet of the afternoon was broken as ten trucks, each holding dozens of men in civilian dress drove past us at speed. It was an unusual sight, one that we commented on at the time. Less than a month later, we would realise these men were fighters from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) bussed into Khartoum to battle the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) unleashing hell on the people of Sudan on 15 April 2023. The country has since suffered what UNHCR has described as the most devastating humanitarian and displacement crisis in the world, largely out of sight of media attention.


Entrance to the Grand Hotel, Nile Street, a popular choice for Syrian weddings in the 1950s and 1960s. Photo by Arwa Ahmed.


Eighteen months into my History PhD, I arrived in Khartoum in March 2023 to meet and interview members of the Syrian community whose grandparents or great-grandparents arrived in Sudan from Greater Syria (today’s Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Jordan) at the turn of the twentieth century. I was warmly welcomed into homes with cooling glasses of

karkade

 (hibiscus tea) and

gungulaise

 (baobab juice) served alongside bowls of peanuts and salted plaited cheese before settling into long conversations about multi-generational family histories and the changing fortunes of the community over time.


Shrine to the Virgin Mary at the Melkite Catholic Church on Jumhuriya Street. The church was a central social, cultural, and religious hub until the community’s departure in April 2023. Photo by Arwa Ahmed.


The Syrians were one of several migrant communities – Greek, Italian, Armenian, Jewish – whose prosperity in the early and mid-20

th

 century was underpinned by their commercial activities. The earliest group of Syrians who settled in Sudan in the 1870s were merchants, mostly hailing from Aleppo, primarily operating in interregional trade of goods such as elephant tusks, ostrich feathers, leather, Arabic gum, and Syrian cotton and silk. The 1900s saw a new wave of Syrian migration to the newly created Anglo-Egyptian Condominium of Sudan, driven by anti-Christian persecution, economic opportunities, and government recruitment of physicians and administrators (principally from the Syrian Protestant College, now the American University of Beirut). One of these graduates was Nicola Malouf who opened a pharmacy and clinic on Mek Nimr Avenue in early 1920s next door to the family home. Within the same decade, he acquired substantial farmland outside Khartoum which he developed into a large-scale agricultural enterprise.


Norma Kfouri in her home in Khartoum. Photo by Arwa Ahmed.


By the 1950s, businessmen from the Syrian community such as Nicola Malouf occupied a central role in the Sudanese economy. They were among the nation’s leading industrialists, owning factories specialising in weaving, knitting, and cigarette and soap production, and were active in export trade, raw material extraction, and agricultural and dairy enterprises. My first meeting in Khartoum was with Norma Kfouri, his daughter, the longest standing member of the community. Described to me at a party as ‘Khartoum’s most important ambassador’ given the central role she played in city’s social milieu, she led a vibrant social life heading up a women’s charitable foundation, attending philanthropic events and parties, and hosting gatherings at her pink and yellow villa on the Nile.


The 1950s and 1960s are remembered as the ‘golden years’ when the Syrian community numbered several hundred families and concentrated itself in the capital. A significant number of women interviewed described ‘living like queens’ in this period, facilitated in large part by Sudanese domestic workers who cleaned and maintained homes, shopped and helped prepare meals, and cared for their children.


Mek Nimr Street, home to a number of Syrian families in the 1950s. Photo by Arwa Ahmed.


The

Nadi

 (the Syrian club), churches, and schools were repeatedly mentioned as institutions which forged enduring friendships and a strong sense of identity as the ‘Syrians of Sudan’ which continues to bind the community, despite its dispersal today. The

Nadi

 was the …

author: labor4pal
title: A fightback is building as crackdown deepens against civil liberties (Workers’ Voice)
content:
Dozens of activists are accused by the federal government of contributing to bogus “criminal conspiracies.” In Minnesota, two separate conspiracy cases accuse 54 people of participating in illegal conspiracies for participating in protest and journalistic activities. The Minnesota 15, Righteous 39, Michigan 8 (now 12), Spokane 3, and Prairieland Defendants are the most well known cases in the ongoing crackdown. All of these cases are attacks on organized labor.

The California Faculty Association and the Graduate Employee Organization at University of Michigan (GEO-AFT 3550) are facing frontal attacks on their unions by the right-wing press and FBI. Doctored video of a CFA meeting was leaked to Trump booster Bari Weiss’s Free Press in an attempt to scandalize the union with false accusations of antisemitism. The Department of Justice first charged GEO President Hiab Teshome with felonious financial crimes. Those bogus charges were dropped the same day that a grand jury subpoenaed GEO’s books, including all member lists, meeting minutes, and financial records. The union is fighting to retain basic privacy rights.

Fueled by National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, U.S. intelligence and police apparatuses are being explicitly targeted at anyone standing for basic democratic rights, immigrant communities, and racial justice. As the world drifts closer to major inter-imperialist conflict and expanding zones of overt imperialist military occupation takes hold in the semi-colonies, Western imperialisms are tightening restrictions on protest, speech, and organizing for progressive movements.

While there are many additional cases of “lawfare” and anti-protest policing, it is worth taking a moment to review two of the cases mentioned above to understand the tactics and scope of the current crackdown.

Around two dozen protesters held a noise demonstration on July 4, 2025, outside of the Prairieland Detention Center in Texas. As the protest was winding down and many of the participants had left, Alvarado Police Officer Thomas Gross sped onto the scene and almost immediately aimed his gun at a demonstrator moving away from him. Video evidence indicates that Gross discharged his weapon, something that would appear to have been covered up by the judge and prosecutors.

In response to seeing a potentially lethal attack on a protester, Marine Corps veteran Benjamin “Champagne” Song let out a warning shot into the ground away from the officers. Gross went to the hospital for superficial wounds that the government alleges resulted from being shot by Song, but video evidence released after sentencing indicates Gross was likely hit by shrapnel produced from his own weapon’s discharge.

Using the presence of guns and defensive action of Song as pretext, 22 people were ultimately indicted as part of an alleged conspiracy to attack cops and carry out an armed prison break. One person, Daniel “Des” Rolando Sanchez Estrada, was not at the protest at all. Des was convicted for “corruptly concealing a document or record” and sentenced to 30 years for possessing legally protected political materials.

After arrests, pressure and legal sabotage was mounted by the judicial system against the defendants. Many were initially held in solitary confinement, with one reporting that human feces coated their cell. U.S. District Judge Mark Pittman blocked the defendants from retaining a private attorney, meaning they had to use public defenders. Song’s legal team was not allowed to make an argument that the warning shot was taken in self-defense. Eight defendants became cooperating witnesses, providing coerced testimony to validate the government’s made-up conspiracy theories.

Before the trial even began, the deck was stacked against non-cooperating defendants. In an explicit “warning” to the left, Judge Pittman laid down ridiculously high sentences of between 30-100 years to non-cooperating defendants.

From the war on drugs to the war on speech: Minnesota 15

The Minnesota 15 are 15 activists accused of a “conspiracy to impede or attack federal agents.” The majority are current or recent union members and all are community activists. They are not accused of participating in or coordinating any acts of violence. Instead, the original 92-page indictment against them lists “evidence” including participating in rapid response group chats, protests, and mutual aid activities. author: Mag
title: Militarisierung der Hochschulen und Zivilklauselbewegung
content:
Dossier


Die Initiative „Hochschulen für den Frieden – Ja zur Zivilklausel“ hat sich im Mai 2011 gegründet. In ihr setzen sich Gewerkschaften, Studierenden- und Wissenschafts- sowie Friedensorganisationen für zivile Hochschulen als Ort für Studien, Lehre und Forschung ein, in denen sinnvolle Beiträge zur friedlichen Lösung der Probleme und Konflikte dieser Welt geleistet werden. Die verstärkte Ausbreitung militärischer Forschung und Lehre an Universitäten trägt nicht zum Wohle der Menschen bei. Die Initiative kämpft für Hochschulen, die in Wissenschaft, Forschung und Lehre ausschließlich dem Frieden verbunden sind. Dazu bedarf es einer breiten Diskussion um die gesellschaftliche Verantwortung der Wissenschaft. Siehe alle Informationen über die bundesweite Zivilklauselbewegung auf der

Homepage der Initiative „Hochschulen für den Frieden – Ja zur Zivilklausel“


  und hier dazu:


Trotz Protesten: „Werteklausel“ löst an der Uni Kassel die Zivilklausel ab und hält die Hochschulleitung nicht von Strafanzeige und Polizeigewalt bei der Räumung des besetzten Hörsaals ab


Beschäftigteninitiative verurteilt gewaltsame Räumung friedlicher Studierendenproteste


„

Gestern stimmte der Senat der Uni Kassel für die Abschaffung der Zivilklausel. Die Studierenden hatten seit Monaten Kritik am intransparenten und wenig repräsentativen Verfahren geäußert. In einer studentischen Urabstimmung mit hoher Wahlbeteiligung stimmten 82% für den Erhalt der Zivilklausel. Ihr Votum wurde nicht gehört. Wir widersprechen der Darstellung der Hochschulleitung, dass es sich bei der Neufassung um einen Kompromiss handelt. Die Zivilklausel der Universität existiert nicht mehr. Künftig sind militärische Forschung und Lehre hier möglich.


Als Protest besetzten darauf etwa Hundert Studierende einen Hörsaal im Campus Center. Erst nach Stunden wurde den Studierenden Wasser und Essen zugänglich gemacht, weitere Stunden später durften sie schließlich die Toiletten benutzen. Die Besetzung und die angemeldete Versammlung vor dem Hörsaalgebäude wurden schließlich in der Nacht zum 05.11.2026 gewaltsam von der Polizei auf Anordnung der Universitätsleitung geräumt. Nachdrücklich kritisieren wir dies als Ausdruck der Zunahme an Versicherheitlichung und autoritären Praktiken in der Hochschule.


Anil Shah von der Initiative Zivile Uni Kassel: „Wir verurteilen das Vorgehen der Hochschulleitung und die daraus folgende Eskalation aufs Schärfste.


Hörsaalbesetzungen zählen zum zivilen Ungehorsam und sind seit Jahrzehnten Teil studentischer Protestkultur.“ Statt den Studierenden Raum zu geben für selbst organisierte Informationsveranstaltungen, Vorträge und Diskussionen, entschied sich das Präsidium für einen Polizeieinsatz und die Eskalation der Lage. Vermittlungsversuche von Lehrenden wurden größtenteils abgelehnt.


Stefan Stache, Senator an der Universität, gestern selbst vor Ort und als Schlichter im Campus Center, beurteilt die Situation so: „Der Einsatz der Polizei war unnötig und schädlich für die demokratische Kultur der Universität. Zuvorderst müssen nun die Anzeigen wegen Hausfriedensbruchs von der Universitätsleitung zurückgezogen werden. Es bedarf dringend einer Sondersitzung des Senats, um die Vorgänge aufzuarbeiten. Darüber hinaus brauchen wir eine Debatte über Demokratie an Hochschulen und eine Reform der Hochschulverfassung.

““

Pressemitteilung von ‘Zivile Uni Kassel’ vom 5.11.2026

 


Polizei räumt Hörsaal nach Protesten an der Uni Kassel

In Kassel protestieren Studenten gegen eine mögliche Zusammenarbeit mit Rüstungsfirmen. Gegen 47 Studenten, die einen Hörsaal besetzt haben, wird ermittelt.


Die Polizei hat einen von protestierenden Studenten besetzten Hörsaal der Universität Kassel geräumt. Am Mittwochabend hielten sich laut einem Polizeisprecher etwa 40 bis 50 Personen in dem Hörsaal auf und verließen ihn auch in der Nacht nicht. Die Protestierenden seien aus dem Hörsaal herausgetragen worden und hätten dabei »teils erheblichen Widerstand« geleistet, teilte die Polizei mit. »Nach derzeitigem Kenntnisstand wurden bei den Einsatzmaßnahmen sechs Polizeibeamte leicht verletzt.« Gegen drei Personen »aus dem Kreis der Besatzer« seien Strafanzeigen wegen tätlichen Angriffs auf Vollstreckungsbeamte erstattet worden, gegen 47 Personen werde wegen Hausfriedensbruchs und Verstoßes gegen das Hessische Versammlungsfreiheitsgesetz ermittelt. title: Rural communities face continuing violence amid militarization
content:
Photo by Viggo Sarmago/Bulatlat

Under the blazing sun in front Camp Aguinaldo, palay hats stood out together with the line of banners. It was not a celebration for peasants — but a plea to end militarization, violence, and to serve justice for Negros 19 killed in Toboso, Negros Occidental on April 19, 2026.

Farmers and fisherfolk play a vital role in sustaining the nation’s food security and economy, yet they are the ones who struggle the most to survive.

Pamalakaya’s National Vice Chairperson Ronnel Arambulo stated in his speech during the fourth day of peasant month protest on October 19, that the administration does not aim to protect the life and rights of the people, farmers, and fisherfolk, but to protect the ruling class, the foreigners, and the people in power for their own personal interest.

Fisherfolks are also facing harassment that disrupts their lives. According to Arambulo, there are recent reports of intimidation in Binangonan, Rizal, where fisherfolk were called by Maritime Police to appear at the municipal hall. They were later summoned to renounce and abandon Pamalakaya.

This kind of intimidation is not confined to the province of Rizal, as similar deployments have also been reported in other regions.

Nida Barcenas from Karapatan-Bicol stated that the 9th Infantry “Spear” Division of Philippine Army or at least ten battalions of men in uniform were scattered around six provinces in Bicol region.

During the “Stakeholder and Media Fellowship Night: Episode 1 – Kaakibat sa Kapayapaan,” event of 9th Infantry Division held on April 18, 2026 at Camp Elias Angeles, Maj. Gen. Aldwine I. Almase recognized the efforts of national agencies, local government units, media personalities, and other stakeholders in countering alleged local terrorist activities to ensure peace and safety in the Bicol region.

For Karapatan-Bicol , however, these achievements actually meant human rights abuses against farmers communities. As of March 2026, Karapatan has recorded 46 political prisoners in Bicol — 9 of them are women, with 22 arrested under Marcos Jr. administration. In his four year term in the government, two enforced disappearances and 38 extrajudicial killings have also been documented.

Red-tagging, violence, and land grabbing continue to disrupt the lives of Bicolanos, Barcenas said.

“To this day, residents of Masbate continue to appeal for help amid alleged land grabbing by Governor Kho. Farmers are being driven off their lands, and those who resist are killed and red-tagged as NPAs, [New People’s Army]” Barcenas said.

The issue involving Governor Antonio Kho is also part of the problem regarding land dispute over the Pecson Estate in Cawayan, Masbate. Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) stated that Kho took over a portion of 1,807-hectare estate, forcing more than 100 farmers off the lands they have cultivated for years.

The agrarian conflict has also been associated with reports of killing involving peasants in Cawayan. A human rights report from Karapatan revealed cases including killings of farmers named Pancho Versaga and Renard Remulta on October 28, 2022 in Sitio Villaluna, Barangay Itom-Bato, Cawayan. These two were among more than 100 farmers tilling a 450-hectare portion of the Pecson Estate within land seized by Kho in Masbate.

Karapatan has declared Masbate as Bicol’s killing fields due to an increasing number of victims who had been killed under Marcos Jr. regime’s counter-insurgency war on the province.

One of the heinous cases was the killing of a farmer couple Aimee and Jover Villegas, a two-hectare land caretaker. The military said that the couple died under armed encounters. However, their injuries contradict this claim as Aimee’s throat, chin, and neck had been slashed, while Jover sustained gunshot wounds in the nape and back.

Echoing this concern, Grace Nabian from Amihan-Negros called for a stop to the militarization in rural communities.

She questioned killings, abduction, and threats against farmers, stressing that land reform, and access to quality education for their children are what they need.

She also pressed his demand to hold Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) accountable for various deaths in their land including Negros 19.

author: hsa_oryx
title: SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!
content:
Oh, wait… sorry. The Judge already did that in court.


John ‘Pinocchio’ Henty’s case ends in acquittal

.


Thank you to


South Suffolk Hunt Sabs


for this guest article.


A court case brought by former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty against a hunt saboteur has ended in a resounding victory for the defence, with the saboteur found NOT GUILTY.


John Henty outside court.


Following allegations made to police, former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty pursued a prosecution alleging abusive and threatening behaviour under Section 5 of the Public Order Act. The case followed an incident on a quiet country lane in which Henty pursued the hunt saboteurs’ vehicle, blocked it in, approached it and attempted to provoke a reaction.


What followed was a lengthy legal process based on Henty’s account of events. However, when his evidence was examined in court, serious questions arose about the credibility of that account and whether the alleged behaviour actually amounted to a criminal offence.


A case that should never have reached court?


The Judge was highly critical of the way the case had been handled by the CPS and the police officers involved, making clear that the alleged actions did not meet the legal threshold required for a criminal offence.


Both the prosecution and the defence barrister sought to discontinue the case on more than one occasion. The case was nevertheless directed to proceed. The circumstances surrounding that decision raise serious questions about why so much time and public money were spent pursuing a prosecution that ultimately failed.


Former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty is now at The Ludlow Hunt.


The evidence tells a different story


Henty submitted two video clips, recorded by himself, which were played in court. The footage showed Henty pulling his vehicle alongside the hunt saboteurs’ Land Rover, getting out of his own accord and filming the encounter.


Our saboteur told Henty to ‘f*ck off’ before closing the vehicle door. Rather than disengaging, Henty continued filming and engaging with the occupants. Despite claiming under oath that he had been alarmed and distressed, the circumstances captured on his own footage told a different story.


The prosecution was unable to produce further evidence demonstrating that Henty had experienced the alarm or distress alleged.


Henty spun a yarn of lies that should never have made it to court.


The judge’s conclusion


Having heard Henty’s evidence under cross-examination and considered the footage and relevant law, the Judge concluded that:


Henty had parked his vehicle alongside the saboteurs’ vehicle of his own accord.


He had got out of his vehicle voluntarily.


He had chosen to film the encounter.


He had continued the interaction of his own accord.


He had not contacted the police immediately, instead reporting the incident to 101 approximately two hours later.


These circumstances were central to the Judge’s assessment of Henty’s claim that he had experienced fear, alarm and distress. Following Henty’s evidence and cross-examination by the prosecution and defence, the case concluded without our hunt saboteur needing to take the stand.


The verdict

:

Not guilty. Acquitted.


After all the allegations, the police involvement, the CPS proceedings and the considerable expenditure of public resources, the case ended in an acquittal. A considerable amount of time, money and public resources had been spent pursuing this matter, only for the court to reach a conclusion that raises serious questions about why the prosecution was pursued in the first place.


Hunt saboteurs will not be intimidated out of exposing illegal hunting. And they will not be silenced by allegations that cannot withstand scrutiny in court.


The South Suffolk One stands vindicated.


SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!


South Suffolk Hunt Sabs remain steadfast and will not be intimidated or silenced.


Show some support to

South Suffolk Hunt Sabs.

SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!

 appeared first on

Hunt Saboteurs Association

.
