SAMHAIN. Pronounced “sow-ween” or “sow-ain”, the term is the old Gaelic name for this time of year. Today it is better known as Hallowe’en, All Hallows Day, All Saints’ Day, and All Souls’ Day, and covers the time between October 31 to November 2 inclusive.

It is a lot more than going from door to door begging for candy, although this enjoyable modern ritual also has its place, binding us to our ancestors’ other children (especially those who still are children!).

But it goes much further than that.

This week, I thought I would simply open a Samhain Open Memorial Thread amongst the Anti-Capitalist Meetup community. On this day, when the ancient, pre-Christian Lore of the Celtic peoples of Western Europe teaches that the Veil between the living and our dead Ancestors is thinnest, it is appropriate to bring those Ancestors to remembrance by name that our memories of them and our debts to them may live on. Let us remember them, love them, revere them, and give them our gratitude in Solidarity for what their lives have given us.

I thank ZhenRen for his contributions to our Diary of two weeks ago, which I have taken the liberty of adapting to this week’s Diary by making a very small set of textual changes to expand the poetry to cover all of our Ancestors instead of just one.

From this Comment by ZhenRen, I open our Memorial this evening:

Come, you ancestors! Brothers, sisters, comrades, come! Come you all, for the Veil is thinnest On this very night of nights! Come ye, that we may love you again That we may bond with you again That we may share Solidarity with you again For: “Our heart is with you! Our anger is fuelled by your strength. We are all here. We are all here. It’s just your bodies which will stay where they are. You will be with us forever. You will be our light and illumination forever.”

— words after “For:” adapted from Emel’s eulogy of Ali Kitapci

I offer the text from Istanbul Indymedia in Ali Kitapci’s memory as a lesson tonight:

It’s raining. On all our memories with Ali… It’s raining. Yet yesterday the killers have washed away the blood on the street long ago. It’s raining. All those drinks we had together, all those actions we went, all those slogans we shouted, all that gas we breathed. Ali’s asthma crisis.. It’s raining. State attacks. It’s raining so badly. All the comrades, we are together just like we did 20 years ago. We are together, just like it happened in 1936! Ali had given his life to the class struggle, to the trade-union movement. He was one of those unnamed “heroes” struggling to transform the anarchist movement from a weak breath into a lively alternative of freedom. Let his memory be our comrade… We won’t forget, we won’t forgive!

To this I add: We are all together, just like it happened in 1936….. and 1886…. and 1917…. 1914….. 1940…. and many, many other times!

On this night, all of our comrades are together; we living reaching out to you who live no more as we live; but …

author: Unknown
title: Рикардо Флорес Магон - Революция
content:
Автор

: Рикардо Флорес Магон

Название

: Революция

Дата

: 19 ноября 1910

Источник

: Regeneración


 Вот-вот упадёт вполне созревший плод внутреннего мятежа; плод горький для всех, кто возгордился положением, которое приносит почести, богатства и награды тем, кто основывает свои наслаждения на страдании и рабстве человечества; но плод сладкий и отрадный для всех, кто так или иначе ощутил на своём достоинстве копыта тех зверей, которые в одну ночь, длившуюся тридцать четыре года, крали, насиловали, убивали, обманывали, предавали, скрывая свои преступления под покровом закона и уклоняясь от кары под сенью официальной власти.


 Кто боится Революции? Те же самые, кто её вызвал; те, кто своим гнётом или своей эксплуатацией народных масс довёл до того, что отчаяние овладело жертвами их подлостей; те, кто несправедливостью и грабежом возмутил совесть и заставил бледнеть от негодования честных людей земли.


 Революция вот-вот разразится. Мы, столько лет следившие за всеми событиями общественной и политической жизни мексиканского народа, не можем обманываться. Симптомы грозного катаклизма не оставляют места сомнению в том, что нечто вот-вот возникнет и нечто вот-вот рухнет, что нечто воспрянет и нечто вот-вот падёт. Наконец, после тридцати четырёх лет позора, поднимет голову мексиканский народ, и наконец, после этой долгой ночи, обратится в развалины чёрное здание, чья тяжесть нас душила.


 Сейчас уместно снова сказать то, что мы говорили так часто: нужно сделать так, чтобы это движение, вызванное отчаянием, не стало слепым движением того, кто делает усилие, чтобы сбросить с себя вес огромной ноши, – движением, в котором инстинкт почти полностью господствует над разумом. Мы, либертарии, должны позаботиться о том, чтобы это движение приняло направление, которое указывает Наука. Если этого не сделать, поднимающаяся Революция послужит лишь тому, чтобы заменить одного Президента другим Президентом, или, что то же самое, одного хозяина другим хозяином. Мы должны помнить, что нужно, чтобы у народа был хлеб, было жильё, была земля для обработки; мы должны помнить, что никакое Правительство, сколь бы честным оно ни было, не может декретировать отмену нищеты. Именно сам народ, именно голодные, именно обездоленные должны отменить нищету, в первую очередь вступив во владение землёй, которая по естественному праву не может быть прибрана к рукам несколькими, но является собственностью всякого человеческого существа. Невозможно предсказать, до какого предела дойдёт дело восстановления прав в грядущей Революции; но если мы, борцы доброй воли, несём намерение продвинуться по этому пути как можно дальше; если, берясь за винчестер, мы идём решительно не к возвышению очередного хозяина, но к восстановлению прав пролетариата; если мы несём на поле вооружённой борьбы стремление завоевать экономическую свободу, которая есть основа всех свобод, которая есть условие, без которого нет никакой свободы; если мы несём это намерение, мы направим грядущее народное движение по пути, достойному этой эпохи; но если из желания легко победить; если из стремления поскорее закончить борьбу мы уберём из наших устремлений тот радикализм, который делает их несовместимыми с устремлениями чисто буржуазных и консервативных партий, тогда мы совершим дело разбойников и убийц, ибо пролитая кровь послужит лишь тому, чтобы придать больше силы буржуазии, то есть касте, владеющей богатством, которая после победы снова наденет цепь на пролетариат, чьей кровью, чьей жертвой, чьим мученичеством она завоевала власть.


 Итак, необходимо, пролетарии; необходимо, обездоленные, чтобы вы не обманывались. Консервативные и буржуазные партии говорят вам о свободе, о справедливости, о законе, о честном правительстве и говорят вам, что, если народ сменит людей, стоящих у Власти, на других, у вас будет свобода, будет справедливость, будет закон, будет честное правительство. Не давайте себя обмануть. Вам нужно, чтобы вам обеспечили довольство ваших семей и хлеб насущный; довольство семей не сможет дать вам никакое Правительство. Это вы сами должны завоевать эти блага, с самого начала вступив во владение землёй, которая есть первоисточник богатства, а землю не сможет дать вам никакое Правительство, – поймите это хорошо! – потому что закон защищает

право

 тех, кто удерживает богатство; вы должны взять её сами, вопреки закону, вопреки Правительству, вопреки мнимому праву собственности; вы должны взять её во имя естественной справедливости, во имя права, которое имеет всякое …

title: Muslim, Jewish Groups Warn “Right to Worship” Bill Could Undermine Free Speech

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: ‘It’s all fake, It’s all rhetoric:’ MP Billy Morin doesn’t have much good to say about Budget 2026
content:
Conservative MP Billy Morin says

 Budget 2026

 reveals a pattern of performative reconciliation that leaves Métis governments on the sidelines.


Morin, the opposition critic for Indigenous Services and former chief of Enoch Cree Nation in Alberta, went further while holding a copy of the budget.


“It is ironic that it says ‘Masters of Our Destiny,’ he said. “I have crossed out destiny and put the masters of our deficit, debt, and deceit. And when it comes to Indigenous people in particular, the deceit one really, I think, is highlighted.”


In Thursday’s budget, the federal government announced nearly $50 billion in spending over the next ten years, with $32 billion in new investments for First Nations housing and infrastructure.


“The prime minister said he was going to do $32 billion of investments, and he portrays that as new spending. I see very minimal new spending in that… All he did is keep the funding going. They had two options: cut it or keep it going. And they portray it as an investment or new funding. It’s not.”


APTN reached out to Indigenous Services Canada to ask whether the $32 billion announced in the budget was new spending or not. We were told that, at the moment, all questions related to the budget are to be directed to Finance Canada.


According to the department that responded after the story was published, “Budget 2026 newly allots $32 billion worth of new cash into community infrastructure that wasn’t previously there. This includes $1.3 billion of new money going towards First Nations off reserve, Inuit, Métis and modern treaty and self governing partners to invest in affordable, supportive and transitional housing – which represents 10% of BCH’s new capital,” said the department. “How that money was derived or pooled is immaterial to the point, what matters is that community money that wasn’t available just yesterday now is – and is already flowing into Indigenous communities across the country. But let me be clear: this is new money. Suggesting otherwise is patently false.“


 


Métis reaction


Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand said Friday that his government was “appalled” by being left out of the budget.


“In recent years, Canada has finally started to address the long-overlooked needs of the Red River Métis in areas such as housing, early learning and childcare, and post-secondary education,” Chartrand said in a statement. “However, a significant gap still exists between our Nation and the general population. There’s no doubt our people will be angered that their needs have been dismissed by this Budget.”


The MMF noted that Métis appear only once in the 532-page document — “as part of the title for a piece of legislation, An Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families – a piece of legislation that Canada has claimed they do not have a mechanism to fund us for.”


“The hugely successful distinctions-based approach has vanished, and government is reverting to phrases like ‘Indigenous’ when, in reality, they mean First Nations and Inuit,” Chartrand said. “The Red River Métis pay billions in taxes in this country, yet we have been forgotten by this government.”


Read More:


Budget 2026 delivers $32B to First Nations, but Métis, Inuit largely left out


Manitoba Métis Federation ‘appalled’ they were left out of budget


The MMF said it had met with “numerous Ministers as well as the Prime Minister” ahead of the budget to discuss infrastructure, housing, health, and child and family services.


Morin said he understands the Métis questioning the government.


“How serious is this government about partnering with the Métis when they can’t even put them and acknowledge them in the budget? Morin said. “President Chartrand has every right to be appalled with this budget because every indication from this government is just like it treats First Nations people; it’s all fake. It’s all rhetoric and they don’t really mean it.”

‘It’s all fake, It’s all rhetoric:’ MP Billy Morin doesn’t have much good to say about Budget 2026

title: Kongra Star: Protecting our children and students is a social and historical responsibility
content:
Kongra Star issued a statement to condemn the attacks against student protesters demonstrating for their right to education in their mother tongue in Hesekê.


The statement said: "The blatant attack on student protesters demonstrating for their right to education in their mother tongue in Hesekê, and the actions of terrorist gangs and sectarian incitement, a dangerous conflict that threatens the social peace and stability of the region.


Recently, the city of Hesekê has been facing a dangerous security and social crisis, due to systematic attacks carried out by destructive, terrorist and chauvinist groups against the Kurdish component. This tension was manifested today in a blatant attack on a peaceful sit-in by school students in front of the Directorate of Education and the Governorate, as they were exercising their legitimate and legal right to education in their mother tongue, resulting in a number of students being injured.


The use by these rogue groups of extremist slogans and terrorist threats inspired by the ‘ISIS’ ideology, including the threat of beheading and sectarian incitement, It shows an explicit call to spread chaos and strike at communal coexistence and social peace. These violations do not just target students; they are a dangerous continuation of the fascist ideology of ISIS. And a clear violation of all international principles and agreements that guarantee the right to education and peaceful expression."


Kongr Star declared its official position and stressed the following demands and principles:


"We call upon all our free mothers, our heroic people, civil society forces and all democratic sectors to rally around the courageous students. The right to education in the mother tongue is a red line that must not be crossed, and protecting our children and students from ideological and physical terrorism is a social, moral, and historical responsibility.


-We hold the Transitional Government and the authorities fully legally and morally responsible for the situation that has arisen in Hesekê, especially after the recent integration and establishment operations; as these destructive groups continue to carry out daily provocations, incitement to sectarianism and disruption of social peace, in full view of and with the knowledge of official institutions, without any hindrance or genuine accountability. Silence in the face of these acts is an explicit complicity in the crime.


-We make an urgent and explicit call on the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and all relevant international organisations for human rights and child protection, to intervene swiftly and protect students and children in Rojava from terror. We also call for the establishment of international monitoring and investigation committees to document the systematic violations and crimes targeting predominantly Kurdish areas. – There is a risk of repeat of scenarios of systematic “purges” and incitement – as previously occurred in Girê Spî and Serê Kaniyê, and are now being attempt once again in Hesekê.


-With conclusive evidence, our people’s children have tracked the suspicious movements of elements affiliated with the terrorist organisation ISIS, who roam the city of Hesekê with complete freedom, particularly with the simultaneous acts of sabotage and attacks on peaceful demonstrations. Therefore, we strongly and urgently call upon the Internal Security Forces to intensify security campaigns, arrest these terrorists, and to uproot sleeper cells that threaten the security and safety of society."

title: Gülten Kaya: Art requires the courage to engage with life
content:
Gülten Kaya has always been at the heart of music, poetry and stories of her homeland, both through her own personal journey and as Ahmet Kaya's life partner and Yusuf Hayaloğlu's sister.


Gülten Kaya, with whom we discussed the transformation of the music world, said that digital platforms also generated ethical and moral problems of their own. She identified creating works in one's mother tongue as one of the most important pillars of collective memory.


Gülten Kaya said of Ahmet Kaya's music: "It is socially conscious, it bears witness, it is authentic, literary, recent history, poetry, emotion and sacrifice. His music reflects both recent history and all the suffering experienced by society." She also criticized the reduction of art to an apolitical industry: "All creative fields, from painting to literature, cinema to music, require the courage to engage with life. Art is one of the fields in which the greatest courage is needed to bear witness to life, particularly in countries like ours."


ANF spoke to lyricist and music producer Gülten Kaya about the transformation of the music world and the impact of digitalization on music production and consumption habits.


The music industry has evolved toward a digitalized, algorithm-driven market model in recent years. How is this transforming music's role in creating collective memory and fostering social empathy?


Digital environments and platforms also generate ethical and moral problems of their own. We can consider these problems from both human-centered and system-centered perspectives, and the two are not independent of each other. Technology undoubtedly has a significant impact on how people perceive the world and is increasingly determining that perception. Although we cannot yet speak of a fully developed music industry in Turkey, looking at the global music industry, we can say that its participation in this new process, which could be described as a digital revolution, has begun, albeit belatedly. The music industry is an important stakeholder in cultural heritage. Competition and the necessity of participating in this transformation seem to be unfolding simultaneously.


For me, one of the most important pillars of collective memory is creating works in one's own mother tongue. As for fostering empathy, that is achieved through good, high-quality creative work rather than through the digital process itself.


Does the culture of singles that are rapidly consumed and forgotten negatively affect the soul of music?


I do not think such a generalization would be particularly sound, because this format alone is not what affects the soul of music. Focusing on anything that is quickly consumed and forgotten, including singles, diverts our attention from the multilayered nature of the problem. The fundamental issue here is the quality of creative work. An artist may produce hundreds of works or just one. Therefore, the lasting value of a work cannot be explained by its format.


The disposable culture introduced into our lives by popular culture, the trap of speed in our era, the emphasis on quantity rather than quality in production, the failure to establish an emotional connection with listeners, simplistic and unliterary lyrics written over nearly identical musical arrangements, and the way such works circulate despite cultural and musical ignorance, only to disappear just as quickly... There are dozens of factors we could mention.


As in every field, concepts such as "good" and "right" are, of course, relative in art. But anything that connects with and touches your inherited cultural identity deserves a unique place in your personal repertoire of experiences.


Does the use of artificial intelligence to generate voices and music concern you? What consequences could it have?


Frankly, it worries me considerably. Replicas of art, design and all creative fields have already been circulating for quite some time, in a way that has almost begun to gain legitimacy. Life seems to be moving toward a time when even human beings may be cloned. This process, which is advancing while creating its own market and economy, is beginning to take the place of authenticity in every field. Once again, what we most need to hold on to is ethics and conscience. We need the intellectual capacity, education and cultural knowledge to recognize the difference in value between what is genuine and what is artificial, and to appreciate that difference.

title: DEM Party: Abolish the Council of Higher Education, a vestige of the 1980 military coup
content:
In a written statement, the DEM Party’s Education Policies Commission called for the abolition of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), a vestige of the 12 September 1980 military coup.


The statement said: “Established on 6 November 1981, in the aftermath of the 12 September military coup, the Council of Higher Education (YÖK) has continued for 45 years to be one of the principal institutions through which a centralised and tutelary system of governance is imposed on universities.”


The statement noted that, particularly under AKP rule, this structure had become one of the instruments through which the political authorities intervened in university affairs, and added: “It is unacceptable that young people are pushed out of politics, that their freedoms of association and expression are restricted, and that universities are transformed into institutions that produce obedient individuals. Young people are not merely the social and political actors of the future; they are actors in society and politics today.”


The DEM Commission outlined the kind of university it envisions as follows:


"A university in which YÖK is abolished, and centralised tutelage comes to an end; in which rectors are elected through the democratic will of the university community; in which academic and scientific freedom is guaranteed; in which students, academics and university workers have a voice and a role in decision-making. A university founded on education in one's mother tongue, pluralism, equality and a libertarian understanding of secularism and in which education is organised around the public interest rather than market demands."


The statement concluded: “On the anniversary of YÖK's establishment, we reiterate once again: universities are not ideological instruments of those in power, nor are they institutions to be shaped according to the needs of capital. Academic freedom is one of the fundamental conditions for the democratisation of society. End the trustee-appointed administration model, political tutelage and academic repression! Abolish YÖK! Establish autonomous, democratic, free and public universities! Let young people have a say! Let universities be free!”

title: Nilüfer Koç: Council of Europe must consider the new process
content:
A total of 845 signatures from 50 countries have been collected as part of the "Freedom for Abdullah Öcalan, a Political Solution to the Kurdish Question" campaign. International support, including that of 109 Nobel Prize laureates, has been brought to the Council of Europe. Most recently, 620 signatories from 29 countries sent a letter to the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers.


ANF spoke to Nilüfer Koç, Co-Spokesperson for Foreign Relations of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK), about the results of the international campaign, diplomatic initiatives to be pursued at the Council of Europe, steps toward implementing the right to hope, and upcoming efforts aimed at securing Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom.


Nilüfer Koç commented on reports that Abdullah Öcalan had been moved to a new building on Imrali Island, stating that his transfer to a larger space did not constitute a fundamental change in his conditions. She emphasized that the arrangement amounted only to an expansion of his physical surroundings and that access to Imrali Island and visits remained under state control.


Koç pointed out that the island was surrounded by the sea and that the state decided who could travel to and from it. She said, "The state will take you there whenever it wants and will either allow or deny permission to those wishing to visit. This is a situation entirely under state control. That alone is a problem. Changing the size of a cell on the island is not a particularly decisive factor either. In my view, this amounts to little more than a delaying tactic."


Koç emphasized the importance of Abdullah Öcalan's political struggle reaching society and the political sphere, stating that the existing conditions prevented this from happening. She noted that Abdullah Öcalan had taken considerable risks to build democracy and peace in Turkey and had been engaged in political struggle for many years. She stressed that changing his physical surroundings would not be sufficient to enable this struggle to reach society.


Koç also stated that the isolation conditions on Imrali prevented the idea of peace from taking root in society and becoming an effective part of the political agenda. She emphasized that meaningful change would only be possible if Abdullah Öcalan were allowed to establish contact with the outside world.


Koç said, "His relocation is also a cosmetic measure in this respect. It does not change the course of the process. Establishing connections with the outside world, as Abdullah Öcalan himself has requested, would genuinely contribute to the process. Such a development could further strengthen the Kurdish people's confidence in the process."


Koç reiterated that the changes to Abdullah Öcalan's physical conditions had not altered his imprisonment or isolation. She said, "Abdullah Öcalan remains a prisoner on Imrali Island. The conditions of his captivity have not changed. He has simply been transferred from one cell to another. We should not be misled by this."


'Abdullah Öcalan's status must be clarified for the process to advance'


Nilüfer Koç pointed out that the steps taken by the Kurdish side in the Peace and Democratic Society Process were clear, while the state had maintained a slow and uncertain approach to taking concrete measures. She emphasized that Abdullah Öcalan's status needed to be clarified for the process to move forward, recalling that numerous proposals had been presented since 27 February to advance the process.


Koç stated that Abdullah Öcalan had put forward calls and proposals on major issues, including the establishment of commissions, legislative arrangements, the burning of weapons and the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). She said that he had addressed the entire political spectrum in Turkey in his efforts toward peace. Koç emphasized that clarifying his status was essential for these efforts to continue and for him to maintain the role he had undertaken in the process.


Koç said that the state had not yet made a definitive political decision on resolving the Kurdish question and that the prevailing uncertainty and repeated delays stemmed from this indecision. She pointed to growing contradictions within the state, referring to debates surrounding corruption allegations and the fund crisis, and argued that the state under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government was experiencing serious internal decay.

title: Executions and prison sentences continue in Iran
content:
The Kurdistan Human Rights Organisation has published a report on Iran’s repression of Rojhilatê Kurdistan (Eastern Kurdistan) and Iranian citizens.


The report states that courts in Tehran and Mashhad have sentenced five protesters, Alireza Rezai, Vahid Kehermani, Mehdi Jalali, Metin Şebani and Emir Dilşad, to death. All five were arrested during the January 2026 protests.


According to the report, all five were convicted of “collaborating with enemy states”. Two female prisoners tried in the same case, whose identities have yet to be established, were each sentenced to 30 years in prison.


Mehdi Jalali, who previously served as an imam, was reportedly sentenced to death by the Special Court for Clerics on charges of apostasy.


Meanwhile, 19 religious scholars held in Urmia Central Prison (Yakup Muradi, Ibrahim Jiyani, Areş Agahi, Esed Muhammediyan, Awine Kaytarani, Çiya Nasrullahi, Resul Yusuf, Siyamend Alipur, Hemin Ahmedi, Emin Dilnişin, Şehriyar Hızır, Cafer, Vezir Zersaw, Rahim Asare, Afşin, Areş Kulizade, Mihran Nirumendi, Kamyar Şeyhi and Mevlud Ateşbar, as well as Saadet Taşke) have reportedly been sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to ten months.


The report also states that the prisoners have been denied leave, limited freedoms and the right to receive medical treatment outside the prison.


The report further states that two athlete brothers, Emirali and Emad Zakeriferd, who were arrested during the January protests, were transferred to Ilam Central Prison after being subjected to severe physical and psychological torture by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). A court reportedly sentenced the brothers to 33 and 35 years in prison, as well as flogging.

title: MKG: Repression against women journalists continued in October
content:
According to the October 2026 report on rights violations published by the Mesopotamia Women Journalists Association (MKG), one woman journalist was arrested and imprisoned, two women journalists were detained, and another journalist’s home was raided in Turkey last month. In addition, one woman journalist was subjected to ill-treatment, and one incident of obstruction of news coverage was documented.


The report stated that an investigation was launched against one woman journalist, another was sentenced to 18 months in prison, and nine women journalists continued to face trial in nine separate cases. It emphasized that prosecuting journalists for reporting on violence and rights violations against women constituted an infringement of the public’s right to information.


Digital censorship and dismissals


Highlighting the continued digital censorship targeting the free press, the report documented the blocking of two websites and restrictions on access to 20 news articles. It stated that these measures made it more difficult for information about rights violations against women to reach the public.


The report noted that 162 journalists lost their jobs. However, it was not possible to determine how many of them were women. MKG drew attention to the precarious working conditions and discrimination faced by women journalists.


Eight women journalists behind bars


In its report, MKG stated that eight women journalists were currently imprisoned and called for their release, effective investigations into sexist attacks, and an end to policies of impunity.


The association emphasized that it would continue to fight against the criminalization of journalistic activities and strengthen its efforts to defend press freedom.

title: Karayılan: Our martyrs are our greatest values
content:
Following the announcement of the identities of nine guerrilla fighters from East Kurdistan (Rojhilat) who lost their lives at different times during the Kurdish freedom struggle, Murat Karayılan issued a statement addressing their families and the public. The commander of the central headquarters of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG) paid tribute to the fallen fighters’ contributions to the Kurdish freedom movement and recalled the historical significance of the participation of people from Rojhilat in the collective liberation struggle across all parts of Kurdistan.


Karayılan also addressed the current political situation in East Kurdistan and Iran. In light of regional developments, he called on the people to place their trust in their own collective strength, build structures of solidarity, and organize independently of external powers. He also described the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan as a development whose significance extended far beyond North Kurdistan.

Murat Karayılan’s statement reads as follows:


“First of all, I would like to extend my greetings and respect to our people in Rojhilat in particular. Among those who have fallen in recent times, some of whose names have already been announced while others have not yet been made public, are several of our comrades from Rojhilat. On behalf of the leadership of our movement and our central headquarters, we extend our condolences to the families of the martyrs whose names we are now announcing. Our sympathies also go out to the entire population of Rojhilat.


On behalf of all our fallen comrades, we remember Heval (Comrade) Artêş (Muhammed Fevzi) and Heval Sila (Zehra Ismaili) with respect, admiration, and gratitude. We bow before their memory and renew our promise to them, the promise we made together as comrades. We will remain faithful to that promise. We will fight to the end to realize their hopes and dreams and bring their cause to success. We will carry their struggle to victory and, in doing so, immortalize their memory.


They gave their lives for their homeland


Dear comrades, esteemed families,


All those whose names we are announcing at this time resisted under extraordinary circumstances and fell in that struggle. As we have already emphasized, this holds particular significance. I would like to express my appreciation to all the families who raised such courageous individuals. We extend our greetings and respect to the mothers and fathers of the martyrs.


The fact that young people from Rojhilat joined the struggle throughout Kurdistan, particularly in Bakur (North Kurdistan), and demonstrated such great willingness to make sacrifices reflects an honorable stance. They did not act out of personal interest. They gave their lives for their homeland. That is why these comrades are especially precious to us, and we bow before their memory. Through their deaths, they have also left us a message that we must put into practice.


As I have explained before, people from Rojhilat began joining our movement in 1989. However, a decisive development took place during the international conspiracy against Rêber Apo [Leader Abdullah Öcalan]. Although our movement had not yet established its own organizational structures in Rojhilat at the time, the people rose up. Protests and uprisings broke out across East Kurdistan, marked by great determination and willingness to make sacrifices.


This stance deserves the highest recognition. At that time, our comrades and our entire people felt that we had support and that Rojhilat stood by our side. The people of Rojhilat understand the significance of political leaders and their historical responsibilities. They had already gained this experience during the time of Qazî Mihemed and Abdurrahman Qasimlo. That is why they also understood the capture of Rêber Apo as a historic turning point and rose up against it.


Rojhilat’s contribution to the collective liberation struggle


Following this period, the participation of young people from Rojhilat in the guerrilla movement continued to increase. We must not forget comrades such as Doctor Afat and Dilxwaz, who fought and fell in East Kurdistan. We also remember Heval Şivan Gever and his many years of work in the region.

title: Ciwan İbrahim is Rojava
content:
“I am a child of Serêkaniyê. My mother’s name is Enisa, and my father’s name is Abdurrahim. Who are you? Where do you come from?” These were the words Ciwan İbrahim addressed to the militants of Jabhat al-Nusra. It was 2012, and the battle for Serêkaniyê was underway. Despite being wounded in the hand, Ciwan refused even to have his injury bandaged and would not abandon his fighters. “If I withdraw, my comrades will be affected. I am putting all my strength into this battle,” he said, as he considered how to continue directing the fighting with his other hand.


Ciwan İbrahim’s 18-year journey, stretching from Serêkaniyê to Lebanon, from Garê to the resistance tunnels of Zap and the Rojava Revolution, was marked by this determination. Throughout this journey, he distinguished himself at different times as an accomplished journalist, a commander, and one of the leading figures among the people.


Some of us came to know him when he announced the establishment of the People’s Defense Units (YPG), others as a commander of the Asayish (Internal Security Forces), and still others as he rode his motorcycle through the streets of Qamişlo.


Today, Rojava mourns the loss of this legendary commander.


From Lebanon to the mountains of Kurdistan


Ciwan İbrahim (Nosican İbrahim) was born on October 3, 1983, in Serêkaniyê. He had two sisters, Lorîn and Şirîncan, and a brother named Dilciwan. As the eldest child, he was the apple of his family’s eye. Both his mother and father were teachers, and he received his primary and secondary education from them.


From an early age, he became familiar with the Ba’ath regime’s policies that denied the existence of the Kurdish people. Through the activities carried out by Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan in Rojava and his efforts to raise political awareness among the population, Ciwan became acquainted with the Kurdish Freedom Movement. In 2001, two years after the international conspiracy against Öcalan, he returned to Kurdistan from Lebanon.


After spending a considerable period in the Garê region, he moved to Zap. In 2010, he joined the Special Forces (Hêzên Taybet), where he underwent profound ideological and military development in accordance with the principles of self-sacrificing militancy.


In 2011, as the Rojava Revolution began to take shape, he once again turned toward his homeland, Rojava, to take a leading role in revolutionary activities. This return marked the beginning of a new chapter in his life.


The early days of preparations for the revolution


That year, meetings were being held across Rojava, young people were brought together, and efforts were underway to organize the population. The institutions of the revolution had not yet been established. Much of the work was carried out through clandestine meetings and training sessions. The home of Ciwan’s father, Abdurrahim İbrahim, was among the places where these meetings took place.


Ferhad Şamî, former press spokesperson for the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), first met Ciwan during this period. Recalling those days in an interview with ANF, Şamî said, “I met him during the first meetings in 2011. We were attending training sessions with Mazloum Abdi, Martyr Hisen Çavuş, and Henife Hisen. At the time, the Ba’ath regime wanted to launch attacks, but we were taking precautions.”


He contributed to every field


Ciwan’s activities during those years extended across the fields of media, youth organizing, and self-defense. Programs were developed to provide young people with media training, and training sessions were organized in various cities across Rojava.


Şamî also joined these efforts at Ciwan’s request. He continued:


“We prepared a program and began the training sessions. We provided media training to young people in Serêkaniyê, Dirbesiyê, and Til Temir. We then traveled to Hesekê and Qamişlo, eventually reaching Dêrik.”


While media training continued, organizing communities in the cities and developing self-defense initiatives were also of great importance. As part of these efforts, youth groups were formed during the process of removing regime soldiers from the cities. Ciwan, Martyr Hemze Tolhildan, Martyr Serhed, Martyr Seydo, Martyr Goran, and Martyr Lewend took on this responsibility.


For all of Kurdistan


Journalist Dîlan Osman also recalls that they were still young at the time and eager to take part in preparations for the revolution. She describes the arrival of Ciwan and his comrades in Rojava …

title: Veysi Aktaş: A struggle disconnected from society cannot succeed
content:
What role can literature, language, and intellectuals play in shaping a democratic peace? This question is at the heart of an international conference that began on Friday in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). Under the title “The Role of Literature, Language and intelligentsia in Processes of Dialogue, Reconciliation, Peace and Equality,” writers, academics, and representatives of civil society organizations and political parties have come together. Discussions focus on the social responsibility of cultural figures, the freedom of the Kurdish language, and the prospects of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


The event, held at the Ali Emiri Conference Hall, is organized by the international writers’ association PEN, the Kurdish PEN Center (PENa Kurd), Amed Metropolitan Municipality, and the district municipalities of Sur, Yenişehir, Bağlar, and Kayapınar. It began with a moment of silence.


Peace requires linguistic and cultural freedom


At the opening, Ömer Fidan, a writer and chair of PENa Kurd, stated that literary figures must take responsibility for building a dignified peace. He said the conference aimed to strengthen the social and cultural dimensions of the peace process.


Mürüvet Demir of the Peace Mothers’ Council recalled the decades-long suppression of the Kurdish language and said: “People were subjected to repression and violence simply for speaking Kurdish. The opportunities available today to use and develop the language publicly are the result of a long struggle by society.”


Writer Mizgin Ronak drew attention to the situation of imprisoned literary figures. She said numerous writers remained in Turkish prisons and that their works must be made accessible to the public. She emphasized that Kurdish literature has a rich historical and cultural heritage whose development must continue even under repressive conditions.


Writer Ilhan Sami Çomak, who himself spent many years in prison, described freedom to use one’s mother tongue and the release of political prisoners as essential prerequisites for a successful peace process. He particularly highlighted the situation of people who have been imprisoned for decades, as well as seriously ill prisoners.


Serra Bucak, co-mayor of Amed Metropolitan Municipality, also stressed that peace would not be possible without linguistic equality. She said everyone must have the freedom to speak, sing, and create literature in their mother tongue.


Literature as a means of fostering social understanding


The panel titled “Literature, Language and Universal Rights in Peace Processes,” moderated by Diba Keskin, then began. Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International, spoke about the responsibility of writers in overcoming social conflicts. “Writers from different countries can help develop a common language of peace and support processes of mutual understanding across national and cultural boundaries,” he emphasized.


Author Bêrîvan Doskî highlighted the importance of the mother tongue for identity, culture, and the future of society. She said that despite decades of attacks, the Kurdish language had continued to develop. To strengthen this development, she called for joint cultural and arts festivals, greater literary engagement with social struggles, and exchanges with writers from other communities.


Aktaş: Intellectuals must not distance themselves from society


In his speech, Kurdish politician Veysi Aktaş critically examined the role of intellectuals in the current peace process. He warned against separating cultural and academic work from social struggles.


“The peace process is of great importance to all peoples. Intellectuals have an important role to play in its success. Their responsibility is to open up new paths for society and provide guidance. However, if they lose touch with social realities, they develop an elitist attitude that distances them from the people.”


Aktaş, who was imprisoned for several years alongside Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan on the Turkish prison island of Imrali, called for a more comprehensive examination of the social conditions necessary for peace, freedom, and coexistence based on equality.


In his assessment, the contributions made by intellectuals so far have been insufficient. Although efforts are underway, he said, they needed to be deepened and more closely linked to grassroots organizing.

author: Unknown
title: IHD documents hundreds of human rights violations in Turkish prisons
content:
The Human Rights Association (IHD) documented a total of 899 human rights violations in Turkish prisons between July and September 2026. The most frequently reported violations concerned access to food and drinking water, protection against ill-treatment, and the right to communication. The organization warned of a further deterioration in prison conditions and accused the Turkish government of allowing problems to persist even when they could be easily resolved.


The report on the human rights situation in prisons across the Marmara region was presented at a press conference held at the IHD branch office in Istanbul’s Beyoğlu district. Gülseren Yoleri, a member of the IHD Central Executive Board, Meral Nergis Şahin, co-spokesperson for the Prison Commission, and commission member Sevilay Yılmaz Birgin took part in the presentation.


The investigation was based on complaints and submissions from prisoners and their relatives, as well as publicly available information. The report noted that prisons were operating beyond their designated capacities.


Ill-treatment and inadequate living conditions


Most of the documented rights violations concerned prisoners’ basic living conditions. In 293 cases, the IHD recorded inadequate access to food and clean drinking water, as well as deficiencies in hygiene and personal care. Another 258 violations involved physical assaults, ill-treatment, degrading treatment, and torture.


Restrictions on fundamental rights also accounted for a significant proportion of the violations. The organization documented 136 violations of the right to communication, including cases of isolation. In 117 cases, the right to healthcare was violated. These were accompanied by 39 violations involving unlawful detention and unequal treatment in the enforcement of sentences, as well as 28 cases in which prisoners’ access to justice was obstructed or denied.


In addition, the IHD recorded six violations related to hunger strikes and three violations of the right to life. Another 15 rights violations were identified through an analysis of publicly available online sources. The individually listed categories add up to 895 cases. However, the IHD reported a total of 899 rights violations. The discrepancy of four cases is not explained in the available summary.


Political causes of prison abuses


In its assessment, the Human Rights Association linked increasing prison overcrowding to the deterioration of detention conditions. According to the organization, both the prison population and the number of documented rights violations are rising. The IHD particularly criticized the fact that even problems that could be resolved through relatively simple measures remained unaddressed.


“This demonstrates that the underlying cause lies in the persistent continuation of government policies that give rise to human rights violations in general and violations of prisoners’ rights in particular,” the report stated.


The IHD therefore considers strengthening social mobilization and human rights advocacy against these violations a key prerequisite for bringing about change.


‘We want to give prisoners a voice’


The Prison Commission emphasized that its reports were not intended merely to compile statistics.


“We prepare these reports not simply to provide information. Our primary goal is to give those behind prison walls a voice, at least to some extent, to make their pressing problems visible, raise awareness, and help prevent rights violations.”


At the same time, the IHD acknowledged the limited scope of its investigation. It said the documented cases were based on a relatively small number of complaints and submissions from the prisons examined. The actual number of rights violations could therefore be significantly higher.


According to the organization, the investigation covered 16 prisons. These included the Marmara/Silivri, Bakırköy, Kandıra, Edirne, Tekirdağ, Ümraniye, Metris, and Maltepe prison complexes. The published list also included facilities outside the Marmara region, including those in Izmir and Bolu.


In conclusion, the Prison Commission stressed that the struggle to secure humane prison conditions must not be left to prisoners alone: “Human rights violations in prisons cannot be prevented solely through the struggle of prisoners themselves. This also requires support through struggles outside prison walls. This report is also our call for solidarity with prisoners and their families in the …

author: Unknown
title: Court overturns fine imposed on Syriac Orthodox church in İdil
content:
The Syriac Orthodox Church of the Virgin Mary in İdil district of Şırnak province has secured a preliminary legal victory against the AKP-run municipality. The Şırnak Administrative Court has suspended the enforcement of a fine of approximately 1.17 million Turkish lira (around 20,800 euros), which had been imposed on the church foundation over a guesthouse allegedly built without a permit. The main proceedings are still ongoing.


In June, the municipality imposed an administrative fine of 1,170,743.24 lira on the foundation of the historic Syriac Orthodox Church of the Virgin Mary and sealed the guesthouse in October. The foundation subsequently challenged the measure in court.


In its ruling, the Administrative Court found that the municipality had failed to adequately investigate who had actually constructed the building in question. According to the court, the mere fact that the building lacked a construction permit was not sufficient to hold the church foundation responsible.


The court criticized the incomplete examination of the facts and ordered the suspension of the fine without requiring a security deposit. As a result, it concluded, the penalty cannot be enforced until further notice. A final decision on its legality has yet to be made.

author: Daron Letts
title: MLAs wrap up fall sitting
content:
The fall sitting of Nunavut’s legislative Assembly wrapped up Thursday, with MLAs passing into law seven bills they introduced, leaving four to be dealt with later. 


“Thank you, each and every one of you, for working hard for the two weeks of what we did,” said Speaker David Joanasie, the MLA for South Baffin, as he closed the session at the end of the day.


MLAs looked at 11 bills over the two weeks that that they sat, beginning on Oct. 22, including legislation to increase the student loan limit, changes to the membership of the board of inquiry that governs medical professionals, and an approval for capital expenditures.


Among the bills that were passed were:


Bill 15: an act to amend the Student Financial Assistant Act to double the limit of loans made to a person who is eligible to receive other loans to $300,000.


Bill 14: an amendment to the Medical Profession Act to update the membership composition of the Board of Inquiry, set out term limits for members of the Board of Inquiry, establish hearing panels, and modernize the law’s language. 


Bill 10: Appropriation (Capital) Act, a bill that authorizes capital expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2028.


The policymakers are scheduled to return to the Legislative Assembly in the new year on Feb. 27.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Clyde River grieves hamlet councillor, victim of Iqaluit homicide
content:
Community members in Clyde River are grieving the death of Sandra Aipellee, who was the victim of what police say was a homicide in Iqaluit in October. She was a hamlet councillor, who had just been sworn in this summer.


Steven Aipellee, her brother, said she had been visiting Iqaluit with her partner when when she was fatally stabbed on Oct. 17.


“It’s unbelievable, that happening to the family,” he said in a phone interview from Clyde River on Friday. She had one sister and five brothers.


Nunavut RCMP had reported her death to the public on Oct. 19, but didn’t identify her then. Police

charged

 32-year-old Christie Nutarariaq with second-degree murder. She was taken into custody and had a court appearance scheduled for Nov. 17, an RCMP news release said.


Steven Aipellee said police told the family that Sandra knew the accused.


He described his sister as a social person who looked out for those around her, and as a dedicated caregiver to her mother. She leaves behind three children, he said, one young girl and two teenage boys now being cared for by their grandmother.


“Sandra was kind to everyone,” her brother said. “She had love when she talked to people, whoever they were, children, elders or adults. A lot of people knew her.”


On Oct. 19, flags at the hamlet office were lowered half mast in her honour, said Billy Palluq, the hamlet’s chief administrative officer.


“We were shocked and we’ve been saddened,” he said, saying she had joined council in early July.


She had recently earned a certificate from the Piqqusilirivvik Inuit cultural school, he said, and was an active member on the hamlet’s recreation committee.


“She was doing an excellent job,” he said.


Dr. Anna Banerji, a Toronto-based pediatrician, has since launched a Go Fund Me fundraiser in support of the family.


Banerji described Aipellee as part of her extended family, saying she was the aunt of her late adopted son Nathan, also from Clyde River. She said the money raised will go to supporting Aipellee’s three children.


“Financially, it’s very difficult for them, plus emotionally very traumatic to lose your mother in such a tragic way,” she said in a phone interview from Toronto. “I know the cost of living is so high, and if there’s anything we can do to help to make it a little bit less difficult, then why shouldn’t we?”


The fundraiser has set a goal of raising $16,000, and has raised just over $2,000 as of Friday.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Ottawa renews Inuit Child First Initiative funding, tops up Nutrition North
content:
The federal government is committing $575 million over five years to Inuit children’s services and more than $610 million over four years to northern food subsidies in this year’s federal budget.


The Liberal government released its budget for 2026-27, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” on Thursday.


It proposes renewing the Inuit Child First Initiative and transitioning it to Pirutsiagutiit, an Inuit-designed program developed with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami and the four Inuit treaty organizations.


The $575-million commitment would begin in the 2027-28 fiscal year. Pirutsiagutiit is expected to begin April 1, 2027, and will be operated by the treaty organizations or their designates, according to ITK.


Launched in September 2018, the Inuit Child First Initiative provides health, social, educational and other support to Inuit children and youth. Funding for the program ran out in 2025 and it

has received

 one-year top ups since then, with the

promise to retool

 it.


ITK had requested $600 million over five years for Pirutsiagutiit in its pre-budget submission. 


The budget also proposes $610.3 million over four years, beginning in 2027-28, for Nutrition North Canada and associated initiatives. It includes another $118.1 million in 2031-32, followed by $117 million annually.


Nutrition North subsidizes shipping costs for eligible food and essential goods in remote northern communities and supports harvesting and community food programs. 


It spent $163 million

subsidizing nutritious food

 in 124 northern communities in the 2025-26 fiscal year, including in communities in Nunavut and Nunavik.


Ottawa also announced a $30-million top-up in February.


The funding comes as the government considers changes

following a review

 led by former Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Aluki Kotierk.


She recommended

expanding the subsidy

 to all items sold in eligible communities, rather than limiting it to products classified as nutritious. Her review also questioned whether retailers passed the full value of subsidies on to consumers.


The budget describes the new funding as an expansion and stabilization of Nutrition North and related initiatives.


This approach to Nutrition North will “maintain the inefficiencies of the current program,” with no funding identified for reforms to address food insecurity in Inuit Nunangat, ITK said in a Nov. 5 news release.


ITK also criticized the lack of Inuit-specific housing and infrastructure funding, noting the budget allocates $30 billion for First Nations housing and infrastructure but does not mention comparable investments for Inuit communities.


“Aside from the welcome funding for Pirutsiagutiit, the broader sustainability of our communities is not reflected in this budget,” ITK President Natan Obed said in the release. “Building projects is not enough. The lack of investment in building healthy Inuit communities is a risk to this country.”


Conservative MP Billy Morin, the party’s shadow minister for Indigenous services, called the Nutrition North funding “a Band-Aid,” saying the program is not audited effectively.


“What a Conservative government would do is truly sit down with northerners, Inuit people and jurisdictions and groups and organizations and governments, to let it be defined more by them,” he said Friday in an interview.


ITK’s pre-budget submission also called for a $7,500 refundable tax credit for low-income residents of Inuit Nunangat, legislation to establish Inuit Nunangat University, funding for a national Inuit identity card and Inuit-led justice services.


It also proposed a $1-billion fund for Inuit housing and infrastructure. Budget 2026 does not include specific commitments for those proposals.


Liberals MPs Mandy

Gull-Masty, who represents the Nunavik region, and Nunavut’s Lori Idlout were not available for interviews about the budget, nor was NDP northern affairs critic Leah Gazan.

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s declaration on abolishing the Indian Act an ‘absurd distraction’
content:
At the noon break at the First Nations First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew quoted to Karl Marx as he forwarded his call to action.


“Abolish the

Indian Act

,” Kinew said. “You have nothing to lose but your chains.”


This week on APTN News InFocus, our guests Pam Palmater and Veldon Coburn argue First Nations have much to lose.


“There are thousands of bylaws and codes, and other laws that First Nations have passed to govern their communities under the Indian Act that have to be addressed,” said Palmater, a lawyer and chair in Indigenous Governance at Toronto Metropolitan University. “All of these things are constitutionally protected.


“So, you literally cannot say, ‘Hey, let’s just abolish it’. That alone, dealing with that intricate web of laws and constitutional issues, that’s going to take a long, long time.”


Canadian leaders have been toying with abolishing or amending the Indian Act for more than 70 years.


As Palmater notes, there’s a pattern.


“During the 1969 White Paper, you had [former prime minister] Pierre Elliot Trudeau who wanted to make Canada self-sufficient in oil and gas. That was his big agenda item,” Palmater said. “All of a sudden, well, Treaty rights might stand in the way, and First Nations, so let’s get rid of the Indian Act.”


Premier Wab Kinew is seen holding up his status card at the First Nations First Ministers meeting in Ottawa, Oct. 21, 2026. Photo: APTN.


Decades later, the Conservative government under prime minister Stephen Harper unveiled an unsuccessful plan to repeal the Indian Act.


Hayden King at the Yellowhead said the latest attempt to abolish the Indian Act was when former prime minister Justin Trudeau tried to move First Nations “toward self-government by encouraging a piece-meal devolution of administrative powers from the Federal (and in some cases provincial) governments to First Nations.”


As Coburn, who chairs the Indigenous Relations Initiative at McGill University, argues, it’s about strategy.


“Especially in this particular political moment in the geopolitics of the day where they tie national security to our economic advancement because of the souring relations with our largest trading partner… and the desire to build a deep-sea port in Churchill, Man., to get a pipeline across northern Manitoba,” Coburn said. “It sounds a bit conspiratorial, but there are First Nations who have Aboriginal rights within the territory, but also title to the territory itself that burdens the Crown’s underlying claim.


“Eliminating status [is] one big step. It doesn’t eliminate everything, but it goes a long way to ensure that the Crown can give corporate developers what they want.”


Read More: 


Indian Act controversy lingers more than a week after abolishment was raised in Ottawa 


What would approaching this in a good way look like? For now, Palmater said, “please don’t.”


“I don’t know a single First Nation person who is like, ‘yes, we love the Indian Act, we love paternalism, and control, and racist history and oppression.’ None of us like it,” Palmater said. “We all know that at some point, there needs to be alternatives to that.


“But it has to happen when First Nations want it.”


InFocus reached out to Kinew’s office for an interview on his statement several times. We never received a response.

author: El Surtidor
title: Como a quebra do banco Ueno, no Paraguai, acabou com o governo do presidente Santiago Peña
content:
Na terça-feira, 3 de novembro de 2026, quase 3 milhões de paraguaios — cerca de metade da população — acordaram sem poder usar o seu dinheiro.

 Às 3h24 da madrugada, o Banco Central do Paraguai (BCP) anunciou no X/Twitter o fechamento do Ueno Bank, banco digital ligado ao presidente Santiago Peña, por falta de solvência. As economias de milhares de famílias estavam depositadas ali, assim como 800 milhões de dólares em recursos públicos.


Naquele mesmo dia, o Ministério Público emitiu uma ordem de prisão contra oito dirigentes do banco, a partir de uma denúncia do Banco Central.

O principal apontado é Federico Miguel Vázquez, primeiro vice-presidente do Ueno e fundador e acionista majoritário do Grupo Vázquez

 — um conglomerado de pelo menos 28 empresas que fazem parte de um suposto esquema de captação de recursos e fraude bancária. O empresário está sendo apelidado de “Vorcaro do Paraguai”, pelas semelhanças com o escândalo brasileiro do

Banco Master

.


Na quarta-feira, 4 de novembro, o Ministério Público imputou a 27 dirigentes do grupo os crimes de conduta indevida em situações de crise e lesão de confiança, incluindo os oito primeiros. À tarde, deputados da oposição apresentaram o projeto de impeachment contra Peña e, nas ruas da capital, a polícia reprimiu manifestantes com balas de borracha, gás lacrimogêneo e caminhões-pipa.


Às 10h da manhã de quinta-feira, 5 de novembro, a Câmara dos Deputados deu início ao processo de impeachment para destituir o presidente. Mas, às 13h30, Peña renunciou antes que fosse afastado. O Senado tentou aceitar sua renúncia, mas prevaleceu a linha do impeachment, que continua nesta sexta-feira. Paralelamente, um juiz decidiu pela prisão preventiva dos oito dirigentes do Ueno.


Na mesma manhã de quinta-feira, senadores da oposição apresentaram uma denúncia contra Peña ao Ministério Público especializado em crimes econômicos, o mesmo que investiga os dirigentes do Ueno Bank. “Que ele seja indiciado e tenha seus bens confiscados. O dinheiro que roubaram precisa ser recuperado e usado para pagar as pessoas”, afirmou a senadora oposicionista Esperanza Martínez. A denúncia também inclui integrantes da diretoria do BCP, como Carlos Carvallo Spalding, que foi dirigente do Ueno Bank antes de assumir a presidência do Banco Central durante o governo Peña.


Se a investigação do Ministério Público comprovar os crimes atribuídos aos dirigentes do Ueno e do Grupo Vázquez, assim como a cumplicidade de Santiago Peña e de integrantes do BCP, esse caso será tão grave quanto ou maior que o do Banco Master, no Brasil

, ligado a

Flávio Bolsonaro

 e que afetou quase 2 milhões de brasileiros. Há, além disso, um temor latente de aprofundamento de uma crise social e econômica, com diversas ramificações a médio e longo prazo.


Miguel Vázquez, executivo do banco Ueno, está em prisão preventiva


As manobras que permitiram um esquema de fraude com recursos públicos


O crescimento do Ueno Bank e do Grupo Vázquez foi meteórico. Em menos de cinco anos, o grupo alcançou uma carteira de milhões de clientes.

Mas esse aumento contou com o apoio do poder político a partir da chegada de Santiago Peña à presidência, em agosto de 2023.

 Desde então, diversas manobras legais e políticas permitiram a expansão desse grupo econômico:


Manipulação das normas do Instituto de Previdência Social em benefício do banco Ueno.


Três meses depois da posse de Peña, o jornal ABC Color denunciou que o conselho da instituição de seguridade social havia

reduzido

 as exigências para que um banco pudesse receber seus recursos, o que permitiu que o Ueno se qualificasse. Um ano depois, também foi eliminado o limite patrimonial que o IPS podia depositar em um banco.


O Ueno ficou com cerca de 350 milhões de dólares do Fundo Comum de Aposentadorias e Pensões, aproximadamente 9% do dinheiro dos aposentados atuais e futuros. Agora, com o fechamento do banco, não se sabe qual será o destino desse dinheiro nem por quais mecanismos ele poderá ser recuperado.


Alteração da lei de conflitos de interesses e das portas giratórias


No final de 2023, o Congresso enfraqueceu a lei de conflitos de interesses, o que

facilitou

 a nomeação de ex-funcionários do banco Ueno e do Banco Basa — do ex-presidente Horacio Cartes — para cargos estratégicos na economia, além da distribuição de licitações ao Grupo Vázquez, no qual Peña tinha ações.

author: Jan Daalder
title: Queimaduras, terror psicológico e salários atrasados em data centers na Europa
content:
Sandu Dumitrescu* olhou para o relógio. Ele estava terminando os últimos 15 minutos de seu turno em uma obra de data center do Google em Saint Ghislain, Bélgica, em março, quando recebeu uma ligação. Tinha acabado de realizar verificações elétricas nos ventiladores do

hall

 quando seu gerente comunicou um pedido final: fazer dois testes rápidos antes de sair.


O funcionário de 34 anos já havia trabalhado quase 10 horas. No ambiente altamente pressurizado de GBL-6, o sexto data center Google em um vasto campus avaliado em 5 bilhões de euros, pedidos de última hora como esse eram normais.


“Eu não tinha escolha”, diz Sandu. “Pessoas foram demitidas por dizer não.” Ele acreditava que os supervisores no local, da empresa irlandesa Dornan Engineering, não aceitariam bem uma recusa. Como ele dependia de seu contrato semanal, e tinha esperanças de conseguir ligar para sua esposa e filho pequeno na Romênia naquela noite, decidiu executar o trabalho.


Era uma tarefa que ele havia feito muitas vezes antes e envolvia uma série de testes para medir a segurança e integridade da fiação elétrica. Era para ter levado cerca de uma hora. Sandu diz que o pedido lhe foi feito verbalmente, por um intermediário. Um traje protetor estava guardado em uma sala de equipamentos. Ir ao ocal para buscá-lo teria adicionado mais 15 minutos ao trabalho, diz ele, e havia pessoas esperando.

Na pressa, Sandu decidiu não ir pegar o traje.


Na sala de tensão, Sandu diz que os gerentes confirmaram que as linhas haviam sido desenergizadas. Na primeira rodada, tudo correu conforme o planejado. Mas, no segundo teste, enquanto segurava uma pinça isolada, ele conectou os cabos. Mas desta vez, os cabos de energia estavam ligados.


A explosão foi imediata e catastrófica. Em milissegundos, 400 volts e 12 mil amperes atingiram o rosto de Sandu e atravessaram o lado direito de seu corpo. Um colega que estava embaixo da plataforma e presenciou o incidente contou à

Investigate Europe

 ter “ouvido um barulho alto, muita fumaça e o visto [Sandu] gritando de dor”.


“Fiquei completamente cego”, relembra Sandu. “Disse aos gerentes três vezes que não conseguia enxergar. Mas nenhum deles respondeu”, diz ele. De acordo com a testemunha que procurou ajuda – enquanto desembaraçava Sandu dos cabos com seu corpo queimado – os gerentes fugiram, ao passo que Sandu se contorcia de dor no chão.


Trabalhadores se apressaram para levar Sandu para a ambulância. Quando os médicos o receberam no Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, ele foi colocado em coma induzido por cinco dias.


Registros hospitalares acessados pela

Investigate Europe

 mostram que o choque havia queimado 12% do corpo de Sandu, com queimaduras de segundo grau no rosto e pescoço, além de queimaduras de terceiro grau no ombro direito e nos dedos. Fotografias mostram orelhas queimadas e lábios inchados e em carne viva, com o braço cheio de hematomas e pele coagulada.


Quando Sandu acordou na unidade de tratamento intensivo uma semana depois da cirurgia, sua mulher estava à beira de sua cama. Ele diz que todo o seu corpo parecia uma “bolha branca e escaldante… Era tanta dor. O coração humano não consegue compreender”, relembra.


Sandu fotografado em outubro de 2026, meses depois de a eletrocussão por arco elétrico ter queimado 12% do seu corpo


Dois dias após acordar do coma, representantes do Google, da irlandesa Dornan e de uma agência de recrutamento holandesa, a Wanted, vieram visitá-lo. Sandu diz que enquanto estava deitado em uma maca de hospital, enfaixado, Google e Dornan tomaram declarações dele sobre o acidente. Segundo Sandu,

o funcionário do Google lhe disse que tinha sorte de estar vivo.


A descarga elétrica sofrida por Sandu foi brutal e assustadora.

Até hoje, porém, não há registro de nenhuma multa ou sanção pelo incidente.

 Inspetores federais do trabalho na Bélgica encerraram sua investigação sobre o acidente no final de outubro e não encontraram irregularidades. Sandu diz que nunca foi entrevistado diretamente pelas autoridades trabalhistas.


Apesar de ter pedido o relatório sobre seu acidente à Wanted e ao Google, ele ainda não recebeu o documento. Um mês após o acidente, o recrutador enviou uma mensagem a Sandu perguntando como estava. E perguntaram:

“[A empresa] está recrutando mais testadores (talvez você conheça pessoas?)”.


Um porta-voz do Google disse à

Investigate Europe

: “Nosso código de conduta de fornecedores e contratos exigem que todos os fornecedores cumpram as leis …

author: Daron Letts
title: Experts decry Nunavut’s ‘Band-Aid’ approach to foster care
content:
The broken child welfare system in Nunavut is rooted in the territorial government’s colonial approach to the problem, say some with years of experience with the system.


“The taking of Indigenous children never stopped at residential school,” said Jeremy Young, who was separated from his mother as a child. “It only continued with foster care.”


Young spoke to Nunatsiaq News about his experience in Nunavut’s foster care system Thursday in response to the latest

report

 by the federal auditor general

 i

nto the territorial government’s handling of youth in its care.


Tuesday’s report, the fifth over 15 years, shows little has changed. The Nunavut government is failing to account for the number of children in its care, failing to do consistent check-ins and failing in its duty to make sure every foster child is put into an appropriate home.


Young, now 26 years old, was taken from his mother as a child in Pangnirtung even though she did her best, Young said.


He blamed overcrowding and poverty for his family’s situation, saying his mother tried for 12 years to get housing for her family but ultimately could not.


“Society has failed Indigenous people,” he said. “That’s why we live in poverty. That’s why we go through the traumas we went through.”


Young believes Inuit self-government is the antidote to the problems in the foster care system.


Rankin Inlet researcher and academic Peter Williamson and Arlene Hache, an advocate with decades of experience working with Indigenous women agree.


Williamson said even if the territorial government finally heeds the auditor general’s

recommendations

 for fixing foster care, which includes

getting a handle

 on its own information management system, it wouldn’t solve the root causes that lead to the removal of children from their families? It would only streamline the system.


“They are identifying the Band-Aid solutions in government instead of fixing the root causes in the communities,” Williamson said.


Unstable housing, low education, unemployment and poverty are risk factors for removing children from their families, Williamson said, citing peer-reviewed studies by North American and Nordic researchers.


“Those are prevalent in Nunavut,” he said.


Mothers forced to enter emergency housing have an even greater risk of having their children taken from them, he added.


Hache agreed, calling the current system a form of “genocide” of Indigenous people.


“When [government workers] go into a family or a community, they are searching for all these problems,” she said. “Because of their colonial mindset and their racism.”


An alternative is an Inuit-led, community-based model that “supports families, recognizes their value and their ability to recover, and provides support, mentorship, and training,” she said.


“Let’s persuade people that they can grow from the place they are to a new place. That’s how elders in Inuit communities think.”


Shortly after the territory’s inception in 1999, the Nunavut government invited Hache on a territory-wide tour to share information about this approach to foster care, she said.


It wasn’t a new idea. Developed and adopted in Hawaii in 1979, it is still in use today.


“It was a well-evidenced model based on world-Indigenous understandings of families and children,” Hache said. “It wasn’t like it was radical or new. But everything in the North is radical and new if it’s not colonial.”


Nunavut rejected the model.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “En esta causa alguien tiene que caer”: las presiones a un policía que declaró en el juicio por la golpiza a jóvenes Qom
content:
Un efectivo denunció que recibió amenazas de sanciones y sumarios por parte de sus superiores cuando debía declarar sobre el allanamiento ilegal y brutal golpiza perpetradas por un grupo de uniformados contra jóvenes de la comunidad Qom de Fontana, Chaco, en mayo de 2020. En la sexta audiencia también declaró un comisario retirado que identificó a varios de los imputados en los registros audiovisuales incorporados al expediente.


La frase expone una arista hasta ahora no conocida del juicio por la golpiza y los hechos de violencia institucional sufridos por integrantes de la comunidad Qom en el barrio Banderas Argentinas de Fontana: las presuntas presiones dentro de la propia fuerza policial para condicionar testimonios durante la investigación. “En esta causa alguien tiene que caer”, habría sido la advertencia que recibió uno de los efectivos que declaró ante el tribunal.


El episodio salió a la luz durante la sexta audiencia del juicio oral y público, realizada el martes, en la que prestaron declaración dos policías que se desempeñaban en Fontana cuando ocurrieron los hechos, en mayo de 2020. Uno de ellos, el oficial principal Héctor Ariel Velázquez, denunció que sus superiores lo amenazaron con sanciones y actuaciones sumariales cuando debía aportar información sobre el procedimiento investigado.


La jornada también dejó otro aporte relevante para la reconstrucción de lo sucedido: el comisario retirado Orlando Ismael Trangoni, quien era segundo jefe de la Comisaría Tercera, reconoció en los registros audiovisuales a varios de los efectivos que hoy están sentados en el banquillo de los acusados.


Las presiones 


Velázquez fue el primero en declarar. En 2020 prestaba servicios en la Comisaría Segunda de Fontana y había intervenido en actuaciones vinculadas con los hechos que ahora se juzgan.


Durante su exposición manifestó tener dificultades para recordar distintos detalles de los procedimientos, una situación que atribuyó a la cantidad de intervenciones policiales en las que había participado. Sin embargo, el interrogatorio dejó al descubierto contradicciones entre sus respuestas ante el tribunal y la declaración que había brindado el 13 de octubre de 2020.


En aquella oportunidad, el efectivo había identificado a integrantes de la fuerza a partir de los registros audiovisuales que hoy forman parte del expediente. Ese antecedente fue confrontado durante la audiencia con sus actuales manifestaciones.


En ese contexto, Velázquez reveló que había recibido presiones de sus superiores cuando debía prestar declaración ante mandos policiales. Según relató, lo amenazaron con sanciones y la apertura de actuaciones sumariales.


Entre los superiores que mencionó se encuentran el comisario mayor Godoy y el comisario Ariel Alejandro Gonzalo González. El testigo describió el mensaje que, según sostuvo, le transmitieron en aquella instancia: “En esta causa alguien tiene que caer”.


La denuncia abre un interrogante sobre el comportamiento de la propia estructura policial durante la investigación y las condiciones en las que se recogieron los testimonios de los efectivos que podían aportar información sobre el operativo.


Reconoció a los policías


El segundo testimonio correspondió a Trangoni, quien se desempeñaba como segundo jefe de la Comisaría Tercera de Fontana al momento de los hechos. Al comenzar, manifestó desconocer los motivos precisos de su citación y expresó dificultades para recordar distintos aspectos del procedimiento.


No obstante, la exhibición de los registros audiovisuales incorporados a la causa permitió avanzar en la identificación de los policías que participaron de los operativos, tanto en la vivienda como dentro de la dependencia.


A partir de esas imágenes, el excomisario reconoció a Diego Adrián Latorre, Orlando Sergio Martín Cabrera, Cristian Eduardo Foschiatti, Cristian Benítez, Cristian Borda y Marcelo Eduardo Blanco. También identificó a Sofía González, a quien señaló como responsable de la guardia.


Trangoni reconoció, además, las maniobras utilizadas por el personal policial para trasladar a las personas aprehendidas hacia el interior de la comisaría.


Otro tramo de su declaración estuvo relacionado con los protocolos que deben aplicarse cuando una persona detenida presenta lesiones. En ese sentido, ratificó que, conforme a las normas de actuación policial y a la Ley de Seguridad Pública, corresponde trasladar inmediatamente a toda persona lesionada a Sanidad Policial.
