title: Προβληματισμοί για τη χάραξη της γραμμής 4 στα Εξάρχεια & γιατί πρέπει να ανοίξει η πλατεία Εξαρχείων
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης:

Προβληματισμοί για τη χάραξη της γραμμής 4 στα Εξάρχεια & γιατί πρέπει να ανοίξει η πλατεία Εξαρχείων


Η εκδήλωση θα μεταδοθεί από το OmniaTV

:


YouTube


PeerTube


Facebook


Η γραμμή 4 του μετρό, το μεγαλύτερο δημόσιο έργο της χώρας, έχει εκτροχιαστεί. Οι σοβαρές ζημιές στα κτίρια της Κυψέλης,  η απόρριψη της μελέτης για τον σταθμό Ριζάρη από το ΣτΕ, οι δικαστικές διαμάχες σε Γουδί, Αλεξάνδρας και Εξάρχεια αποκαλύπτουν ότι ο τρόπος σχεδιασμού του δεν έγινε προς το συμφέρον των ανθρώπων της πόλης, αλλά με γνώμονα τα υπερκέρδη των μεγαλοεργολάβων, θυσιάζοντας την ασφάλεια και την ποιότητα ζωής όλων μας.


Η επιλογή χάραξης της γραμμής – των σημείων που κατασκευάζεται η σήραγγα και που βγαίνουν οι σταθμοί –  οι ελλιπείς και σε κάποιες περιπτώσεις ανύπαρκτες μελέτες για το υπέδαφος, τα κτίρια, το περιβάλλον, η αδιαφορία για τα «θέλω» και τις ανάγκες των ανθρώπων των γειτονιών διαμόρφωσαν εξαρχής ένα ασφυκτικό πλαίσιο. Οι γειτονιές μας έχουν μετατραπεί σε απέραντα εργοτάξια, οι ελεύθεροι χώροι μας καταστρέφονται, τα σπίτια μας, τα σχολεία και τα δημόσια κτίρια κινδυνεύουν. Σε όλα αυτά έρχεται να προστεθεί και η εκτίναξη του κόστους του έργου, που ήδη υπολογίζεται στο μισό δισεκατομμύριο ευρώ, σε συνδυασμό με τις καθυστερήσεις παράδοσής του, αφού πια γίνεται λόγος για το 2036 και αν.


Οι γειτονιές αντιστέκονται και τα Εξάρχεια ήταν από την αρχή μπροστά. Η ανοιχτή συνέλευση «Όχι μετρό στην πλατεία Εξαρχείων» εδώ και 5 χρόνια, με έρευνα και πολλή δουλειά, έχει ξεσκεπάσει με κάθε μέσο που διαθέτει την σκανδαλώδη επιλογή κυβερνήσεων, ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΟ ΜΕΤΡΟ και αναδόχων του έργου να χρησιμοποιήσουν τη γραμμή 4 ως μέσο αλλαγής φυσιογνωμίας της γειτονιάς μας. Η επιλογή κατασκευής του σταθμού στην πλατεία,  όπου ο σταθμός δε χωράει ακόμα και με τεχνικούς όρους, η υποβάθμιση της ζωής των κατοίκων της με την κοπή των δέντρων, τις λαμαρίνες, το κλείσιμο δρόμων κ.ο.κ., η απομόνωση και πραγματική υποβάθμιση των συνθηκών κατοικίας και δραστηριοποίησης στην περιοχή είναι πλέον εμφανείς ακόμα και στους πιο δύσπιστους. Και βέβαια η απάντηση σε όλα αυτά από την πλευρά της κυβέρνησης είναι η καταστολή.


Η πλατεία Εξαρχείων πρέπει να απελευθερωθεί! Όποιος ακόμα επιμένει ότι το έργο αυτό πρέπει ουσιαστικά συναινεί στην καταστροφή όλων αυτών που ορίζουν τι είναι η γειτονιά.


Την Πέμπτη, 5/11, παρουσιάζουμε και συζητάμε μελέτες που αποδεικνύουν την επικινδυνότητα συνέχισης του έργου με τους υπάρχοντες όρους στα Εξάρχεια, ενημερωνόμαστε και προχωράμε ένα βήμα πιο κοντά στην τελική νίκη! Κανείς πλέον δεν μπορεί να ισχυριστεί ότι δεν ήξερε. Όλοι και όλες μαζί θα σώσουμε την πλατεία Εξαρχείων, την ύπαρξή μας στη γειτονιά όπως εμείς την ορίζουμε.

author: Lance Selfa
title: Trumpism swamped at the ballot box
content:
The US midterm elections were a stunning rebuke to President Trump and the Republican Party.

Votes are still being tallied around the country. But the extent of the Democratic Party’s victory is becoming clear. In Congress, Democrats will take office in January 2027 with majorities in both houses that were at the upper end of expectations before the election.

In fact, the national popular vote margin in favour of the Democrats is the largest since the mid-1970s Watergate era, and Democrats could end up with as many as 56 (of 100) senators, up from their current number of 47. That would be the largest Senate majority of either party since 2009. Media estimates predict a House majority of at least 250 Democrats (of 435 House members). That would be the largest House majority for either party since the early 1990s.

Democrats won Senate seats in longtime conservative Republican strongholds like Kansas (which hadn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932), Texas and South Carolina. Democrats made gains in every demographic group and region, compared to Kamala Harris’s performance in the 2024 presidential election.

In 2024, Harris lost a close race to Trump largely because, as the incumbent vice president, she carried the can for the Biden administration’s inability to tackle the inflation eroding working-class living standards. Key to Trump’s victory was his ability to add small, but significant, numbers of inflation-strapped voters among young people and people of colour (especially Latinos) to his “base” of white, middle-class Christian conservatives.

But Trump’s policies—from his erratic tariffs to the war against Iran, to huge cuts to medical assistance to fuel tax cuts to the rich—worsened the ability to afford necessities. What’s more, the administration’s unleashing of camouflaged thugs to arrest, imprison and deport hundreds of thousands of immigrants outraged millions. Democrats also tapped into disgust with the open corruption of Trump and his cronies, along with their disdain for the struggles of ordinary people.

The impact of these Trump actions repulsed all the groups who took a chance on Trump in 2024. Going into the 2026 midterms, opinion polls showed Trump to be the most unpopular president since Harry S. Truman in 1946. So, a pro-Democratic “wave” election wasn’t really in doubt. The question was how high the wave would be when it crested.

As has happened historically, Democratic gains rode atop a surge of Black (and more recently, Latino) voters. After the Supreme Court eviscerated the Voting Rights Act last summer, many civil rights advocates feared the return to political Jim Crow and a strengthening of one-party Republican rule in the southern states. But Black voters’ outrage expressed on 3 November had the impact of breaking through Republican domination in states like North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and even Mississippi.

In Texas, Latino voters forced a generational change and statewide sweep of the state that had become the cradle of post-civil-rights-era Republican politics. If the Republicans, as they are currently constituted, “lose” Texas, they will lose any sort of national political viability for a generation.

The 3 November results do not undermine the case for new civil rights and voting rights protections to undo the damage Trump and the Supreme Court have inflicted on the gains of the 1960s civil rights movement. But they show that breaking what former AFL-CIO political director Michael Podhorzer calls the “

Greater Confederacy

” is possible.

Trump and the Republicans had nothing positive to offer to voters. And they and their deep-pocketed donors spent billions attempting to excite their base with non-stop anti-trans and racist messaging against their Democratic opponents. Abdul el-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, took the full brunt of an Islamophobic campaign against him—not only from his Republican opponent, but also from pro-Israel Democratic Party politicians and operatives.

But all of this failed to rescue Republicans, even in their longtime strongholds. The voting majority rejected these “culture war” appeals, seeing them as deliberate attempts to distract from Republican malfeasance and catering to the rich. When all is said and done, Elon Musk will have figuratively lit half a billion dollars on fire.

It’s important to understand the election as a repudiation of Trump and Republican rule, not an endorsement of whatever it is the …

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: The End of the Trump Era: The Democratic Sweep of the Midterm Elections
content:
Early this morning, I was woken up by a text from my daughter in Atlanta, nine hours behind Sharjah, UAE, where I’m currently located. Dems are leading, she exclaimed. Can you chat for a quick second? Before I called her, she sent another text, saying, it’s breaking news: Keisha Lance Bottoms is the projected winner as Governor of Georgia. My daughter, who has lived in Atlanta since she went to university there in the early 2000s, was ecstatic beyond measure.


Our celebratory chatter woke up my wife, a political scientist and keen observer of American politics. The ancestors must be smiling, she proclaimed with giddy excitement. We switched on the television and followed the elections on American stations we had access to, including CNN International and Bloomberg, while simultaneously perusing newspapers including The New York Times and The Guardian.


The more we talked and thought about the unfolding election results, I couldn’t help and filtering the elections through Africanist and global lenses, the clearer it became that this stunning blue wave, which polls had been predicting, represented political triumph in five dimensions, what I would the 5Ds: democrats, democracy, diversity, demography, and development.


The Democratic Victory


The Democrats won a resounding victory. Their victories swept the electoral map in Congress and across red states, as they held on to their constituencies. It was a political tsunami that routed President Donald Trump and the Republicans in a stunning rebuke of their failed policies and divisive politics, in which diversionary and inflammatory cultural wars trumped the deteriorating material conditions and interests of the electorate.


Democrats seized both chambers of Congress. Their candidates flipped seven Republican seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas, red states some of which had not elected a Democrat in decades. They retained seats in five states, namely, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, and Virginia.


At the time of writing, the Democrats had flipped 35 seats previously held by Republicans in the House, including multiple seats in states won by Trump by more than 10 points such as Texas, Iowa, Florida, and Pennsylvania, along with key wins in Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio, and Utah. They successfully defended all or nearly all of their incumbent districts , including 22 that were considered vulnerable because Trump carried them by more than 10 points in the 2024 election, and are projected to win 242 to 258 seats when all the votes are counted, 40 more than they need to form a majority.


In a tectonic shift, at the time of writing, with 32 of the 36 seats contested, Democrats had also flipped five state governorships from Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, and Nevada, and successfully defended 15 states. They won a total of 29, earning a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010.


So far, with final calls still processing, Democrats have flipped 12 of the 88 state legislative chambers on the ballot from Republican control in Pennsylvania (Senate; they already controlled the House), Wisconsin (both chambers), Arizona (putting Republicans in a legislative minority for the first time in 26 years), North Carolina (House), and drastically broke Republican supermajorities in states like Florida, South Carolina, and Indiana. They successfully defended 25 legislative chambers, including competitive ones in states like Maine, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington, where they were able to preserve existing Democratic trifectas.


Similarly, Democrats dramatically outperformed Republicans in races for attorney general and secretary of state offices. For the former, the biggest upsets were in Texas and Georgia, while key defensive holds included Nevada and Michigan. Democrats also won the majority of contested secretary of state offices, seizing several from Republicans and holding those they held before.


The Resurgence of Democracy


America’s beleaguered democracy won. Electoral democracy in the United States has always been compromised by gerrymandering, voter suppression, politicization of the judiciary, and the financialization of politics. funding. This is why a conservative outfit like The Economist considers the United States a flawed, rather than a full, democracy compared to its increasingly alienated Western allies such as Canada.


Gerrymandering spectacularly backfired for Republicans …

title: Tekirdağ'ın Saray ilçesinde taşkın: Köprü kapatıldı, mahsur kalan 2 kişi kurtarıldı

Safaalan Mahallesi'nde ise su baskını tehdidi altındaki bir ev ekipler tarafından boşaltıldı. Evde yaşayan 6 kişilik aile, Saray Belediyesi tarafından otele yerleştirildi.

Sağanağın etkili olması beklenen ilçede belediye ekipleri, yaşanabilecek olumsuzluklara karşı tedbir amacıyla hazır bekletiliyor.

author: Unknown
title: Şüpheli şekilde yaşamını yitiren Nurcan Akpirinç’in dosyasında 5 aydır gelişme yok
content:
Diyarbakır'ın Bağlar ilçesinde 20 Haziran’da evinde şüpheli bir şekilde ölü bulunan 23 yaşındaki Nurcan Akpirinç’in ölümüne ilişkin soruşturma sürerken, aradan geçen 5 aya rağmen otopsi raporu hâlâ çıkmadı. Anne Asiye Akpirinç, kızı ve katledilen tüm kadınlar için adalet talebinde bulundu.

Olay günü mahalleye ambulans geldiğini 4 ay sonra öğrendiklerini belirten Asiye Akpirinç, birinin 112'yi arayıp yardım istediğini, ambulanstakilerin mahalleye gelip arayanı bulamayarak geri gittiğini söyledi. Kızının sağlık ekiplerini arayıp yardım istediğine inandığını ifade eden anne Akpirinç, bu durumun ve 112 çağrısının detaylı bir şekilde araştırılmasını istedi.

Kızının ölümünün üzerinden 5 ay geçmesine rağmen otopsi raporunun hâlâ çıkmadığını ve verdikleri dilekçelere her seferinde "incelemede" yanıtı aldıklarını kaydeden Asiye Akpirinç, "Kaç defa dilekçe verdik, otopsi raporunu istiyoruz. Kızımın 112’yi arayıp yardım istediğinin araştırılmasını istiyoruz. Neden hâlâ bize bir cevap verilmiyor?" diye tepki gösterdi.

Kızının alnında ve sağ kulağının arkasında darp izleri gördüğünü belirten anne Akpirinç, M.A. ve annesi C.A. tarafından sürekli şiddete uğradığını ifade etti. Olay günü kendilerine bilgi verilmediğini, kızının evde olmadığının söylenerek köyde aranmasının istendiğini, saatler sonra ise aynı evde yaşamını yitirdiğini öğrendiklerini aktaran Akpirinç, "Kızımın intihar ettiğine inanmıyorum" dedi.

Sorumluların açığa çıkarılmasını ve cezalandırılmasını talep eden Asiye Akpirinç, "Adalet istiyorum. Hükümet sesimizi duysun, savcılar, hâkimler sesimizi duysun. Sadece kızım için değil, katledilen bütün kadınlar için adalet istiyorum. Başka annelerin canı yanmasın. Bu işin peşini bırakmayacağız, sonuna kadar mücadele edeceğiz" ifadelerini kullandı.

Diyarbakır'ın Bağlar ilçesinde 20 Haziran’da dini nikahla evli olduğu aktarılan M.A. ile tartıştıktan sonra annesini arayan Nurcan Akpirinç ailesinin yanına gitmek istemişti. Kızlarından haber alamayan ailenin evine gitmesi üzerine Nurcan’ın evde olmadığı söylenmiş, yaklaşık iki saat sonra ise evin misafir odasında yaşamını yitirdiği ortaya çıkmıştı. Aile, Nurcan’ın daha önce defalarca tehdit edildiğini belirtmesine rağmen 5 aylık süreçte otopsi raporunun çıkmadığı ve yalnızca aile bireylerinin ifadesinin alındığı bildirilmişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Mekke Anlaşması Meclis’te: İlk madde Genel Kurul'dan geçti
content:
Türkiye, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan arasında imzalanan Mekke Ortak Savunma Anlaşması'nın onaylanmasına ilişkin kanun teklifi Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi (TBMM) Genel Kurulu'nda görüşülüyor.


Genel Kurulda, teklifin tümü üzerinde görüşmelerin tamamlanmasının ardından maddelerinin görüşmelerine geçildi.


Teklifin ilk maddesi de gece saatlerinde kabul edildi. Bunun üzerine TBMM Başkanvekili Celal Adan, birleşime ara verdi. Diğer maddeler üzerindeki görüşmeler bugün 14.00’te devam edecek.


Ancak dün akşamki görüşmeler tartışmalı geçti. İktidar ve muhalefet partileri anlaşmanın Türkiye açısından nasıl askeri yükümlülükler doğuracağı ve ülkeyi bölgesel çatışmalara dahil edip etmeyeceği üzerinden tartıştı. 


AKP ve MHP anlaşmanın bölgesel güvenliği ve caydırıcılığı güçlendireceğini savunurken, CHP de barış ve iş birliğine katkı sağlayacağı gerekçesiyle destek vereceğini açıkladı.


YENİ Parti, DEM Parti, İYİ Parti ve Yeni Yol ise Türkiye'nin üstleneceği askeri yükümlülüklerin belirsizliğine ve bölgesel çatışmalara dahil olma riskine dikkat çekti. Askerin yurt dışında görevlendirilmesi ve olası savaş riskleri üzerinden tartışmalar yaşandı.


Genel Kurul görüşmelerinden öne çıkanlar


AKP Kayseri Milletvekili Hulusi Akar, anlaşmanın Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan'la mevcut askeri iş birliklerini kurumsallaştırmayı amaçladığını belirterek, "Bu anlaşma hiçbir şekilde NATO'ya alternatif vesaire değil; bu tamamlayıcı bir birliktelik ve hiçbir ülkeye de karşı değil" dedi. Akar,  askerin yurt dışında görevlendirilmesinin söz konusu olması halinde bunun "mutlaka Meclisin iznine tabi" olacağını söyledi.


MHP Erzurum Milletvekili Kamil Aydın da anlaşmanın "kolektif caydırıcılığı artıracağını" savunarak MHP grubunun teklife destek vereceğini açıkladı.


CHP Grup Başkanı Faik Öztrak ise anlaşmanın yeni çatışmaların değil, bölgesel barış ve iş birliğinin aracı olması gerektiğini söyledi. Öztrak, "Bu iş birliğinden doğan güç yeni savaşlar açmak için değil savaştan caydırmak, barışı sağlamak, sınırlarımızı korumak ve ticareti geliştirmek için kullanılmalıdır" diyerek CHP'nin anlaşmaya olumlu oy vereceğini açıkladı.


İYİ Parti ise anlaşmanın sınırlarının belirsiz olduğunu savundu. Grup adına konuşan Lütfü Türkkan, "Bizim itirazımız işbirliğine değil, belirsizliğedir, ortak savunmaya değil sınırları çizilmemiş yükümlülükleredir" dedi. Türkkan, Türkiye'nin askeri ve mali yükümlülükleri ile bölgesel çatışmalara taraf olma riskine karşı güvencelerin açıklığa kavuşturulmasını istedi.


DEM Parti Antalya Milletvekili Saruhan Oluç da Türkiye'nin yeni vekalet savaşlarına dahil edilmemesi gerektiğini belirterek, "Türkiye herhangi bir vekalet savaşının parçası olmamalıdır, bunu reddediyoruz" dedi. DEM Parti Diyarbakır Milletvekili Ceylan Akça Cupolo ise partisinin "hayır" oyu vereceğini açıklayarak, "Gözümüz kapalı bir şekilde savaşa gitmeyi reddediyoruz" ifadelerini kullandı.


Yeni Yol Grubu'ndan Hasan Karal, savunma iş birliklerinin güçlendirilmesini desteklediklerini ancak askeri yükümlülüklerin ve Meclis'in denetim yetkisinin açık biçimde belirlenmesi gerektiğini söyledi. Karal, "Bu konulardaki belirsizlikler giderilmediği için kanun teklifine mevcut haliyle olumlu yaklaşamadığımızı ifade ediyorum" dedi. Aynı gruptan Selçuk Özdağ da anlaşmaya ret oyu verdiklerini açıkladı.


YENİ Parti İstanbul Milletvekili Namık Tan ise anlaşmanın Türkiye'yi sınırları belirsiz askeri operasyonlara sürükleyebileceğini savundu. "Mehmetçik'in asli görevi Suudi vatanını değil, kendi vatanımızı korumaktır" diyen Tan, anlaşmaya karşı olduklarını söyledi.


TBMM Dışişleri Komisyonu Başkanı Fuat Oktay ise eleştirilere yanıt verirken anlaşmanın otomatik olarak asker gönderilmesi anlamına gelmediğini savundu. "Anlaşma onaylandığı takdirde, Suud çöllerine Türk askerini, Mehmetçik'i gönderiyoruz... Böyle bir uygulama da söz konusu değil, böyle bir şey de yok" diyen Oktay, olası adımların tarafların değerlendirmesi ve oydaşmasıyla belirleneceğini söyledi. Oktay'a göre destek; istihbarat ve tecrübe paylaşımından ekipman desteğine veya askeri karşılığa kadar farklı biçimler alabilecek.


Oktay ayrıca, anlaşmanın ilk 10 yılında çekilmeye getirilen sınırlamayı savunarak bunun uzun vadeli stratejik anlaşmaların doğasından kaynaklandığını söyledi. "10 yıl süre içerisinde de herhangi bir konuda oydaşma sağlanamazsa [...] Türkiye'nin arzu etmediği bir konunun uygulamaya alınması asla ve asla mümkün değildir" dedi.

author: Menchani Tilendo
title: Women tending the Kasibu barricades against large-scale mining
content:
At the barricade, she has found her place by turning its often-invisible work of care into a collective act of resistance.


KASIBU, Nueva Vizcaya – In this third class municipality some 300 kilometers north of Luzon, land is life. It feeds families, sustains Indigenous communities, and carries generations of history. Yet under Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s banner of “development,” mining expansion threatens to dispossess communities of the very land that keeps them alive. 


In defense of their land, the people of Kasibu set up the people’s barricade against large-scale mining. Their steadfastness was met with force when on

August 28

this year, police arrested 11 locals of Barangay Paquet for blocking the entry of North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC).


They were later released on bail, but the crackdown has not ended because members of the community continue to face

trumped-up criminal charges

 or what advocates consider as Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP). 


The NLMRC is the seventh company to attempt exploration in the area. It holds a government-issued exploration permit covering 4,456 hectares across parts of Kasibu, where it seeks to explore for gold, copper, and other minerals. 


It is no coincidence that mining companies have their eyes on Kasibu. Beneath its mineral-rich mountains lie the farmlands and watersheds that sustain its people. Known as the Citrus Capital of Luzon, the municipality grows calamansi, other citrus fruits, and vegetables, while the 18,417-hectare Kasibu Watershed forms part of a vital network of watersheds in the Sierra Madre. 


For farmers already struggling with high production costs and potential losses of P25,000 ($392.63) to P150,000 ($2,355.75) per cropping cycle, mining threatens to worsen their hardships. They fear contamination of soil and water, as well as landslides, droughts, and floods. The drive to extract mineral wealth destroys the land that feeds communities and sustains generations. 


But the people of Kasibu have never surrendered their land. Their resistance dates back to 2007, when the Kasibu Inter-Tribal Response for Ecological Development (KIRED) emerged from the community’s struggle against large-scale mining. Alongside the Alyansa ng Novo Vizcayano para sa Kalikasan (ANVIK), they have helped sustain a network of barricades against successive mining ventures. 


There are currently six barricades standing across Kasibu, positioned along routes that mining operations could use to advance into community lands. The main barricade in Barangay Paquet has drawn more than 100 regular members, with more joining when the community calls for reinforcements.


Women play a central role in sustaining this resistance. 


At least 300 women are part of the wider community barricades, taking on leadership roles and helping sustain their operations. As mining threatens their livelihoods and ancestral lands, these women are fighting for their families’ right to remain on, live from, and care for the land they call home.


Nanay Linda: Never giving up


Nanay Linda, 60 years old.


At 60, Linda Kuruko knows the weight of a life spent working the land. Born in Lamot, Ifugao, she grew up in poverty before her family settled in Kasibu in search of a better life. She has spent years as a farmer, making ends meet even when harvest prices fall. 


“I’m still strong—if I don’t work, I won’t have anything to eat,” she told

Bulatlat

 in Filipino. 


Despite the exhaustion that comes with age, she continues to climb the mountain to join the barricade. She and her son have even built a small hut uphill so they can stay close to the community’s defense line.


Her determination is rooted in what she has witnessed in Didipio, a neighboring village in Kasibu where

OceanaGold

operates a large-scale gold and copper mine. She has seen how mining can damage the land and leave slopes vulnerable to erosion and landslides during heavy rains. She fears Kasibu’s communities will suffer the same fate if mining operations continue. 


But fear has never been reason enough for Nanay Linda to surrender. She knows the hardship of living harvest to harvest, and she knows what losing the land would mean for families who depend on it. Despite the harassment and the strain of waiting at the barricade for possible confrontations, she continues to stand with her fellow defenders.


“Sometimes, I feel hurt by what they do to us, but I try to keep my composure so I don’t …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Protecting the mangrove paradise in Tacloban
content:
For Gilda Salazar Laag, if it were not for the mangroves, more would have been dead from Yolanda.


By Agatha Canape


CANCABATO BAY, Tacloban City – Gilda Salazar Laag, 69, recalled that she and her fellow volunteers found human bones when they tilled the muddy soil to plant the mangrove seedlings in Paraiso, which literally means paradise, a couple of months after supertyphoon Yolanda (international name: Haiyan) struck. 


On November 8, 2013, the storm surge in Tacloban began at 7:00 a.m. and lasted until 8:30 am, submerging the city in seven meters of water. “Atop their roof, we witnessed the cries of people who could not be rescued as they were swept by the floods,” Laag said. The typhoon left thousands of people dead, millions displaced, and destroyed 90 percent of the city. Twenty-three people of those killed were from Paraiso.


Laag’s home was totally destroyed by the typhoon. Originally from Catarman, Northern Samar before she married, Laag was asked by her extended family to come back to her hometown while the city has yet to recover. She refused as her family feared losing whatever was left of their home. They rebuilt their home on the same lot where it was destroyed using materials that could be salvaged from its ruins.  


Besides, Laag was tasked to deliver relief to households in the barangay. As a barangay health worker, she was knowledgeable about the number of people and needs of every household, and the nooks and crannies of the barangay.


Gilda, 69 years old, served as a barangay health worker in Paraiso for more than half of her life. She is one of the members of the local organization that started the mangrove reforestation in Paraiso in 2014, only a couple of months after Typhoon Yolanda.

 (Photo by Agatha Canape)


Relief and recovery efforts bled into the next year. In February 2014, they were gathered by their barangay captain to look after the mangroves next. 


Yolanda flattened the two-hectare mangrove forest in Paraiso to 0.2 hectares (2000 square meters), or merely 20 percent of the original coverage. The reforestation team started with 25 people, eight of whom were women. 


The barangay, with support from international non-government organizations, procured seedlings which they potted, tended to in a nursery for two years before planting along the land at the edge of Cancabato Bay. Through their hands, they have grown back the mangrove forest and made it denser than before.


Paraiso was brought back to life. Between 2015 and 2018, approximately 30,000 mangrove seedlings were planted. According to a study, the mangrove forest cover in Paraiso increased by 80 percent compared to its pre-disaster state, expanding from two hectares to 5.18 hectares. In 2019, the Paraiso Mangrove Eco-Learning Park was opened to the public.


Satellite image of the mangrove forest in Paraiso, November 10, 2013. (Google Earth image)


Satellite image of the mangrove forest in Paraiso, November 3, 2026. (Google Earth image)


Mangrove rehabilitation and reforestation in Paraiso began in early 2014, a couple of months after Yolanda. In 2019, the Paraiso Mangrove Eco-Learning Park was opened to the public.

 (Photo by Agatha Canape)


Today, Paraiso is once again under threat. The multi-billion Tacloban Causeway Project, a 2.55-kilometer road embankment and land reclamation project that will directly connect the Daniel Romualdez Airport to downtown Tacloban, is slowly killing the Cancabato Bay. 


The city government, in the first volume of the Tacloban City Comprehensive Land Use Plan 2017-2025 claimed that the bay is “polluted and dying” to justify the plan to reclaim and convert it into a new central business district. (The plan has since been revised into a third volume where this claim has been removed. It is the only version available on the city government’s website.) 


Rodolfo “Rudy” Delliva, 71, debunked the city government’s claims.


Delliva, a fisher who earns his living by catching blue swimming crabs, was among the volunteers who restored the mangroves along Cancabato Bay.


“Alive. It’s very much alive,” Delliva said about Cancabato Bay. He then enumerated the sea creatures he has known in the bay:

danggit

 (rabbitfish/spinefoot),

iito

 (catfish),

lumong

 (whipfin silverbiddy),

tamban

 (sardines),

mangagat

 (mangrove red snapper),

tingag

 (grouper),

aguyong

,

kirawan, punaw

 (clam), and many more. 


The efforts of the community for the past decade have revived the mangrove …

author: Jerome Small
title: Debt angst is class war
content:
A flood of water, meant to symbolise debt, flows from the Victorian parliament, inundating suburban streets and living rooms while a scared child watches on. AI-generated ads like this, sponsored by right-wing outfit Fix Victoria, will be familiar to anyone in the state. 

Overwhelmingly, the media narrative is that Australia in general and Victoria in particular is drowning in debt. We’re told there’s no choice except brutal cuts to health, education, and other government spending. 

This is a powerful narrative, but a false one. 

It is being used by the ruling class to force workers to accept cuts, and to attack Labor governments federally and in Victoria. Labor is already bowing to this pressure by implementing cuts to vital services and implementing sharp cuts to real wages, except where union revolts threaten a crisis. 

Contrary to this right-wing myth, neither Victoria nor Australia is drowning in debt. Total government debt (combining both federal and state) has 

risen

 from 40 percent to 52 percent of gross domestic product over the past decade. But this level of debt is still relatively low by international standards—well below the UK (102 percent of GDP), Spain (97 percent), Canada (115 percent) and plenty of others. According to the International Monetary Fund, the “advanced economies” have an average government debt of 107% of GDP, more than double that of Australia.

Around the world, however, ruling class concern over debt levels—and who will pay that debt—has been sharpened by the sudden spike in global inflation and interest rates since mid-2021. The inflationary surge was fuelled initially by dislocations from the pandemic, and then by a series of “geopolitical shocks”—a euphemistic term for brutal imperialist wars—first Russia invading Ukraine in 2022, and more recently the US and Israel’s attack on Iran. These disrupted energy markets and pushed up the price of oil and gas, causing a global price shock. 

Surging demand for capital to fuel the AI bubble is also pushing global inflation and interest rates higher, as are rapidly expanding US deficits to fund Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and rearmament to prepare for war with China. 

None of these factors driving borrowing costs higher were created by working-class people, let alone by those of us who happen to live in Victoria. But around the world, and in every state, it’s working-class people who are expected to endure the increased cost of finance—through below-inflation wage rises, and by seeing vital services cut. 

In Victoria, Labor’s ambitious infrastructure agenda is at the centre of the right-wing campaign against the government. Initially, though, there was little serious ruling-class concern over this. 

Few disputed the need to update Melbourne’s rail infrastructure, or remove its plentiful level crossings. Melbourne still has nearly 

100

, despite the extensive program of removals, compared to just a 

handful

remaining in Sydney. Notably, removal of level crossings is a boon to road transport of all sorts—including major freight companies and small businesses, as well as commuters of all classes. 

Prior to Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel, the last major expansion of the city’s rail infrastructure was the City Loop, built under the state Liberal governments of the 1960s and 70s and opened by Labor in the early 1980s. And despite the river of anti-union propaganda about the construction unions, it's simply 

not the case

 that cost overruns on Victoria’s Big Build are substantially different to similar projects in New South Wales or elsewhere. 

Victoria is also far from the only state which financed infrastructure by taking out loans during a period of historically low interest rates. Victoria’s debt of $160 billion is 

higher

 than New South Wales at $117 billion, but both states have the same 

debt rating

 from international agencies—along with every Australian state except Western Australia, which enjoys massive royalty flows from iron ore and gas. Liberal and Labor governments in New South Wales in recent years found $65 billion for a series of massive new 

Metro rail projects

, $20 billion for the gigantic WestConnex tunnel, and a few billion here and there to help pay for a new international airport, a city tram system, and sundry other projects.

Former Premier Daniel Andrews’ approach to achieving its ambitious infrastructure agenda did not depend on increased taxes when it was launched. Instead, like similarly …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: The women of Davao Oriental protecting Balete Bay
content:
Amid the warming climate and the looming impacts of large-scale extractive mining projects, women like Peralez, Millomeda, and Decena, from fishing, farming, and religious backgrounds across Mati City have come together to protect one of the most ecologically critical areas in their town. 


By Michelle Mikiko Pagaran


Along the coast of Balete Bay, women farmers, fisherfolk, advocates, and church workers across Mati, Davao Oriental are coming together and turning to collective action and organic farming to protect their coasts, and adapt to extreme weather impacts of climate change.


A small mangrove grows amid thick aerial root networks in Balete Bay, Davao Oriental

.

(Photo by Michelle Pagaran)


Tucked quietly along the coast of Mati, Davao Oriental is Balete Bay, a small inlet along the southern border of the province. Known as a breeding ground for various fish species, reef species and lobsters, the bay is of great ecological significance. A marine inlet, its cove-like structure hosts seagrass beds, diverse reef fisheries, and abundant mangroves.


A sanctuary of corals, mangroves, and commercially vital fisheries, the bay is important for local fisherfolk who depend on it for their livelihood. It serves as a breeding ground for shellfish and wild lobster fry.


In 1994, it was declared a NIPAS protected area as part of the 20,873.43 hectare Pujada Bay Protected Landscape and Seascape, through Presidential Proclamation 431. It is an inlet of the larger Pujada Bay which was declared one of the Most Beautiful Bays in the World in 2020.


Amidst its ecological importance, locals in Mati near the coast and further upland experience the growing impacts of climate change amid a backdrop of looming impacts from extractive industries surrounding the area.


Low tide at the Balete Bay. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)


Mangroves and Marine Resources Crucial to Local Fisherfolk


Christine Peralez recalled her fondest memory of the bay.


“My fondest memory of the bay is playing among the mangroves when we were children. We would play amongst its roots. The mangrove was our playground. We would play pretend. We gathered shells that cling to the roots, collected them, and those were what we pretended to sell”, she said in an interview with Bulatlat.


Peralez was born in Bigue. She recounted her childhood growing up in a fishing community in sitio Bigue, one of the communities along Balete Bay. She would help her parents catch fish and play amongst the mangroves in the coast of the bay.

Their house before was right by the sea. Whenever there was high tide, the sea would go under their house.


“As kids we would bathe right under our house every time it was high tide. That’s why my hair was always bleached yellow,” she said.


Peralez, 32, grew up along the coast of Balete Bay, helping her father, a fisherman, catch fish and sea cucumbers. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)


“Before, we hardly felt how difficult life was, thanks to our parents’ hard work. My father was a fisherman. Mostly gathering shellfish and sea cucumbers. He was the go-to person for people looking to order shellfish and sea cucumbers, or what we call bat. Sometimes when he couldn’t go diving, he would go line fishing or spear fishing. That’s really how we survived. Through his fishing,” Peralez said.


She recounted that her father would catch fish for their own consumption. Her father’s catch was also enough for selling at the market to provide for their daily needs.


She speaks about her childhood with fondness, recalling how the bay, teeming with fish, gave their father a livelihood and provided their family with food on the table.


“Manginhas”. Locals forage for shellfish, sea cucumbers, and seafood during low tide at the bay. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)


“

I used to join in net fishing back then so that the catch was strictly ours to share, without having to divide it with other people. I heard stories from the old days that before, fish would almost swim up to you. Because they were so abundant, fish back then would reach right up to the shore,” Peralez said.


But times have changed since then. Fishing has been harder, especially amid the rising heat. 


She said that back then, her father did not have to go far to gather shellfish. She recalled how easily her father could get shellfish across their house in Bigue. 


“Today my father can no longer fish right across from our house. He has to go far to get to more abundant areas of shellfish.” …

author: Kodao Productions
title: The Philippines’ ‘solar surge’ leaves many Filipinos behind
content:
Amid increasing energy prices, Filipinos are turning to solar – but upfront costs mean it remains out of reach for those who most need savings


By

Samantha Beltran / Dialogue Earth


ids Salvador Badilles, a doctor in Las Piñas, a city just south of the Philippines’ capital Manila, transitioned to solar power and electric vehicles to offset rising costs from the energy crisis. In June, her family installed a 12.6-kilowatt, 20-panel system, as well as a 12-kilowatt solar hybrid inverter and 32-kilowatt-hour batteries.


“We are saving so much already on gas and monthly electric consumption,” Badilles tells Dialogue Earth. Her family now saves PHP 20,000 (USD 315) each month for a system that cost them PHP 700,000 (around USD 11,000), she notes: “Even air conditioning [for the whole day] is not a problem anymore.”


Jovi Solomon, a café owner in Bataan province, installed a 40-kilowatt (KW) solar panel system to offset her business’s electricity costs, setting her back PHP 880,000. She says this allows her to save PHP 10,000 a month on her power bill.


Interest in solar power has surged as Filipinos grapple with skyrocketing electricity rates that have worsened since the Gulf conflict began in late February. However, the trend has also highlighted the stark gap between those who can afford solar options and those who are priced out.


A

Reuters report

 from June 2026 indicated that the Philippines imported USD 407 million worth of solar panels from China between March and May, a year-on-year increase of 145%. It estimates that the median Filipino household now spends around 12% of its monthly income on electricity.


Residential installations – solar panels that are below 100 KW or are registered under the Philippines Net-Metering Program – make up around 245 megawatts (MW) of the country’s 1,846-MW solar capacity, according to

2025 data

 from the Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities. While the majority of that capacity is from utility-scale installations (projects above 1 MW), residential installations have outpaced commercial installations (projects above 100 KW).


= = = =


What is net metering?:

A billing mechanism that credits solar panel owners for excess energy produced that is sent back to the grid


= = = = =


A

survey

 of 20 solar companies in April by clean energy non-profit New Energy Nexus said that customer inquiries were up by an average of

582%

. Weekly rooftop installations rose 170% on average from before the energy crisis began, it noted.


Alnie Demoral, Asia energy analyst at the think-tank Ember, says that with the Philippines’ largest electricity provider Meralco’s rates at around PHP 14.5 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in

June

, “a household rooftop system now pays for itself in about three years”. The utility’s rates have since

risen

 to nearly PHP 15.1 per kWh, a 16% increase from January.


“Our earlier

estimate

 of roughly 1,300 MW of rooftop solar by April is likely conservative today,” she says.


While updated official figures have yet to be released, “every indicator we’ve seen since May points to Filipinos adopting rooftop solar faster than ever”, Demoral adds.


Interest, not installations


Despite the spike in interest in solar power adoption, it remains inaccessible to many in the Philippines.


A single solar panel unit capable of powering direct current devices like lights and mobile devices could cost PHP 4,000-6,000 (USD 63-94) each, according to John Mark Napao, an electrical engineer and founder of Solar Hope, a non-profit that provides off-grid electrification to rural and Indigenous communities through solar power.


That amount is a considerable fraction of the

national average minimum wage

 of PHP 510 a day or PHP 11,100 a month as of April, as aggregated by the Ibon Foundation, a think-tank. A solar power system with an inverter – needed to run appliances such as air conditioners and refrigerators – would cost much more. For example, a basic, 630-watt-peak grid-tie solar system from Solaric, which is connected to the utility grid,

starts

 at PHP 114,000.


Sheryl Estella, program manager at New Energy Nexus Philippines, says that while the non-profit has been observing strong consumer interest in solar, this does not necessarily translate into actual installations.


“The upfront cost of a solar PV [photovoltaic] system can represent several years of electricity expenses for a household, making the initial investment difficult for many families …

author: Leanne Sanders
title: AFN, other defendants delaying lawsuit by former national chief, lawyer says
content:
It has been five months since a judge issued a court order requiring the Assembly of First Nations and the other parties named in a lawsuit by former national chief RoseAnne Archibald to produce their documents by July 31.

Nearly three months later, Archibald’s lawyer says they’re still waiting.

David Shiller said the AFN and the other parties remain in breach of that order, forcing the matter back before the court for another case conference and another delay.

“Oral examination for discovery (was to) occur, between November second and November 9th,” Shiller said in an interview with APTN News. He added that they’ve still not received the required documents. On July 31, 2026, what they delivered to me was what they called a draft affidavit of documents, and it was only purporting to be from the AFN.

“There was nothing delivered on behalf of the individual defendants who were the individual members of the executive committee.”

The affidavit of documents is a form that comes from the court that discloses relevant evidence related to a case.

“What they delivered was a document that says ‘I, blank, of the town of blank, in the county of blank, affirm I am the blank, of the Assembly of First Nations.’ It wasn’t a sworn affidavit of documents. It was a draft,” Shiller said. “And that’s not just a technical difference. The whole point of making each side swear an affidavit is to get them to tell the other side and the court that they have done a diligent search of their records.

APTN reached out to AFN for comment and received a statement that said it can’t comment on a legal case but that the organization ”remains committed to meeting its legal obligations to the courts.”

Archibald launched the lawsuit June 14, 2022, naming the regional chiefs of the AFN at the time of her dismissal. Those regional chiefs include Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, Paul Prosper, Ghislain Picard, Glen Hare, Joanne Bernard, Kluane Adamek, Terry Teegee, Bobby Cameron, Darlene Bernard, Junior Gould and Gerald Antoine.

Woodhouse Nepinak is now the national chief, Prosper is a sitting senator, while Picard and Bernard are retired.

She also named the AFN as a whole, as well as the National Indian Brotherhood and the executive committee comprised of the regional chiefs.

Archibald is seeking damages of $5 million for “breach of contract and oppression; indemnity for the legal fees incurred by the plaintiff from July, 2021 through June, 2022 in connection with the campaign to sideline her and oust her from the Assembly of First Nations,” according to the statement of claim.

She is also seeking the legal fees she incurred in order to respond to her “unlawful suspension of her employment and the unlawful prohibition imposed on her by the Executive Committee of the Assembly of First Nations in connection with the 2022 Annual General Assembly and the Chiefs and Assembly meetings,” according to the statement of claim.

In its statement of defence, filed in Ontario Superior Court on Feb. 6, 2026, the AFN and the other defendants said they “deny each and every allegation contained in the Statement of Claim…” and that “the relief sought in paragraph 1 of the statement of claim is grossly excessive, exaggerated, inflated, and too remote and not commensurate with any losses, damages, or expenses, if any, sustained by the Plaintiff.”

The statement also said the defendants specifically deny that they initiated or engaged in any campaign of retaliation against Archibald and they have “no knowledge of any campaign to sideline and oust” Archibald from the Assembly of First Nations and that she must offer “strict proof” of the allegation.

They also deny that the defendants conspired to trigger workplace-harassment complaints against the plaintiff and also denies that the four complaints themselves were part of any conspiracy and that the Executive Committee exceeded its jurisdiction… or that there was an abuse of power by the Executive Committee as alleged.”

Archibald served as the AFN regional chief for Ontario from 2018 until she ran for national chief and won in 2021. She butted heads with then national chief Perry Bellegarde over “serious issues regarding the way the AFN and the Executive Committee were run,” according to her statement of claim.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Mississaugas of the Credit invests $15M million to become shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada
content:
Mississaugas of the Credit in Ontario has invested $15 million in First Nations Bank of Canada, becoming one of the bank’s largest shareholders with an ownership stake of approximately 10 per cent.

The $15-million dollar investment for an approximate 10 per cent stake values First Nation Bank of Canada at roughly $150 million

The deal, announced Wednesday at Canadian Club in Toronto, completes a $50 million capital raise by the bank and brings the total number of First Nations and shareholders to 117.

Chief Margaret Sault said the investment is part of the Nation’s long-term economic strategy.

“This investment represents an important step forward in our Nation’s commitment to building a strong and sustainable economic future for our people,” Sault said. “By becoming a major shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada, we are investing in an opportunity to build long-term wealth for our community with a partner who understands our needs and aspirations.

“Meaningful participation in the Canadian economy includes having ownership in the institutions that help drive and shape its future. We see this investment as an opportunity to create lasting benefits for future generations,” she added.

FNBC president and CEO Bill Lomax said the addition of Mississaugas of the Credit strengthens the bank’s founding vision.

“Today, we are building a growing national bank, supported by First Nations and Indigenous shareholders from across the country, and well positioned to pursue the significant opportunities ahead.”

“For 30 years, First Nations Bank of Canada has been focused on building a strong, successful financial institution dedicated to serving Indigenous communities,” Lomax said. “With the addition of Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation as a major shareholder, that founding vision is stronger than ever.”

According to Lomax, the investment will allow FNBC to loan more money to First Nations businesses for community infrastructure and economic development.

The bank, founded in 1996, is Canada’s only Indigenous-owned chartered bank. It operates 22 branches and service centres across six provinces and three territories, manages more than $1.625 billion in assets.

Fintrac imposes penalty on First Nations Bank of Canada

For First Nations, equity ownership in a federally regulated bank represents a shift from being primarily clients of mainstream financial institutions to being owners.

Lomax has described the institution as doing “the economic part of reconciliation and the financial part of nation-building.”

Other First Nations have said that having a stake in the bank gives them the ability to keep money within the community rather than extracting it.

Mississaugas of the Credit, the sole Treaty holder in the Greater Toronto and Golden Horseshoe region — an area that generates roughly 25 per cent of Canada’s GDP — framed the investment as both “economic and generational.”

The announcement included a fireside discussion with Sault, Coun. Larry Sault, Lomax and was moderated by Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers.

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

title: At least 25 people executed in Iran within six days
content:
The “No to Executions on Tuesdays” campaign, which is being organised by political prisoners in 66 prisons across Iran and is now in its 145th week, announced that at least 25 people had been executed across Iran and Rojhilatê Kurdistan (Eastern Kurdistan) over the past six days.


It was reported that Şehab Zuhedi, Omran Amani, Emin Pirdal, Arman Merefeti, Şayan Shekibayi and Metin Farinyan, along with numerous other political prisoners whose names have not yet been made public, have been sentenced to death.


The campaign's statement said: “Neither threats nor death sentences will be able to silence the voices raised against inhumane punishments. We demand the immediate abolition of all death sentences and all forms of killing in Iran.”


Two young protesters executed in Isfahan


Iranian judiciary-affiliated Mizan News Agency has announced the execution of two detained individuals, Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein.


The report stated that the death sentences handed down to Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court.


Shahrzad Shahbazi, one of the lawyers involved in the case, emphasised that none of the defendants had been directly accused of murder and that the trial proceedings had not been fair.


Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein were arrested by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in January 2026, during popular protests held at Alihan Square in the city of Isfahan.

author: Unknown
title: Ağbayır: Those invoking Dar al-Salam must take responsibility for peace
content:
Muslim feminist Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır, one of the signatories of the "Women Side by Side, Discussing the Future" conference held in Ankara, spoke to ANF about the importance of the conference, what peace means for women and the role of the women's struggle.


Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır, who spoke to ANF on the second day of the conference, expressed her happiness at being among its signatories. She said that the first day had exceeded expectations and that they had placed greater emphasis on forums to enable participants to take a more active role in the discussions.


 


'We have a common aspiration'


Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır said, "We actually have a common aspiration here," and added: "This conference emerged from the question of how we, as women who have been discussing the ongoing process, growing inequality in Turkey, poverty, economic violence and all the problems that come with them separately, can speak with one another despite our different political views, positions and disagreements."


Ağbayır said that the discussions in the forums had demonstrated how useful this approach was, noting that they had come together with many women throughout the day, from Söke in Aydın to Ankara, and from Bodrum to Diyarbakır (Amed).


Ağbayır said that the conference had provided an opportunity to hear about issues they had not known about or previously considered. 


Ağbayır said: "Women are engaged in a political struggle everywhere, from inside their homes to the streets. Sometimes they find themselves confronting the challenges of simply being women, sometimes women's poverty, and sometimes the very reality of child poverty.


That is why we planned today's session around a panel followed by forums, creating a space where we can speak and listen together. What will emerge from this? How can we move forward? We envision a process in which the women here have a say and are the ones speaking today. I hope it will turn out very well."


'We think peace is an issue only certain groups can discuss'


Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır challenged the perception that peace was an issue only certain groups could discuss, emphasizing that peace had not been achieved within society itself. She drew attention to the following problems: "We tend to think that peace is something only a particular group can talk about. But peace does not exist within this society either. We are talking about a society that lacks internal peace. We are talking about a system in which a child can go to school in the morning carrying a pump-action shotgun. We are talking about a world where addiction is increasing and children are left in desperate conditions on the streets because of it. At the same time, we are discussing violence against women. The very existence of male violence often places us under this oppression. The system does not distinguish between Muslim women, secular women or any other women when it does this.


The system does this because it sees you as vulnerable simply because you are a woman. And we really are among the most vulnerable groups. That is another aspect of the issue. Although we are not on the side of the oppressors but among the oppressed, we are women who continue to struggle."


Ağbayır continued: "As a Muslim woman, I believe we live in a society where those who constantly take pride in Islam as a language of peace and repeatedly invoke Dar al-Salam, meaning the abode of peace, should perhaps question why peace does not exist in this society and take responsibility."


She added: "I am still at a point where I cannot call this a peace process. That is something I also want to discuss here. I am among those who believe that peace must be achieved, that we must discuss what kind of peace we want, and that all women must be able to speak freely at that table."


'We will not allow peace to be framed as a story centered on men'


Ağbayır said, "We will not allow peace to be framed as a story centered on men," and emphasized that the issue was not merely about preventing loss of life. She stressed that Muslim women must assume social responsibility in accordance with their faith and help build a peaceful future based on equal citizenship for everyone.


Ağbayır said that faith itself demanded such responsibility: "Faith itself commands this. I say that nothing inhumane can be part of Islam. So where do we stand? What kind of peace do we want? We are the ones who will discuss this. Peace cannot exist where one side is victimized, ignored or …

title: The anatomy of special warfare and paths to youth liberation in the Middle East
content:
Special warfare is not an overt military operation carried out with tanks and artillery. It is a system of psychological and social destruction that directly targets society's consciousness, culture and moral values. Within this system, the most strategic targets of dominant and colonial powers are young people and young women. This is because youth is the dynamic driving force of social transformation, while young women are the founding subjects of a free society. The state mentality and dominant powers seek first and foremost to paralyze this revolutionary and pioneering force in order to permanently establish their hegemony over the will of peoples.


As Abdullah Öcalan, whose ideas have become central to the political and philosophical discussions of the Kurdish people, the Middle East and peoples around the world, has strongly emphasized, unless a radical consciousness of "self-defense" is developed against this systematic process of social degradation, society will be completely severed from its historical and moral foundations.


The following sections examine, point by point, the reality into which young people have been pushed, the social destruction caused by the instruments of degradation described as the "three horsemen of the apocalypse," and the paths to liberation, with the aim of providing every young person with a guide to action.


The situation of young people and young women: What has the system reduced them to?


Warmongering and extremist forces originating from capitalist colonial states, which have now become direct instruments of special warfare, have subjected young people to a system of comprehensive control through systematic policies that are "flexible and soft" on one side and "brutal and militaristic" on the other.


Lack of ideology and spiritual emptiness:

Life is reduced to the superficial mentality of "live for today and consume," with the aim of preventing young people from reflecting on the future of their countries.

A sense of helplessness, expressed through the idea that "We cannot change anything; the system is too powerful," is instilled in young minds, forcing society's leading force towards submission, passivity and escape through migration abroad.


Loss of identity and alienation:

 Through policies of cultural destruction, young people are pushed into a cycle of shame concerning their own languages, historical roots and social values. Their potential is confined within a cage of "physical appearance and makeup," depriving them of their pioneering roles.

author: Unknown
title: Iran attacks Komala base in Balîsan
content:
Iran attacked a base belonging to the Komeleya Şoreşgerên Zehmetkêşên Kurdistanê (Association of Revolutionary Toilers of Kurdistan) in Balîsan, southern Kurdistan, this morning. According to the party, the attack took place at around 8:40 a.m. and involved two explosive-laden drones.


Komala stated that no one was injured or killed in the attack northeast of Hewlêr (Erbil). However, the organization reported that the attack caused significant damage to property at the base.


Since the outbreak of the war between Iran, the United States, and Israel, Tehran has repeatedly attacked targets in various parts of southern Kurdistan. More than 30 people have reportedly been killed in these attacks so far.

author: Unknown
title: Students demanding education in mother tongue attacked in Hesekê
content:
A demonstration demanding the right to education in the mother tongue was attacked in the northeastern Syrian city of Hesekê. Students had gathered outside the provincial administration building to demand education in their own language. Forces affiliated with the Syrian transitional government intervened against the gathering and fired shots into the air.


According to information obtained by the ANHA news agency, a group believed to be Arab residents from the Xiwêran neighborhood initially attacked the demonstrators with stones. Meanwhile, security forces of the transitional government attempted to disperse the protest and prevent it from continuing, using firearms.


The students condemned the intervention and emphasized the peaceful nature of their demonstration. “What have we done wrong to be prevented from doing this? We took to the streets peacefully and are demanding our right to our own language,” they told ANHA. The protesters also made it clear that the attacks would not deter them from demanding education in their mother tongue.


Since early September, students and their families in Rojava have been protesting against restrictions on Kurdish-language education. The protests were triggered by the Syrian transitional government’s decision to scale back Kurdish-language instruction and limit Kurdish classes to three hours per week. Previously, Kurdish had been not only a subject but also a language of instruction in schools administered by the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (DAANES).


The protesters regard the decision as an attack on the linguistic and cultural rights of the Kurdish population. They are demanding that pupils and university students continue to receive education in their mother tongue and that the educational structures established under the autonomous administration be preserved.

author: Unknown
title: Hatimoğulları visits Demirtaş, calls for the release of political prisoners
content:
Ten years after the crackdown on the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), called for the release of all political prisoners in Turkey. Following a visit to former HDP Co-Chair Selahattin Demirtaş, who has been imprisoned since November 2016, at Edirne Prison, she declared that the struggle would continue until no one remained behind bars for political reasons.


The subsequent rally outside the prison was attended by numerous supporters and representatives of left-wing and socialist parties, including Seyit Aslan, Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP).


The gathering marked the tenth anniversary of November 4, 2016, when the Turkish government launched a sweeping crackdown on the parliamentary representation of the Kurdish population with the arrests of the HDP’s co-chairs and several other members of parliament.


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/814f1fab_20261104123621_2026-11-04-edirne-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-edirne-cezaevi-aciklama-1.mp4


Hatimoğulları called for the immediate release of Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ and all those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial. She demanded the implementation of the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).


Hatimoğulları stated that the practice of appointing government trustees had spread across the country since November 4, 2016, and condemned the arrests of elected mayors and the appointment of trustees to replace them.


DEM Party Co-Chair said that Demirtaş would continue to support the Peace and Democratic Society Process despite his imprisonment. “The struggle will continue until all political prisoners are free. Our comrades behind bars are continuing their struggle, and we will continue ours to build a democratic society. Our struggle will continue until not a single political prisoner remains,” she stated.


Labor Party (EMEP) Chair Seyit Aslan also called for the release of political prisoners, an end to the practice of appointing government trustees, and the introduction of a general political amnesty.


“We demand concrete steps to ensure that the Kurdish people can live on equal terms, along with the necessary legal reforms, particularly the recognition of the right to education in the mother tongue. Without these measures, without taking these steps, we cannot achieve or establish peace,” Aslan said.


DEM Party Istanbul MP and Socialist Solidarity Platform (SODAP) spokesperson Kezban Konukçu emphasized the need to strengthen a common platform for collective struggle to advance the peace process. She called on Turkey’s socialist left to unconditionally support the Kurdish people’s demand for peace.


“We must intensify our struggle to improve people’s livelihoods, secure women’s freedom, defend our right to life, and enable the Kurdish people to achieve peace in this country. These demands are inseparably linked,” Konukçu stated.

author: Unknown
title: Kurdistan Region Parliament elects presidency
content:
The first session of the Kurdistan Region Parliament’s sixth term began earlier today after the required quorum was reached with the participation of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and several other parliamentarians.


As Mihemed Silêman of the New Generation Movement and Azad Mihemedemîn of the PUK were absent, KDP member Semîra Hesen, the oldest parliamentarian present, presided over the session.


During the session, held without the participation of the PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan), candidates were nominated for the positions of Speaker, Deputy Speaker, and Parliamentary Secretary.


In a joint statement issued yesterday, the KDP parliamentary group and the Turkmen Reform Party called on all parliamentarians to attend today’s parliamentary session. The Presidency of the Kurdistan Region Parliament announced that only 43 parliamentarians had signed the request for the session and that the meeting could not be held because the required quorum had not been reached.


Responding to the KDP’s call to convene parliament, the PUK stated: “In accordance with our deep commitment to the principles of the rule of law and national consensus, we believe that this meeting is illegal and constitutes an attempt by one side to impose its will.” The PUK also announced that it would not recognize any parliament or government formed following the session unless national consensus was achieved and all elected parties were guaranteed the opportunity to participate in the process under free and democratic conditions.


As the parties had failed to reach an agreement on the allocation of ministerial portfolios, the PUK, the New Generation Movement, the Justice Community (Komela Dadgerî), and several other parties boycotted today’s session of the Kurdistan Region Parliament.


With the participation of 52 parliamentarians, which met the required quorum of 50+1, elections were held for the parliamentary leadership positions. Vala Fardi was elected Speaker of the Kurdistan Region Parliament, Rami Nouri was elected Deputy Speaker, and Mona Qahwachi was elected Parliamentary Secretary.

author: Unknown
title: Call for action on the anniversary of November 4 coup: Comply with ECtHR rulings, release prisoners!
content:
Civil society organizations, professional associations, and bar associations in the Kurdish region gathered outside the Diyarbakır Courthouse on the anniversary of the November 4, 2016 operations targeting the HDP.


During the gathering, participants unfurled a banner featuring photographs of politicians imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial. The banner read: “A requirement of the rule of law, a necessity for democracy: Freedom. Implement ECtHR rulings, pave the way for democratic politics.”


Diyarbakır Bar Association President Sertaç Buluttekin recalled that former HDP Co-Chairs Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, along with HDP MPs, had been detained and unlawfully imprisoned in 2016.


Buluttekin said that Turkey had failed to implement the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) despite the Court’s findings of violations. He emphasized that the continued imprisonment of those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial and the failure to enforce judicial decisions undermined public confidence in social peace.


In a joint statement read by Ercan Yılmaz, Co-Chair of the Diyarbakır branch of the Human Rights Association (İHD), the organizations stated that the Kobanê trial was part of broader efforts to undermine democratic politics through judicial means.


Yılmaz recalled that 27 HDP MPs had been detained in the process following the November 4, 2016 operation, with 15 of them subsequently imprisoned. He noted that five politicians had been released under a ruling issued by the Ankara 22nd High Criminal Court on May 16, 2024, while the cases of 72 politicians had been separated from the main proceedings. He added that 108 people were still facing trial in connection with the case, including 14 who remained in detention.


Yılmaz said that the ECtHR rulings concerning Demirtaş, Figen Yüksekdağ, and other politicians indicated that their detention lacked a legal basis and were politically motivated.


Emphasizing that ECtHR rulings are binding under domestic law, Yılmaz called on the 22nd Criminal Chamber of the Ankara Regional Court of Justice to issue release orders for the imprisoned politicians without further delay.


“This decision is not only a requirement under the principle of legal certainty but also one of the most important steps toward establishing lasting peace throughout our region,” Yılmaz stated.


The statement emphasized that the imprisonment of politicians affected not only individual freedoms but also the political will of voters and their right to democratic representation.


Lawyer Erhan Ürküt stated that the rule of law must be restored to achieve peace. He stressed that the release of politicians imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial was essential for advancing the democratic resolution process.


Batman Bar Association President Abdulhamit Çakan also called for the implementation of ECtHR rulings and the immediate release of Demirtaş and other imprisoned politicians.


Meral Danış Beştaş, Co-Spokesperson of the Peoples’ Democratic Congress (HDK), described the arrests carried out on November 4, 2016, as a coup against democratic politics.


Beştaş emphasized that the freedom of Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ was crucial to paving the way for democratic politics. “Their freedom is a test of the sincerity of the process,” she stated.


The statement concluded by reiterating calls for the release of politicians imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial, the implementation of ECtHR rulings, and the opening of channels for democratic political participation.

author: Unknown
title: Bakırhan visits Figen Yüksekdağ, calls for freedom for political prisoners
content:
Ten years after the wave of arrests targeting the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), representatives of several left-wing and democratic parties gathered outside Kandıra Women’s Prison in the western Turkish province of Kocaeli to demand the release of political prisoners. The gathering marked the anniversary of November 4, 2016, when the Turkish government launched a sweeping crackdown on the parliamentary representation of the Kurdish population with the arrests of then-HDP Co-Chairs Figen Yüksekdağ and Selahattin Demirtaş, along with several other members of parliament.


Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), had earlier visited Figen Yüksekdağ, who has been imprisoned for ten years, together with a delegation. Following the visit, party representatives and numerous supporters gathered outside the prison. Under the slogan “Freedom for political prisoners – for peace and democracy,” they demanded the release of those imprisoned.


Bakırhan: The political crackdown of 2016 continues to have repercussions today


Bakırhan described the arrests of November 4, 2016, as a “political coup” whose consequences have long since extended beyond the Kurdish opposition. He said the process had begun with the lifting of parliamentary immunity on May 20, 2016, a move that had also been supported by sections of the opposition at the time.


“On that day, a deep wound was inflicted on Turkey’s political history,” Bakırhan stated. He argued that the violations of rights committed at the time had since expanded to affect nearly all opposition forces. “What was done to the HDP back then is now being directed against all institutions and individuals engaged in opposition activities.”


“This is not just a peace process”


Referring to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process, Bakırhan stated that the continued imprisonment of opposition politicians contradicted the declared objectives of political reconciliation. He stressed that anyone seeking to overcome social polarization must first address past injustices. This includes, in particular, implementing the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and Turkey’s Constitutional Court, he noted.


“For ten years, we have been standing outside these prisons and making statements. Hasn’t it been enough? In the eleventh year, our friends must once again be able to engage in democratic politics alongside us,” Bakırhan said. He stressed that Figen Yüksekdağ should be able to advocate her political position on peace outside prison. Selahattin Demirtaş, too, should be reunited with his people and his political colleagues, he said.


“This is not just a peace process. It is also a process of democratization,” the DEM Party Co-Chair emphasized. He remarked that prisons must be emptied for Turkey to achieve the rule of law, justice and democracy. Alongside Yüksekdağ and Demirtaş, he named several imprisoned politicians and activists, including Can Atalay, Osman Kavala, Bekir Kaya and Leyla Güven. He stressed that their place was not in prison but in society.


Left-wing parties demand an end to political prosecutions


Representatives of socialist parties also linked their demands for the release of political prisoners to fundamental democratic rights. Sezin Uçar, Deputy Co-Chair of the Socialist Party of the Oppressed (ESP), recalled the decade-long resistance against political persecution.


“Without freedom of expression, protest and organization, we can neither achieve peace nor build democracy,” she stated. Uçar said the ESP was demanding the release of all political prisoners, the repeal of Turkey’s Anti-Terror Law and the removal of all restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and organization. She specifically highlighted those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê and Gezi trials.


Levent Tüzel, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP), described the Kobanê trial as a politically motivated prosecution. He pointed out that the HDP had been justified in calling for solidarity with the resistance against the siege of Kobanê in 2014. According to Tüzel, however, the protests at the time had been manipulated by paramilitary forces, with responsibility for the violence subsequently attributed to the HDP leadership. Tüzel criticized the lengthy prison sentences imposed as a result. He emphasized that the demand of peoples to live together in equality and freedom was at the heart of the current peace process.

title: Peace Mothers: There can be no peace unless Abdullah Öcalan is free!
content:
The Peace Mothers, who traveled to Ankara from various cities across Kurdistan and Turkey, held meetings at the Turkish parliament on Tuesday. As part of their peace initiative, they met with representatives of several parliamentary groups, including the YENI Party, the Yeni Yol parliamentary group, the MHP, and the ruling AKP. The discussions focused on Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom, the release of political prisoners, and concrete measures to advance the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


The meetings followed the Peace Mothers’ gathering in the parliamentary park, where women from 24 cities held a peace vigil on Monday and called on political leaders to advance the Peace and Democratic Society Process through concrete measures.


After a press statement about their meetings, the mothers returned home yesterday, while a delegation representing them remained in Ankara for further talks.


As part of their meetings in parliament, the Peace Mothers met with Speaker of Parliament Numan Kurtulmuş on Wednesday. Peace Mothers Hanife Akpolat, Müzeyyen Bütün and Afife Kartal attended the meeting, which took place in the Speaker’s office. Following their meeting with Kurtulmuş, the mothers held a press statement outside parliament’s Dikmen Gate.


Speaking here, Peace Mother Müzeyyen Bütün said: “The meetings went well. We hope this process will reach a successful conclusion. We repeatedly expressed our demand for peace. We came here for peace, and we thank all the political parties and their leaders. We also thank Speaker of Parliament Numan Kurtulmuş for hosting us. They spoke positively to us, and we believe that peace will come to this country and that we will live together. Until peace is achieved, we will raise our voices and demand peace morning and night, everywhere, in the streets and in the cities. We believe our demands will be met. We also call on the mothers of soldiers and police officers to join us so that we can demand peace together.”


Zeynep Çalıhan, a Turkish mother, said: “There are Peace Mothers all around the world, and they all want peace. We want Mr. Abdullah Öcalan to be free. There can be no peace unless he is free. We want him to regain his freedom. Enough blood has been shed on these lands. It is time to plant saplings in this soil, not bury more people. I also appeal to Turkish women: Come, let us build peace together. We want peace, not war.”
