author: Chris Walker
title: Jeffries Downplays Trump Accountability Push After Democrats’ Midterm Blowout
content:
The potential Speaker of the House has brushed aside plans by Democrats to investigate the Trump administration.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

House minority leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) is downplaying the potential to hold the Trump administration accountable following Democrats’ monumental win in the 2026 midterm elections, despite a large proportion of voters signaling that they believe there are grounds for impeaching President Donald Trump.

In an interview following the midterm elections, Jeffries, who is considered Democrats’ top prospect for Speaker of the House, disregarded plans by high-ranking members of his party to pursue inquiries into the White House’s actions over the past two years.

On MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” program, conservative host Joe Scarborough asked Jeffries how he plans to keep Democrats “focused on the things that got them elected,” listing several affordability issues but rejecting the idea of “retribution” against the administration. Jeffries appeared to agree with Scarborough’s framing.

“The American people don’t want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf, because life is way too expensive,” Jeffries said, adding that the party “won on affordability.”

In his Tuesday night speech celebrating the outcome of the midterms, Jeffries only briefly mentioned a commitment to fighting corruption. Instead, he delivered a reconciliatory message — “This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic moment,” he said. “This is not a blue moment or a red moment. It’s a red, white and blue moment because America has won tonight.”

While the economy was the top issue for voters, a sizable number of Americans stated in polls conducted prior to the midterms that accountability and opposition to corruption was a higher priority for them.

In an Economist/YouGov poll published late last month, for example, more than a quarter of likely voters, 26 percent, said that “presidential leadership,” “corruption and waste,” and “democracy and the rule of law” were their top priorities. Among Democratic voters, 41 percent of respondents said these were their top issues, while around 3 in 10 independent voters (29 percent) counted them as their top priorities.

Americans have also stated that their votes should be seen as a direct check on Trump. According to an NPR/PBS NewsHour/Marist poll published in September, 45 percent of voters said their choices in the midterms should be viewed as a “vote against” the president.

Support for impeaching Trump is high among the electorate, with a Politico survey from October finding that 54 percent of voters believe there are grounds to do so, while only 33 percent disagree.

Despite strong support from voters for the concept, Jeffries appeared to reject impeachment as a possibility in remarks to reporters on Wednesday, claiming that no one in his conference had discussed it with him yet.

“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic caucus talk to me about impeachment. We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and accountability,” Jeffries said.

Economist Paul Krugman wrote on his Substack that Democrats would be mistaken to view the results of Tuesday night’s elections as solely about affordability.

“Trumpflation created by tariffs and the Iran debacle helped” Democrats to win, Krugman said. “But an election swung by public anger over high prices looks like 2024, when Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points. Last night, Democrats appear to have won the popular vote by 13-14 percentage points.”

The outcome suggests that a broad coalition of voters is upset with how Trump is governing overall.

“What drove this amazing victory?” Krugman continued. “Hispanic voters, who swung to Trump in 2024 in the naïve belief that he would bring prices down, turned massively against a regime that is arresting, imprisoning and deporting their friends and families. [Black voters] turned out in droves against a transparently racist party that is trying to take away their voting rights. Americans of every kind were repelled by the administration’s cruelty and its rampant, brazen corruption.”

“MAGA took 2024 as proof that Americans want fascism, and acted on that premise. But tens of millions of Americans in effect said, no, that is not what we want. That is not who we are,” he added.

author: Brad Reed
title: Montana Votes Overwhelmingly to Ban Corporate Cash From Political Campaigns
content:
Supporters have billed the initiative as a way to strike a blow against the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United ruling.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Voters in Montana on Tuesday delivered a major blow to big moneyed interests by overwhelmingly passing a ballot initiative barring corporate cash from political campaigns in the state.

With 87% of votes counted as of Wednesday morning, Montana Constitutional Initiative 194 has received support from more than 65% of voters, with just 35% registering opposition.

The initiative prohibits what it describes as “artificial persons” — which includes corporations, nonprofits, trusts, partnerships, and trade associations — from giving money to political campaigns.

Supporters of the initiative have billed it as a way to strike a blow against the Supreme Court’s 2010 ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which opened the door to unlimited campaign spending in US politics.

“A yes vote on I-194 means that only real people — not corporations, unions, trade associations, nonprofits, or groups with anonymous donors — are allowed to spend money in Montana elections,” the Yes on Initiative 194 campaign explained on its website. “It’s time to kick the oligarchs out of Big Sky country.”

The initiative’s overwhelming victory drew praise from Tom Moore, senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, who congratulated the people of Montana for taking “a historic step toward ending the scourge of corporate and dark money in politics.”

Moore noted that the initiative passed by Montana is similar to a law passed in Hawaii earlier this year that classified corporations as “artificial persons” who do not have a constitutional right to make political donations.

Both states, Moore said, are “setting a bold example for other states to follow suit, sending a powerful message that we don’t have to give corporations unlimited power.”

“The more states that follow this innovative approach,” he added, “the more we can make Citizens United irrelevant.”

Stacy Mitchell, co-executive director at the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, hailed the initiative’s passage as a win for democratic governance.

“We’ve largely forgotten that states define what corporations can do,” Mitchell wrote in a social media post. “Yesterday, Montana voters overwhelmingly stripped corporations of the power to spend money influencing elections. Hawaii did the same in May. Both face court fights. Our nascent citizen muscle is coming to life.”

Adam Bojak, a Democrat who on Tuesday won an election in New York State Assembly District 149, said he’d like to see the Empire State follow the trail blazed by Montana and Hawaii.

“Congratulations to the people of Montana!” Bojak wrote. “I can’t wait to bring this legislation to New York in next year’s session.”

author: Daniel Hunter
title: Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.
content:

Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


The broad strokes of the midterms are clear: a massive repudiation of MAGA’s fascist wave has ended the Trump 2.0 era of congressional complicity with his authoritarian takeover. Trump’s lame duck presidency now begins. 


This lopsided electoral rejection is historically rare: Flipping control of both the House and Senate in a midterm has only occurred

three times since World War II

 (1946, 1994 and 2006). The breakthroughs are astounding:

the first Native American governor and senator

,

five Black governors

, the first

majority of Democratic governors in 16 years

, and critical downballot wins like the first Democrat to win as

Texan oil regulator since 1990

 and the

first openly transgender state legislator in Alabama

.


Authoritarians do not do well when trapped — and with a famously norm-busting president, anything is possible. But, critically, election deniers like

Darline Graham

 and

Greg Abbott

 are conceding their races. Donald Trump is already saying he’s

“absolutely willing”

 to accept the results and

told CBS

, “Congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”


So what do we do now?


1. It’s OK to exhale


These midterms have left me, like many, with abundant free-floating anxieties. The

“what if” scenarios

 have been abundant — and while some of the most extreme versions did not happen, the federal government was weaponized against the election system like never before.


Because the times have been so rough, it can be hard to exhale and accept a win, especially since elections are not material changes — they are promissory notes that the future may be different. Until Jan. 3, we live under the same dangerous authoritarian government, even if the atmosphere has changed.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Before I advocate for you to breathe, let’s affirm all the many hard reasons to not exhale. The wins were not universal, as some big losses cut deep. There’s a reality that all of this is ephemeral if Democrats cannot govern a policy of change — if we only manage an economic status quo it will disillusion and likely result in yet another whiplash election in the other direction. And it’s hard to breathe in a dizzying moment.


Further, the attacks on elections were treasonous. I won’t list the complete litany of federal assaults — but we have a Department of Justice captured by authoritarian forces using its power nakedly for partisan goals. The far right openly prepared

sham legal theories

 to refuse certification of Democratic representatives. While we did not get systematic federal law enforcement terror at polls, we saw National Guard throughout

Washington, D.C.

 We still have too many election officials committed to the Big Lie. And ongoing structural impediments to a fair election are consequential: In Mississippi, the Senate margin remains tiny while any win may be marred by

equipment trouble, poll changes,

 and

voters unexpectedly removed by data purges from the voting rolls

.  


Notably, the election maps themselves have been gerrymandered by racists to ensure power — though their greed rebounded

multiple losses

 in these redistricted seats. (Groups like Black Voters Matter deserve a huge shout-out for fighting in the South and in races Democrats had abandoned.)


Despite all that, we managed a pro-democracy win that was too big to rig. The country delivered a shellacking to MAGA politics — an encouraging sign for all of us who are hoping for a better future. Ultimately, the election proceeded with voters refusing to be intimidated.


Buddhists remind me we can take a breath anytime. But this moment seems as good a moment as any, especially when we remind ourselves exhaling isn’t signaling that things are over. Exhales are how our body gets in tune with this moment and releases the latest tension. Bracing doesn’t make us wiser, just tenser.


So really, take five breaths right now. As you breathe, read in a poem by

Jarod Anderson

: “

You can be still while the world is whirling. / You can be silent while your heart is thundering. / You can be alone while your memory is teeming. / You can live forever in the span of a moment. / You can grow kindness in the soil of hatred. / You can decide purpose. You can decide …

author: Andrea DiP
title: “Em nome do Pai”: evangélicos se afastam de Flávio porque nunca gostaram do filho de Jair
content:
“Esses filhos de Bolsonaro são uns jumentos. Só se aconselham com gente errada! Faz carta, fala bobagem, depois corrige (…) Um bando de amadores babacas”. A frase,

revelada pela coluna de Malu Gaspar para O Globo

 no último dia 28, foi enviada em um grupo de WhatsApp pelo pastor e influenciador político Silas Malafaia, um dos maiores líderes evangélicos do Brasil e aliado de primeiro escalão de Jair Bolsonaro durante seu governo. O comentário foi feito após a fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro aos Estados Unidos e da publicação da carta (ou seria das cartas?) em que o candidato derrotado se apresentava como o verdadeiro presidente do “Brazil”. 


As trapalhadas do 01 têm levado pastores das mega-igrejas protestantes a se posicionarem publicamente em uma tentativa de se distanciar de vez do nome da família Bolsonaro e de sua trilha de escândalos.

 No dia seguinte à eleição de Lula no segundo turno, o bispo Alessandro Paschoall da Igreja Universal publicou o trecho de um culto realizado por Edir Macedo em que ele criticava o lema “Deus, pátria e família” usado pelos Bolsonaro. “Na Universal, nós priorizamos essa hierarquia: primeiro Deus, depois família, e depois o resto. Não concordo com essa teoria “Deus, pátria e família”. Porque se não houver família, vai haver pátria? Impossível. Só há pátria se vier da família, que vem de Deus”, disse Macedo na manhã da votação do segundo turno. 


Curiosamente, o lema – que, vale lembrar, foi usado no Brasil na década de 1930 pela Ação Integralista Brasileira, movimento nacionalista de inspiração fascista liderado por Plínio Salgado –só incomodou o bispo agora. Macedo, que é pragmático e costuma se aliar a quem estiver no poder, foi um apoiador de Jair Bolsonaro em 2018 e em 2022, mas se manteve distante nas eleições deste ano. 


Outro bispo, Abner Ferreira, da Assembleia de Deus, que apoiou Flávio no segundo turno e chegou a participar de um mega culto promovido por seu irmão Bispo Samuel Ferreira, presidente da Convenção Nacional das Assembleias de Deus no Brasil no Maracanãzinho com direito a pedido de voto e a presença de Flávio, reconheceu rapidamente a vitória de Lula e publicou um texto em suas redes sociais na semana passada dizendo que a democracia “exige maturidade, equilíbrio e respeito às decisões populares, independentemente das convicções e preferências individuais”.


Outros bispos e pastores evangélicos também têm se manifestado na mesma direção, como o bispo JB Carvalho, da Comunidade das Nações, igreja de Brasília onde Flávio foi batizado em 2024 e o Líder da Igreja Fonte da Vida, Apóstolo César Augusto, também aliado de Flávio. Ou estão em silêncio.


Mas essa tentativa de afastamento por parte de líderes das principais igrejas evangélicas não começou após a carta golpista. É um movimento que vem se anunciando e que reflete também o desgaste desse apoio descarado entre os fieis.

Parece haver uma avaliação de que o saldo positivo desse apoio incondicional aos Bolsonaro ficou só para a família, enquanto as igrejas tiveram cada vez mais sua reputação atrelada a golpes, violência, escândalos de corrupção, etc. 


Em conversa com a coluna, a professora do Programa de Pós-graduação em Sociologia e coordenadora do LePar (laboratório de estudos em Política, Arte e Religião da Universidade Federal Fluminense) Christina Vital, que é pesquisadora do campo evangélico de longa data, faz uma reflexão sobre esse reposicionamento: 


“O afastamento de líderes evangélicos em relação ao bolsonarismo tem a marca das eleições de 2022. De lá para cá só vimos crescer esse afastamento com críticas veementes como tentativa de se limparem moralmente em relação à truculência e corrupção associadas ao bolsonarismo.

Nas eleições de 2026 isso se agravou e não vimos um investimento continuado e intenso em torno do nome de Flávio Bolsonaro por parte de muitos líderes evangélicos e, logo após a derrota, vimos as críticas públicas se avolumarem. A fuga para os EUA foi o estopim de uma relação que já não se sustentava

”, diz ela. 


Segundo ela,

Flávio Bolsonaro não era um nome desejado por ninguém. Líderes religiosos não viam nele a força e maturidade suficientes.

 Michelle Bolsonaro também não foi uma apoiadora de primeira hora, e chegou a jogar contra com o vídeo de 27 minutos, revelando que as críticas que ela faz ali não são tudo o que ela sabia. 


“Quando o nome de Flávio se consolidou para a presidência, ela passou a apoiar o nome dele, assim como Damares Alves e outras parlamentares e …
